payload.snippet: Sugar and flour need measuring.
options: Use the measuring cups
Guess with a handful
Use a toy cup
Pour the whole bag in
payload.explanation: Measuring cups give the right amounts.

payload.snippet: The muffins are too hot to eat.
options: Wait for them to cool down
Blow on them and eat immediately
Put them in the freezer for one second
Eat them straight from the tin
payload.explanation: Hot food needs time to cool.

payload.snippet: The recipe says crack two eggs.
options: Crack them on the bowl edge gently
Smash them on the floor
Drop them from high up
Squeeze them until they break
payload.explanation: Gentle cracking keeps shell out of the batter.

payload.snippet: Ben's sister wants to help sprinkle icing.
options: Let her have a turn
Pour all the icing on at once himself
Tell her she will do it wrong
Run away with the icing bag
payload.explanation: Sharing baking tasks is fun for everyone.

payload.snippet: The dough is too sticky to roll.
options: Add a little flour to the board
Add water to make it stickier
Throw it in the bin
Hit it with a rolling pin very hard
payload.explanation: A dusting of flour prevents dough from sticking.

payload.snippet: The timer goes off but the cake looks pale.
options: Ask a grown-up to check if it needs more time
Take it out because the timer said so
Put it on full heat for one minute
Eat the pale cake anyway
payload.explanation: Timers are a guide — an adult checks doneness properly.

payload.snippet: Lily wants to try the batter.
options: Ask Mum if it is safe to taste first
Eat a big spoonful straight away
Give some to the dog
Eat it while no one is looking
payload.explanation: Some batters contain raw egg — always ask an adult before tasting.

payload.snippet: The chocolate chips need melting.
options: Ask a grown-up to help melt them safely
Put them in the oven while it is very hot
Melt them over a flame alone
Eat them all before melting
payload.explanation: Melting chocolate needs adult supervision.

payload.snippet: Tom gets flour on the kitchen counter.
options: Wipe it up with a damp cloth
Blow it across the room
Leave it for someone else
Sweep it onto the floor
payload.explanation: Cleaning up as you go keeps the kitchen safe.

payload.snippet: The cake is stuck in the tin.
options: Use a blunt knife around the edges first
Pull it out hard from one side
Shake the tin upside down violently
Eat it straight from the tin
payload.explanation: Loosening edges before turning out a cake prevents it breaking.

payload.snippet: The dough needs kneading for five minutes.
options: Push and fold the dough rhythmically
Throw it against the wall
Stand on it
Leave it alone and hope it kneads itself
payload.explanation: Rhythmic kneading develops the gluten structure in bread dough.

payload.snippet: Zoe wants to decorate the cupcakes.
options: Spread the icing on with a spoon or knife
Squirt it directly from the tube at her brother
Put all the sprinkles on one cupcake
Eat the icing before decorating
payload.explanation: Spreading icing evenly makes every cupcake look good.

payload.snippet: The recipe asks for a pinch of salt.
options: Use two fingers to pick up a tiny amount
Pour the whole salt shaker in
Skip the salt since it is a tiny amount
Use a teaspoon of salt instead
payload.explanation: A pinch means a tiny amount between two fingertips.

payload.snippet: The brownies need cooling before cutting.
options: Wait until they are completely cool
Cut them while hot and they crumble
Put them straight in the fridge for one minute
Eat them from the tray with a fork
payload.explanation: Warm brownies crumble when cut — cooling makes clean squares.

payload.snippet: Sam spills milk while measuring it.
options: Wipe it up right away before it spreads
Leave it and see if it dries
Walk through it
Tell no one
payload.explanation: Spills cleaned immediately prevent slipping and sticky residues.

payload.snippet: Mia wants to plant a seed.
options: Dig a small hole with her finger
Throw the seed on the ground
Plant it upside down in the air
Put it on the shelf
payload.explanation: Seeds need to be in soil to grow.

payload.snippet: The seedling needs water.
options: Use a small watering can
Pour a bucket over it
Throw water from far away
Use a hose on full power
payload.explanation: Gentle watering with a small can doesn't flatten seedlings.

payload.snippet: Tom's pot plant is dry.
options: Check the soil with a finger first
Pour lots of water in quickly
Leave it in the rain only
Give it juice instead of water
payload.explanation: Checking the soil prevents overwatering.

payload.snippet: A seed packet says plant in spring.
options: Wait until spring to plant it
Plant it in winter frost
Plant it in summer heat
Plant it whenever you feel like it
payload.explanation: Seeds grow best when planted at the right season.

payload.snippet: The flower pot has no drainage holes.
options: Ask an adult to make some holes
Fill the pot with rocks instead of soil
Use it without holes anyway
Use a bucket instead
payload.explanation: Drainage holes prevent roots from sitting in water.

payload.snippet: Lily puts too much soil in the pot.
options: Remove some so the plant has room to grow
Push the plant down hard
Add more soil on top
Use a bigger plant instead
payload.explanation: Plants need space to grow in their pots.

payload.snippet: A plant's leaves are turning yellow.
options: Ask a grown-up what is wrong
Pull the yellow leaves off
Water it more
Put it in the dark
payload.explanation: Yellow leaves can mean different things — an adult can help diagnose.

payload.snippet: Ben finds a worm in the garden soil.
options: Leave it alone — it helps the garden
Pull it out and throw it away
Pour salt on it
Put it in the flower pot inside
payload.explanation: Worms improve soil by aerating it.

payload.snippet: The seeds need labelling.
options: Write the plant name on a lolly stick
Guess which is which after planting
Remember them without labelling
Draw a tiny picture on each seed
payload.explanation: Labels help you remember what you planted.

payload.snippet: A sunflower is growing too big for its small pot.
options: Move it to a bigger pot or the garden
Cut the roots to make it fit
Tie the roots into the pot
Put a lid on the top of the pot
payload.explanation: Plants need space for roots to grow.

payload.snippet: Zoe's herb pot has no sunlight.
options: Move it to the sunniest windowsill
Buy a lamp for the herbs
Paint the walls white to reflect light
Give it extra water instead
payload.explanation: Most herbs need sunlight to grow well.

payload.snippet: The soil in the garden feels very hard.
options: Add water and let it soften
Stamp on it to break it up
Use a kitchen knife to cut it
Leave the seeds on top of hard soil
payload.explanation: Softening soil first helps seeds to germinate.

payload.snippet: A carrot is ready to pull from the ground.
options: Pull it gently and straight
Grab it and yank hard from one side
Dig it out with a spade roughly
Cut the top off and leave the rest underground
payload.explanation: Gentle straight pulling avoids breaking the carrot.

payload.snippet: Sam's seedlings are very crowded in the tray.
options: Thin them out so each has space
Leave them crowded — the strongest will survive
Water them more to make space
Pull out all but one seedling
payload.explanation: Thinning seedlings gives the strongest ones room to grow.

payload.snippet: A new plant needs staking because it is leaning.
options: Tie it gently to a bamboo cane
Push it upright with your hands every day
Lean a brick against it
Leave it leaning until it falls over
payload.explanation: Staking supports weak or tall plants.

payload.snippet: The lawn is long and needs mowing.
options: Tell a grown-up the grass needs cutting
Use the garden scissors
Cut it with kitchen scissors
Pull each blade of grass by hand
payload.explanation: Lawn mowers are adult tools — tell an adult when the grass is long.

payload.snippet: Ella plants a seed but nothing grows after two weeks.
options: Read the packet to check how long it takes
Dig it up to check
Plant ten more seeds on top
Throw the whole pot away
payload.explanation: Some seeds take many weeks to germinate — check the packet.

payload.snippet: A slug is eating the lettuce leaves.
options: Tell a grown-up who can put down slug pellets safely
Squash it with your foot
Pour salt directly on the lettuce
Spray the plant with washing-up liquid
payload.explanation: Slug control needs adult guidance to be safe for the plant.

payload.snippet: Oscar waters his plant but the water runs straight through the pot.
options: Check whether the soil has become very dry and compacted
Water it again ten minutes later
Add more soil on top
Put the plant in a bucket of water to soak
payload.explanation: Water running straight through can mean the soil is too dry to absorb — soaking is sometimes needed.

payload.snippet: The plant is getting too much sun and the leaves look scorched.
options: Move it to a spot with indirect light
Water it more to cool it down
Cover it with a cloth all day
Leave it since sunlight is always good for plants
payload.explanation: Some plants prefer indirect light — scorched leaves signal too much direct sun.

payload.snippet: The dog's water bowl is empty.
options: Fill it with fresh water
Give the dog juice
Leave it empty
Fill it with milk
payload.explanation: Dogs need fresh water available all the time to stay healthy.

payload.snippet: The cat is scratching at the litter box.
options: Clean out the litter box
Shoo the cat away
Fill the box with water
Move the box outside
payload.explanation: A dirty litter box makes cats uncomfortable; cleaning it keeps them happy.

payload.snippet: The hamster wheel is squeaking loudly.
options: Put a tiny drop of oil on the axle
Take the wheel away
Wake the hamster up
Stuff the wheel with tissue
payload.explanation: A little oil stops the squeak so the hamster can run quietly at night.

payload.snippet: The fish tank is getting cloudy.
options: Do a partial water change
Add more fish food
Turn off the filter
Cover the tank with a cloth
payload.explanation: Changing part of the water removes waste and keeps the fish healthy.

payload.snippet: The puppy is whining by the door.
options: Take the puppy outside for a walk
Give the puppy a treat
Ignore the puppy
Let the puppy into the kitchen
payload.explanation: Puppies whine at the door when they need to go to the toilet or want exercise.

payload.snippet: The cat knocks its food bowl off the shelf.
options: Pick up the bowl and refill it at floor level
Leave the food on the floor
Put the cat outside
Move the bowl to a higher shelf
payload.explanation: Food bowls belong on the floor so cats can eat safely.

payload.snippet: The rabbit's hay rack is empty.
options: Fill the rack with fresh hay
Give the rabbit biscuits
Leave the rack empty
Replace hay with lettuce only
payload.explanation: Rabbits need unlimited hay every day for their digestion.

payload.snippet: The dog's fur is matted and tangled.
options: Gently brush the dog's coat
Cut all the fur off
Wash the dog in the pond
Leave the tangles
payload.explanation: Regular brushing removes tangles and keeps a dog's coat healthy.

payload.snippet: The bird's cage is very dirty.
options: Clean the cage with warm water
Add more food to cover the dirt
Move the bird to a box
Leave the cage dirty
payload.explanation: A clean cage keeps birds healthy and free from disease.

payload.snippet: The guinea pig squeaks and runs to its food bowl.
options: Give the guinea pig fresh vegetables
Tap the cage to calm it down
Add bedding to its bowl
Ignore the squeaking
payload.explanation: Guinea pigs squeak when they are hungry; fresh vegetables are a healthy treat.

payload.snippet: The dog is limping on one front paw.
options: Check the paw for a thorn or cut
Make the dog run to stretch it out
Put a bandage on without looking
Leave it to heal on its own today
payload.explanation: A limp often means something is hurting; checking the paw finds thorns or injuries quickly.

payload.snippet: The cat is sick after eating something outside.
options: Keep the cat calm indoors and call the vet
Give the cat more food to settle its stomach
Let the cat back outside
Put the cat in a bath
payload.explanation: If a cat has eaten something harmful, a vet can advise on the safest next steps.

payload.snippet: The goldfish is swimming sideways near the surface.
options: Test the water quality and call a pet shop for advice
Add extra fish food
Change all the water at once
Take the fish out and put it in a cup
payload.explanation: Sideways swimming usually signals a water quality problem or swim bladder issue; advice before acting prevents further harm.

payload.snippet: The puppy chews on an electrical cable.
options: Gently redirect the puppy to a chew toy and cover the cable
Shout loudly at the puppy
Put the puppy in another room all day
Wrap the cable in tape and leave it
payload.explanation: Puppies chew instinctively; redirecting to safe toys protects both the pup and the home.

payload.snippet: The rabbit has escaped from its hutch into the garden.
options: Move slowly and calmly to herd the rabbit back into a safe enclosure
Chase the rabbit around the garden quickly
Leave the rabbit outside overnight
Call the rabbit loudly from indoors
payload.explanation: Rabbits panic easily; slow, calm movement prevents injury and makes recapture easier.

payload.snippet: The dog refuses to eat its food for two days.
options: Take the dog to the vet for a check-up
Switch to a completely new food right away
Give the dog human leftovers to tempt it
Reduce the portion size and see if it eats less
payload.explanation: Two days without eating is a sign something may be wrong; a vet check rules out illness.

payload.snippet: The cat's claws are getting very long.
options: Trim the claws with special pet nail clippers
File the claws with a nail file
Let the cat scratch on the furniture
Cover the cat's paws with socks
payload.explanation: Regular claw trimming prevents the claws curling into the paw pads, which is very painful.

payload.snippet: The hamster has not come out of its nest for two days.
options: Check that the hamster is still eating and drinking; if not, consult a vet
Move all the bedding to find it
Shine a bright torch into the nest
Shake the cage gently to wake it
payload.explanation: Hamsters sleep a lot but should still eat and drink; a vet call is wise if signs of life are absent.

payload.snippet: The dog is scratching its ears constantly.
options: Examine the ear for redness or smell and visit the vet
Pour water into the ear to soothe it
Ignore it for a few weeks
Give the dog a bath and hope it clears
payload.explanation: Persistent ear scratching often means infection or ear mites, which need veterinary treatment.

payload.snippet: The pet tortoise has not moved or eaten for three days in winter.
options: Check the temperature of the enclosure and ensure it is warm enough
Give the tortoise a cold bath to wake it
Move the tortoise to the garden
Offer the tortoise meat to increase its energy
payload.explanation: Tortoises slow down dramatically if they are cold; maintaining the correct temperature range keeps them active and eating.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour's ball rolls into your garden.
options: Take the ball back to your neighbour
Keep the ball
Kick it over the fence
Hide it in the shed
payload.explanation: Returning something that belongs to someone else is the kind thing to do.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour looks sad sitting on the doorstep.
options: Say hello and ask if they are okay
Ignore them and go inside
Run away
Wave and hurry past
payload.explanation: Noticing when someone is sad and checking on them is being a good neighbour.

payload.snippet: The elderly lady next door is carrying heavy shopping bags.
options: Offer to carry the bags for her
Walk straight past her
Tell her to use a trolley
Take one bag without asking
payload.explanation: Helping with heavy loads is a kind and thoughtful thing to do.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour's dog has escaped through the garden fence.
options: Tell your neighbour straight away
Chase the dog yourself
Ignore it and go inside
Close your own gate and do nothing
payload.explanation: Letting the owner know quickly is the safest way to help get the dog back.

payload.snippet: The baby next door is crying very loudly late at night.
options: Leave it to the parents to handle
Knock on the door at midnight
Shout through the wall
Call the police immediately
payload.explanation: Babies cry — parents know what to do. Knocking late at night would disturb everyone.

payload.snippet: You see your neighbour drop their keys and keep walking.
options: Pick up the keys and call out to them
Keep the keys
Leave them on the ground
Put them through a random letterbox
payload.explanation: Calling out and returning dropped keys is a helpful and honest thing to do.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour's washing has blown off the line into your garden.
options: Hand the laundry back over the fence
Keep the clothes
Leave them on the wet ground
Put them in your bin
payload.explanation: Returning things that blow into your garden is a neighbourly and honest act.

payload.snippet: A new family moves in next door with a child your age.
options: Smile and say hello when you see them
Stare at them and say nothing
Tell them to go away
Run inside and hide
payload.explanation: Welcoming new neighbours with a friendly hello helps them feel at home.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour's cat is stuck up a tree.
options: Tell your neighbour so they can help
Try to climb the tree yourself
Shout loudly at the cat
Walk away and forget about it
payload.explanation: Telling the owner is the safest first step — they can decide how to help.

payload.snippet: You accidentally kick your ball through your neighbour's window.
options: Tell your parent and go apologise straight away
Run inside and pretend it wasn't you
Blame someone else
Wait to see if they notice
payload.explanation: Owning up to accidents quickly is always the right thing to do.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour asks you not to play loud music near their window while their baby sleeps.
options: Move further away or play more quietly
Turn the music up louder
Argue that you were there first
Play music anyway because it's your garden
payload.explanation: Being considerate of others' needs, especially babies sleeping, is good neighbourly behaviour.

payload.snippet: The man next door slips on ice at the bottom of his steps.
options: Ask if he is hurt and tell your parent
Laugh and go inside
Walk past without saying anything
Tell him he should have been more careful
payload.explanation: Checking if someone is hurt and getting a grown-up is the caring and sensible thing to do.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour leaves a note asking you to keep the shared path clear of bikes.
options: Move your bike and say thank you for letting you know
Leave the bikes where they are
Take down the note and ignore it
Write a rude reply
payload.explanation: Respecting shared spaces and being gracious about polite requests keeps neighbours happy.

payload.snippet: You notice the lights in the house next door have been on all night and no one has opened the curtains.
options: Mention it to a parent or trusted adult
Ring the doorbell every hour
Break a window to check inside
Ignore it completely
payload.explanation: Mentioning an unusual observation to a trusted adult is the safe and sensible action.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour grows prize roses and you accidentally break one off playing in the garden.
options: Tell your parent and offer to apologise to the neighbour
Push the broken flower back into the soil
Throw it away and say nothing
Blame the wind
payload.explanation: Honesty and offering an apology shows responsibility and earns respect.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour brings home-baked biscuits to your door as a thank-you for helping them.
options: Say thank you warmly and share them with your family
Say you don't want them and close the door
Take them without saying anything
Give them back and say you don't eat biscuits
payload.explanation: Accepting a kind gift graciously and saying thank you makes the other person feel appreciated.

payload.snippet: A parcel is delivered to your house that is addressed to your neighbour.
options: Bring the parcel next door as soon as possible
Open it to see what's inside
Leave it outside in the rain
Keep it and say nothing
payload.explanation: Returning a wrongly delivered parcel quickly is honest and considerate.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour is away on holiday and their wheelie bin is blocking the shared path.
options: Move the bin to the side so people can pass
Leave it blocking the path — not your problem
Tip the bin over
Go through their garden to move it further away
payload.explanation: Helping with a small inconvenience when a neighbour is away is a kind community gesture.

payload.snippet: You see two children from the street throwing stones at your neighbour's fence.
options: Tell a trusted adult what you saw
Join in
Shout at them yourself
Say nothing because they might bully you
payload.explanation: Telling a trusted adult about property damage is the right action — it's not telling tales, it's being responsible.

payload.snippet: Your neighbour's child falls off their bike right in front of you.
options: Check if they are hurt and help them up
Keep cycling past
Laugh and ride away
Go home and tell your parents later
payload.explanation: Stopping to help someone who has fallen is a basic act of kindness.

payload.snippet: The photo came out very dark.
options: Move to a brighter spot
Close the curtains
Take fewer photos
Put the camera away
payload.explanation: Photos taken in dark places are hard to see. More light makes them much better.

payload.snippet: The picture is all blurry.
options: Hold the camera very still and try again
Shake the camera more
Put a filter on
Make the photo smaller
payload.explanation: Blurry photos happen when the camera moves. Keeping still helps the camera capture a sharp image.

payload.snippet: Your finger is covering part of the lens.
options: Move your finger away from the lens
Keep your finger there
Take the photo anyway
Add a sticker over it
payload.explanation: Covering the lens blocks the view. Always check your fingers are clear before pressing the button.

payload.snippet: The sun is shining right into the camera lens.
options: Turn so the sun is behind you
Close your eyes and press the button
Take the photo straight into the sun
Put sunglasses on the camera
payload.explanation: Shooting into the sun makes photos very bright and hard to see. Keeping the sun behind you gives a much clearer picture.

payload.snippet: The dog keeps moving every time you press the button.
options: Wait until the dog is sitting still
Make the dog run faster
Take a photo of something else
Put the dog in a box
payload.explanation: Moving subjects come out blurry. Waiting for a still moment helps you get a sharp, clear photo.

payload.snippet: The photo shows the inside of your pocket.
options: Take the phone out properly and try again
Keep taking photos in your pocket
Use the front camera
Delete all photos
payload.explanation: Accidental pocket photos happen when the camera button is pressed by mistake. Taking the phone out first solves it.

payload.snippet: You want to take a photo of a rainbow but it is very far away.
options: Zoom in to make the rainbow look bigger
Run towards the rainbow
Only photograph the sky
Wait for another rainbow
payload.explanation: Zooming brings distant things closer in the frame so you can see them better in the photo.

payload.snippet: Your photo has a big shadow across it.
options: Move so your shadow does not fall on the subject
Make the shadow bigger
Add more shadows on purpose
Turn off the lights
payload.explanation: Shadows in photos can block the subject. Moving your position so the shadow falls elsewhere fixes it.

payload.snippet: The colours in the photo look orange and strange indoors.
options: Turn on more lights or open the curtains
Take the photo in the dark
Use only one light
Paint the room a different colour
payload.explanation: Indoor lights can make photos look orange. More daylight or brighter lights help colours look natural.

payload.snippet: You want a photo of your whole family but there is no one to press the button.
options: Use the timer setting so the camera takes the photo automatically
Leave one person out
Hold the camera very far away
Draw a photo instead
payload.explanation: The timer lets you set the camera down, get in position, and have the camera take the photo on its own.

payload.snippet: The photo has too many people's heads cut off at the top.
options: Step back further so everyone fits in the frame
Make the people shorter
Only photograph feet
Tilt the camera upside down
payload.explanation: Stepping back gives more room in the frame so everyone's head and body can fit into the picture.

payload.snippet: It is night time and everything looks black in the photo.
options: Turn on a light near the subject
Take photos only at night
Close your eyes to take the photo
Use the photo as a bookmark
payload.explanation: Cameras need light to capture an image. A nearby light source brightens the subject so it shows up clearly.

payload.snippet: You want a photo of a butterfly but it flies away before you can press the button.
options: Wait very quietly and still for the butterfly to land again
Chase the butterfly waving your arms
Take a photo of a flower instead
Give up and go inside
payload.explanation: Patience is important in nature photography. Staying quiet and still gives wild creatures time to settle.

payload.snippet: The photo has a big pole growing out of someone's head.
options: Move to a different angle where the pole is not behind the person
Cut the photo in half
Saw the pole down
Ignore it
payload.explanation: Distracting objects in the background can be removed simply by changing your position slightly.

payload.snippet: You take a photo of your drawing but the paper looks very white and bright.
options: Move to indirect light instead of direct sunshine
Draw on darker paper
Hold the drawing behind a curtain
Only photograph in the dark
payload.explanation: Direct sunlight bleaches out white paper. Soft indirect light preserves the colours and details of your drawing.

payload.snippet: Your selfie only shows the top of your head.
options: Hold the camera a little higher and tilt it down slightly
Take a photo of just your hair
Ask a friend to take it instead
Stand on a chair
payload.explanation: Holding the camera slightly above eye level and tilting it down creates a flattering angle that shows your whole face.

payload.snippet: The photo is too small to see the details of your model you built.
options: Move the camera closer to fill the frame with the model
Build a bigger model
Put the model far away
Use a smaller camera
payload.explanation: Getting closer to a subject fills the frame with detail, making it much easier to see in the finished photo.

payload.snippet: You want to photograph the moon but it looks like a tiny white dot.
options: Use as much zoom as possible and keep the camera very still
Throw the camera up in the air
Wait until the moon is bigger
Turn off the zoom
payload.explanation: The moon is very far away; maximum zoom combined with a very steady hold gets the best detail.

payload.snippet: Your birthday photo has red glowing eyes.
options: Turn off the flash and use a lamp nearby instead
Give everyone red-eye drops
Use a bigger flash
Add red sunglasses to the photo
payload.explanation: Red eye is caused by flash reflecting off the retina. Using ambient light instead of direct flash eliminates the effect.

payload.snippet: The background of the photo is very messy and distracting.
options: Move the subject to a cleaner spot or step closer to fill the frame
Add more mess to make it fair
Take the photo from below
Edit the background orange
payload.explanation: A clean or simple background keeps the viewer's attention on the subject rather than the clutter behind them.

payload.snippet: You are doing a puzzle and cannot find the last piece.
options: Look under the table and cushions where it might have fallen
Give up and throw the puzzle away
Colour in a piece of paper to replace it
Blame your brother
payload.explanation: Puzzle pieces often fall under furniture. Checking nearby surfaces and the floor is always worth a try.

payload.snippet: Two puzzle pieces look exactly the same but one does not fit.
options: Try both and use the one that clicks in smoothly
Force the wrong one in with your fist
Cut the piece to make it fit
Throw both away
payload.explanation: Similar-looking pieces are common in puzzles. Gently trying each one and feeling for the click tells you which is correct.

payload.snippet: You accidentally sit on one puzzle piece and it bends.
options: Gently flatten it under a heavy book
Throw it away immediately
Keep it bent so you know which one it is
Hide it at the back of the box
payload.explanation: A bent piece can often be flattened by placing something heavy on it for a few minutes.

payload.snippet: The puzzle box has a picture but the pieces are all face down.
options: Turn all the pieces face up before you start
Build the puzzle with the pieces face down
Put all the brown pieces together
Give up because you cannot see the picture
payload.explanation: Turning all pieces face up first gives you the whole picture to work with and makes it much easier to match shapes and colours.

payload.snippet: You are halfway done but need to go for dinner.
options: Leave the puzzle on the table and come back after dinner
Sweep it all back into the box
Take the puzzle to the dinner table
Ask your mum to finish it
payload.explanation: Leaving the puzzle where it is means you can carry on where you left off without losing your progress.

payload.snippet: You cannot tell which side is the right way up for one puzzle piece.
options: Compare it to the picture on the box to find the right orientation
Try all four ways until one looks right
Glue it in anyway
Skip that piece
payload.explanation: The box picture is your guide — comparing the colours and patterns on the piece to the picture quickly shows which way it should go.

payload.snippet: The puzzle is too big for the table.
options: Move to the floor where there is more space
Build only half the puzzle
Cut the board in half
Fold the puzzle up
payload.explanation: Large puzzles need lots of space. The floor gives you plenty of room to spread out and see all the pieces.

payload.snippet: A small child has chewed one puzzle piece and now it does not fit properly.
options: Contact the puzzle maker to ask for a replacement piece
Try forcing it in
Leave a gap in the puzzle
Put the chewed piece at the edge where gaps show less
payload.explanation: Many puzzle companies will send replacement pieces if you contact them. In the meantime, leaving the gap is better than forcing a damaged piece.

payload.snippet: You pick up a piece that looks like it should go in a gap but the colour is slightly wrong.
options: Set it aside and try other pieces first
Colour it in with a marker to match
Jam it in since it almost fits
Tear the hole bigger so it fits
payload.explanation: If a piece almost fits but the colour is off, it belongs somewhere else. Keeping it separate and coming back to it often finds the right spot.

payload.snippet: You have sorted all the edge pieces but now cannot find a corner.
options: Check for pieces that have two flat sides — those are the corners
Start in the middle instead
Assume there are no corners in this puzzle
Empty the box and start again
payload.explanation: Corner pieces are the only ones with two straight sides at a right angle. Looking specifically for that shape finds them quickly.

payload.snippet: The puzzle is of a blue sky and every piece looks the same blue.
options: Sort by the exact shade of blue and look at the shapes
Give up because all sky puzzles are impossible
Use only the edge pieces
Glue all the blue pieces together randomly
payload.explanation: Even a uniform sky has slight tonal and colour variations. Sorting by subtle shade differences, then matching the irregular shapes, is the key to tricky sky sections.

payload.snippet: You drop the puzzle from the table and all the pieces scatter.
options: Collect all the pieces and start sorting them again
Cry and refuse to start over
Glue whatever lands together
Decide the puzzle is done
payload.explanation: Accidents happen. Patiently collecting and re-sorting gives you a fresh start and you will often find pieces you missed before.

payload.snippet: One puzzle piece fits but leaves a visible white gap around its edges.
options: Remove it and keep looking — a slightly different piece will fill the gap completely
Accept the gap as part of the design
Fill the gap with white paint
Declare the puzzle finished anyway
payload.explanation: A visible gap means the piece is almost but not quite right. The correct piece will fit snugly with no gap showing.

payload.snippet: You want to do a puzzle but all the pieces are still in the bag from the shop.
options: Empty all the pieces onto the table first, then turn them face up
Try to build the puzzle with pieces still in the bag
Pour the pieces back into the box and use the box lid as a tray
Only take pieces out one at a time as you need them
payload.explanation: Emptying all pieces and turning them face up before starting gives you the full picture to work from and is much more efficient.

payload.snippet: Your puzzle picture shows a garden and you do not know where to start.
options: Find and build the straight-edged border first
Pick any piece from the middle and work outward
Sort by which pieces you like best

payload.explanation: Building the frame first gives you a defined shape and boundary that makes filling in the middle much easier.

payload.snippet: Two friends both want to do the same puzzle at the same time.
options: Agree to each work on a different section of the puzzle

Divide all the pieces into two equal piles

payload.explanation: Dividing the puzzle into sections lets both friends work simultaneously, making it go faster and keeping everyone involved.

payload.snippet: You have finished the puzzle but one piece is missing even after searching everywhere.

payload.explanation: One missing piece from a finished puzzle is a common experience. The work is still complete and worth celebrating. You can always look for the piece again later.

payload.snippet: The cereal box is empty and it is the only breakfast food you normally eat.
options: Check the cupboard for a different option and eat something rather than nothing
Skip breakfast because your preferred food is gone
Wait for your parent to buy more cereal before eating
Go to school hungry and ask a friend for food
payload.explanation: Any breakfast is better than no breakfast — checking for alternatives takes fifteen seconds.

payload.snippet: Your school has sent a reminder that it is non-uniform day today and you completely forgot until this morning.
options: Choose an appropriate outfit quickly from what is in your wardrobe
Wear your uniform and explain you forgot
Stay at home because you have nothing to wear
Text the school to ask if you can wear uniform instead
payload.explanation: A quick wardrobe decision is the correct response to a forgotten non-uniform day — uniform is always a fallback anyway.

payload.snippet: You cannot remember whether you locked the front door after leaving and you are already five minutes into the walk to school.
options: Text a parent to check or turn back only if no one is home to confirm
Turn back regardless to check even though you will be late
Keep walking and worry about it all morning
Assume it is fine because you usually lock it
payload.explanation: A text or call check takes ten seconds and confirms the answer without necessarily requiring you to turn back.

payload.snippet: The morning news is reporting heavy traffic on the road your parent drives you to school on.
options: Tell your parent early so they can choose a different route or plan
Wait until you are stuck in traffic to mention it
Ask your parent to drive a different way without explaining why
Take the bus instead without telling your parent
payload.explanation: Early information allows a route decision before the car has moved — announcing it in traffic is too late.

payload.snippet: You feel a sore throat coming on but it is a normal school day and you have no temperature.
options: Go to school and mention it to your parent when you get home if it gets worse
Refuse to go to school because of a sore throat
Take cold medicine from the cabinet without telling your parent
Ask your teacher to send you home when you arrive
payload.explanation: A sore throat without a temperature is not normally a reason to miss school — monitoring it is the right response.

payload.snippet: Your water bottle is empty and you forgot to refill it last night before bed.
options: Fill it at the tap in the next two minutes before you leave
Go to school without a water bottle
Buy a bottle of water on the way which costs money every day
Wait until school and use the water fountain all day
payload.explanation: Filling it quickly at home is both free and faster than any alternative.

payload.snippet: You and your sibling both need help from your parent at the same time and your parent is getting the baby ready.
options: Deal with what you can yourself and wait for a genuine blockage
Demand your parent helps you first
Give up on your morning routine entirely
Wake the other parent to get both children sorted at once
payload.explanation: Handling what you can independently before asking for help reduces the morning bottleneck.

payload.snippet: The school gate opens at 8:45 and you arrived early at 8:30 and there is nowhere to wait under cover in the rain.
options: Use a nearby sheltered spot or doorway until the gate opens
Stand in the rain for fifteen minutes
Go home and come back at 8:45
Knock on the school door and demand early entry
payload.explanation: Using nearby shelter is the obvious and free solution to waiting in the rain.

payload.snippet: You have a maths test first period and you realise you left your revision notes at school yesterday.
options: Do a five-minute mental review of what you remember and go in ready to do your best
Stay home to avoid the test
Ring the school to ask if someone can read you the notes
Blame the teacher for not letting you take notes home
payload.explanation: A quick mental review of what you already know is productive in the time available — the notes are gone and the test is not.

payload.snippet: Leo's mum packed a sandwich but he does not like it.
options: swaps with a friend
throws it in the bin
refuses to eat at all
demands a new one now
payload.explanation: Swapping is a polite solution that means neither child wastes food.

payload.snippet: Mia opens her lunchbox and finds her yogurt has leaked all over.
options: wipes it up and eats what she can
throws everything away
leaves the whole mess there
cries and goes hungry
payload.explanation: Cleaning up the spill and eating the salvageable food is the best approach.

payload.snippet: Kai forgot to put his lunch in his bag before school.
options: borrows a school lunch
skips eating for the day
steals another child's food
calls home to complain
payload.explanation: Borrowing a school lunch is the practical solution to a forgotten lunch.

payload.snippet: Nina finds her apple has a small brown bruise on one side.
options: eats around the bruise
throws the whole apple away
refuses to eat any fruit
cries about her ruined lunch
payload.explanation: A small bruise does not make an apple unsafe — you can eat around it.

payload.snippet: Tom's soup spilled inside his bag on the way to school.
options: tells a teacher and asks for help
hides the bag and says nothing
blames the soup flask brand
goes home early for a clean bag
payload.explanation: Telling a teacher means you get the right help to clean up and find food.

payload.snippet: Ava forgot to bring her water bottle to school today.
options: drinks water from the fountain
refuses to eat anything at all
takes someone else's bottle
cries until a teacher gives her one
payload.explanation: Drinking from a water fountain is the simple solution to a forgotten bottle.

payload.snippet: Ben's sandwich has mustard but he asked his mum for none.
options: scrapes the mustard off
throws the whole sandwich away
demands his mum bring a new one
goes home for the day
payload.explanation: Scraping off the unwanted topping is a practical fix.

payload.snippet: Grace packed cold leftover pasta and hopes it still tastes nice.
options: eats it cold without complaining
demands the teacher warm it up
throws it all away uneaten
trades her whole lunch away
payload.explanation: Eating cold leftovers is perfectly fine and wastes nothing.

payload.snippet: Max is sitting next to someone whose lunch smells very strong.
options: moves politely to another seat
tells them their food smells awful
holds his nose loudly all lunch
refuses to eat his own food
payload.explanation: Quietly moving is the polite way to handle a strong smell.

payload.snippet: Lily dropped her fork and it now has dirt on it.
options: gets a clean fork from the counter
uses the dirty fork anyway
eats everything with only her hands
refuses to eat at all
payload.explanation: Getting a clean fork is the hygienic and sensible solution.

payload.snippet: Zoe's sandwich bag is very tricky and hard to open today.
options: asks a friend to help her
gives up eating and goes hungry
rips the whole bag apart
asks the teacher to open it
payload.explanation: Asking a friend for help is friendly and solves the problem quickly.

payload.snippet: Sam brought a delicious-smelling lunch and his friends are curious.
options: shares a little bite with friends
hides it under the table secretly
eats it very quickly to avoid sharing
tells his friends not to look
payload.explanation: Sharing a small taste is a kind and social thing to do at lunch.

payload.snippet: Finn's lunchbox has his name on it but someone else picked it up.
options: tells a teacher what happened
takes another child's lunchbox
goes hungry and says nothing
shouts at the other child
payload.explanation: Telling a teacher is the right and calm way to sort out a mix-up.

payload.snippet: Ruby's mum wrote a little note inside her lunchbox today.
options: reads it and feels happy
throws the note away unread
feels embarrassed and hides it
tells everyone her mum is silly
payload.explanation: A loving note from a parent is something to appreciate and enjoy.

payload.snippet: Owen opens his crisps and finds they are stale from a tiny hole.
options: eats them since they are still safe
throws the entire lunchbox away
demands the school give him new crisps
cries about his ruined snack
payload.explanation: Stale crisps from a small hole are still safe to eat even if less nice.

payload.snippet: Sophie spills her juice box all over the lunch table.
options: gets paper towels to wipe it up
walks away and leaves the mess
blames her friend for bumping her
pretends the spill did not happen
payload.explanation: Cleaning up your own spill is the responsible thing to do.

payload.snippet: Jake finds his crackers crumbled into pieces inside his lunchbox.
options: eats the crumbled pieces from the box
refuses to eat anything not whole
demands his mum bring new crackers
throws away all his food
payload.explanation: Crumbled crackers are still fine to eat — shape does not matter.

payload.snippet: Chloe is very hungry but only brought a very small snack today.
options: eats slowly and asks for more at home
takes food off another child's tray
tells the teacher she is starving
refuses to eat the small snack
payload.explanation: Eating what you have and waiting until home is the right response.

payload.snippet: Ethan's mum packed a brand new food he has never tried before.
options: tries a small bite to see if he likes it
throws the whole thing away untasted
demands his mum never pack new food
refuses it loudly in front of class
payload.explanation: Trying a small bite before deciding is the fair and adventurous thing to do.

payload.snippet: Isla forgot to pack her dessert even though she made it last night.
options: tells her mum after school so she remembers
cries all afternoon about missing dessert
takes someone else's dessert instead
refuses to eat her main lunch at all
payload.explanation: Calmly telling your mum later is the mature response to a small mistake.

payload.snippet: Leo gets on the school bus and his usual seat is already taken by someone else.
options: finds another empty seat without making a fuss
tells the person to move because it is his seat
stands in the aisle refusing to sit elsewhere
refuses to ride the bus and calls his mum
payload.explanation: Finding another seat calmly shows good flexibility and manners.

payload.snippet: Mia's heavy school bag falls from the overhead shelf onto the passenger below.
options: immediately apologises and checks if the person is okay
pretends it was not her bag that fell
laughs and says it was an accident so it does not matter
waits for someone else to deal with the fallen bag
payload.explanation: Apologising and checking on the person shows responsibility and care.

payload.snippet: Kai lost his bus pass and the driver says he cannot ride without it.
options: explains honestly and asks if he can sort it out at school
pushes past the driver and gets on anyway
pretends to look for it and sneaks on
cries loudly until the driver lets him on
payload.explanation: Honest communication with the driver is the right response when you have lost your pass.

payload.snippet: Nina is sitting next to someone who smells strongly of something unpleasant.
options: stays seated and breathes quietly without saying anything rude
loudly tells the person they smell bad
moves seat and points at the person to explain why
puts her scarf dramatically over her nose
payload.explanation: Staying quiet and respectful is the polite response in a sensitive situation.

payload.snippet: Tom is not sure which stop to get off at because the route changed today.
options: asks the driver which stop is closest to his school
gets off at a random stop and hopes for the best
stays on the bus all the way to the final stop
calls his mum in a panic while the bus is still moving
payload.explanation: Asking the driver is the safest and most sensible option when unsure.

payload.snippet: Ava's bus arrives but the queue is long and she might not get on this one.
options: waits patiently for the next bus
pushes through the queue to get on this one
shouts at people in front to move faster
gives up and decides to walk the entire way
payload.explanation: Waiting patiently for the next bus is the safe and fair approach.

payload.snippet: Ben is on the bus and realises he left his school bag at the bus stop.
options: tells the driver at the next stop so he can go back for it
jumps off the moving bus to go back immediately
says nothing and hopes his bag is still there later
blames his friend for not reminding him about the bag
payload.explanation: Telling the driver calmly is the safest way to address a forgotten item.

payload.snippet: Grace finds a mobile phone left on the bus seat beside her.
options: gives it to the bus driver as lost property
looks through the phone to find the owner herself
puts it in her bag to use until the owner is found
leaves it on the seat for the next person to deal with
payload.explanation: Giving the phone to the driver is the correct honest procedure for lost property.

payload.snippet: Max has very smelly trainers and other passengers are noticing.
options: puts his feet flat on the floor so the smell is less noticeable
takes his trainers off on the bus to air them
pretends the smell is coming from someone else
laughs about it loudly with his friends
payload.explanation: Keeping feet flat on the floor is the most considerate option in this situation.

payload.snippet: Lily sees an older woman struggling to lift her heavy bag to the overhead shelf.
options: stands up and offers to help her lift it
watches but does not want to interfere
tells the driver the woman needs help
holds the bag but does not actually lift it up
payload.explanation: Offering to help someone who is struggling is a kind and thoughtful action.

payload.snippet: Zoe's friends are playing music on a speaker and other passengers look annoyed.
options: suggests to her friends that they use earphones
joins in with the music and ignores the annoyed passengers
tells her friends off loudly for being rude
moves to another part of the bus to distance herself from them
payload.explanation: Politely suggesting earphones is a constructive way to resolve the issue without embarrassing friends.

payload.snippet: Sam's bus is running very late and he will miss the start of an important test.
options: texts his parent and asks them to contact the school to explain
gets off the bus and tries to run to school
demands the driver go faster
cries and says there is no point going to school now
payload.explanation: Contacting a parent to inform the school is the most effective and calm action.

payload.snippet: Finn finds a wallet stuffed with cash on the floor under his seat.
options: hands it to the bus driver right away
looks through it for a name and calls the owner himself
keeps the cash and hands in the empty wallet
leaves it there since it is not near his own seat
payload.explanation: Handing the wallet to the driver is the honest and correct action.

payload.snippet: Ruby gets on the bus and friends want her to sit with them but there is only one gap.
options: thanks her friends and sits in the available space
insists a friend moves to another seat to make a better space
stands in the aisle next to her friends instead of sitting
sits on her own feeling upset rather than choosing
payload.explanation: Joining the group in the available space is the social and practical solution.

payload.snippet: Owen is on the bus when a stranger starts asking him personal questions about where he lives.
options: politely says he would rather not say and looks away
answers all the questions honestly to seem polite
shouts at the stranger to leave him alone
moves immediately to sit right behind the driver
payload.explanation: Not sharing personal information with strangers is an important safety habit.

payload.snippet: Sophie accidentally steps on someone's foot getting onto the crowded bus.
options: immediately apologises and checks they are not hurt
keeps moving as if nothing happened
says sorry but then laughs about it to her friend
blames the crowd for making her trip
payload.explanation: Apologising and checking the person is not hurt is the caring and responsible action.

payload.snippet: Jake sees the bus driver yawn several times during the long journey.
options: tells a responsible adult when he gets off the bus
tells all the other passengers the driver is falling asleep
shouts to the driver trying to keep them awake
asks his friend to film the driver yawning as evidence
payload.explanation: Reporting a concern about driver tiredness to an adult after arrival is the responsible action.

payload.snippet: Chloe is on the bus when a fight breaks out between two teenagers a few rows ahead.
options: stays in her seat and tells the driver at the earliest safe opportunity
goes over to try to separate the teenagers herself
films the fight on her phone excitedly
shouts at the teenagers to stop arguing
payload.explanation: Staying safe in your seat and alerting the driver is the right response to a conflict.

payload.snippet: Ethan is on the bus and the person next to him falls asleep on his shoulder.
options: stays still and lets the person rest
pushes the person off immediately
wakes the person up with a loud noise
moves away leaving them to fall sideways
payload.explanation: Letting a tired person rest without disturbing them is a kind and patient choice.

payload.snippet: Isla gets on the bus and notices the floor is wet and slippery near the entrance.
options: tells the driver so passengers can be warned
slips past carefully without saying anything
stands in the entrance blocking everyone while she decides what to do
waits until someone slips and falls before saying anything
payload.explanation: Telling the driver protects all passengers from slipping and is the responsible action.

payload.snippet: Leo wants to buy a toy but he is ten pence short and needs to find a way.
options: asks if he can do a small chore to earn the last ten pence
takes a toy from the shelf and hides it under his coat
cries loudly at the checkout until someone helps him
demands the shopkeeper gives him a discount for no reason
payload.explanation: Earning the last bit of money through a chore is the honest and practical solution.

payload.snippet: Mia finds a twenty pound note on the pavement with no one around.
options: takes it to the nearest shop or police station as lost property
puts it straight in her pocket to spend on herself
leaves it on the ground in case the owner comes back
tears it up so no one else can take it
payload.explanation: Handing in found money to the proper authorities is the honest and correct action.

payload.snippet: Kai is at the checkout and realises he does not have enough money to pay for everything.
options: puts something back politely and pays for what he can afford
runs out of the shop without paying for anything
demands the cashier let him take it all and pay later
causes a scene and refuses to leave until someone pays for him
payload.explanation: Putting something back and paying for what you can afford is the responsible solution.

payload.snippet: Nina is given pocket money and wants to spend it all on sweets right away.
options: buys a small treat and saves the rest
spends every single coin on sweets immediately
loses all her money on the way to the shop
demands more pocket money as soon as she arrives home
payload.explanation: Buying a small treat and saving the rest balances enjoyment with future goals.

payload.snippet: Tom is at a car boot sale and finds something he loves but it costs more than he has.
options: asks the seller politely if the price can be reduced
takes the item and runs away without paying anything
stands there crying until someone buys it for him
deliberately breaks the item so the seller cannot sell it
payload.explanation: Politely asking for a reduced price is a fair and common approach at a car boot sale.

payload.snippet: Ava discovers that her friend always asks to borrow money and never pays it back.
options: kindly explains she cannot keep lending money anymore
gives the money anyway even though she knows it will not be returned
refuses without explanation and falls out with her friend
lends the money but then takes things from her friend secretly
payload.explanation: Setting a kind but firm boundary about lending money is the right thing to do.

payload.snippet: Ben gets twice as much pocket money as usual this week but quickly realises it was an error.
options: tells the grown-up about the mistake and gives the extra back
spends all the extra money as fast as possible before anyone notices
keeps quiet and hopes no one realises the error was made
gives the extra money to a friend to hide it
payload.explanation: Telling the grown-up and returning the overpayment is the honest action.

payload.snippet: Grace wants to buy a present for her friend but her savings are not quite enough.
options: does extra chores to earn the remaining amount needed
takes money from her mum's purse without asking
buys a cheaper present without telling her friend she wanted to get more
demands her parents give her the extra money without earning it
payload.explanation: Earning the remaining money through extra effort is the honest and responsible approach.

payload.snippet: Max is at a shop when he realises he has been given the wrong item at the checkout.
options: goes back and tells the cashier about the mistake politely
keeps the wrong item since it is the shop's fault not his
swaps it himself from the shelf without telling anyone
leaves the shop quickly so no one notices the error
payload.explanation: Telling the cashier politely is the honest way to resolve a checkout error.

payload.snippet: Lily wants to donate some of her pocket money to a charity she cares about.
options: puts money in the collection tin and feels proud
takes money from the collection tin thinking no one will notice
refuses to donate because it is her money
donates all her money and then asks her parents for more
payload.explanation: Donating a portion of your own money to charity is a generous and meaningful act.

payload.snippet: Zoe is at a restaurant when her parents tell her she can choose one thing from the menu.
options: picks something within the price she was told
orders the most expensive thing on the menu
orders several things without asking first
refuses to eat anything since she cannot have everything she wants
payload.explanation: Choosing within the agreed budget shows good understanding of money and boundaries.

payload.snippet: Sam lends his friend two pounds and his friend insists he has already paid it back.
options: checks his notes and calmly discusses what he remembers
accuses his friend of lying loudly in front of everyone
gives his friend another two pounds just to avoid conflict
refuses to speak to his friend until the money is returned
payload.explanation: Calmly discussing the disagreement is the mature way to resolve a money misunderstanding.

payload.snippet: Finn notices that the price tag on a toy at the shop is wrong — lower than it should be.
options: tells the shop assistant about the pricing error
buys as many as possible at the wrong lower price
says nothing and buys one at the lower price
tells all his friends so they can also buy it cheaply first
payload.explanation: Telling the shop assistant about the error is the honest thing to do.

payload.snippet: Ruby finds out her friend is selling homemade biscuits to raise money for a school trip.
options: buys some biscuits to support her friend
tells everyone the biscuits look horrible so fewer people will buy them
steals some biscuits from the stall
asks her friend to give her some for free since they are friends
payload.explanation: Supporting a friend's fundraising by buying their product is kind and helpful.

payload.snippet: Owen is saving to buy new football boots and his little sibling asks him to lend money for sweets.
options: explains he is saving for something important but offers a small amount
gives his sibling all his savings to be kind
refuses and does not explain why he cannot lend the money
lends the money but stays angry about it all day
payload.explanation: Explaining your saving goal while offering a small amount is kind and sets a good example.

payload.snippet: Sophie is given money for her birthday and is not sure whether to save it or spend it.
options: saves most of it and spends a small amount on something she enjoys
spends every single penny on the very first day
saves all of it and never spends any of it at all
gives all of it away to people who ask for it
payload.explanation: Saving most while spending a little is a balanced and healthy approach to money.

payload.snippet: Jake is working at a school bake sale and notices some money is missing from the cash box.
options: tells a supervising adult immediately about the missing money
accuses the person who was helping before him
takes some extra money from sales to make up the missing amount
says nothing and hopes no one notices the amount is wrong
payload.explanation: Telling an adult immediately is the honest and correct response to missing money.

payload.snippet: Chloe helps her mum do shopping and the cashier forgets to charge for one item.
options: tells the cashier they missed scanning one item
stays quiet and enjoys the free item at home
quickly puts the item back before leaving the shop
tells her mum quietly and lets her mum decide what to do
payload.explanation: Telling the cashier about the missed item is the honest action.

payload.snippet: Ethan is offered money to keep a secret that he knows is wrong to keep.
options: refuses the money and refuses to keep the secret
takes the money and keeps the secret
refuses the money but keeps the secret anyway
takes the money and then tells the secret anyway
payload.explanation: Refusing both the money and the pressure to keep a harmful secret is the right and brave choice.

payload.snippet: Isla notices her friend is upset because they cannot afford to come on a school trip.
options: asks a teacher if there are any funds available to help her friend
tells everyone in class that her friend cannot afford the trip
lends her friend money from her own savings
says nothing since it is her friend's personal problem to deal with
payload.explanation: Asking a teacher about support funds is the most helpful and discreet action.

payload.snippet: Leo is walking in the park when a large off-lead dog runs straight toward him barking very loudly.
options: stands completely still, avoids eye contact, and waits for the dog to calm down
runs away from the dog as fast as he can
shouts at the dog to try to scare it away
tries to grab the dog's collar to take control of it
payload.explanation: Standing still and not making eye contact is the safest response to an approaching unknown dog.

payload.snippet: Mia finds a young bird that has fallen from its nest in her garden and is sitting on the grass.
options: tells an adult and watches from a distance without touching it
picks the bird up and puts it in a warm box
tries to put the bird back in the nest herself by climbing the tree
brings the bird inside to keep it as a pet
payload.explanation: Adults can call a wildlife rescue — touching fledglings can make things worse, and the parent may return.

payload.snippet: Kai is at a petting zoo and a goat starts pulling very hard on his sleeve with its teeth.
options: gently pulls his sleeve away and moves to a different area
pulls hard on the goat's ears to make it let go
shouts and hits the goat to make it stop
lets the goat chew his sleeve and laughs about it
payload.explanation: Gently pulling away and moving on is the safe response — goats explore with their mouths and it is normal.

payload.snippet: Nina finds a cat sitting very still with its fur all puffed up and its ears flat back.
options: gives the cat plenty of space and does not approach it
goes over quickly to stroke the cat to calm it down
picks the cat up to comfort it against her body
splashes water on it to make it move away
payload.explanation: A puffed-up cat with flat ears is stressed — giving it space prevents a scratch and allows it to calm.

payload.snippet: Tom sees a swan with its neck arched and wings raised walking toward him near a river.
options: slowly backs away and gives the swan plenty of space
runs toward the river to put distance between them quickly
waves his arms to make the swan go back into the river
throws bread to distract the swan while he passes quickly
payload.explanation: Swans are protective and can be aggressive — slowly backing away is the safest response.

payload.snippet: Ava sees a fox sitting in her garden in the middle of the day looking very still and unwell.
options: tells an adult straight away who can call a wildlife rescue organisation
tries to pick the fox up to take it to the vet herself
shouts at the fox to see if it reacts to noise normally
gives the fox food and water and waits to see if it recovers
payload.explanation: A fox out in daytime acting unusually could be sick — adults and wildlife rescues know the right steps.

payload.snippet: Ben is at the beach when a seagull swoops down very low and snatches food right from his hand.
options: stays calm and does not chase the seagull or wave food around
chases the seagull along the beach shouting
throws his remaining food at other seagulls in retaliation
holds his remaining food very high in the air while walking
payload.explanation: Staying calm and keeping food covered or out of reach prevents further seagull swoops.

payload.snippet: Grace finds a toad in the garden that is struggling to move and looking very dry.
options: calls an adult to help and keeps the garden hose available to gently moisten it
picks it up and runs it under the cold tap forcefully
puts it in a jar with no air holes to carry it to the vet
leaves it and assumes it will be fine without any help
payload.explanation: Toads can dry out in heat — keeping them moist while an adult calls for advice is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Max is on a countryside walk when a herd of cows with calves starts moving toward him and his family.
options: stays calm, moves to the edge of the field, and climbs over the fence if they get too close
runs at full speed directly across the middle of the field
tries to pet the nearest calf to show the cows he means no harm
waves his arms and jacket to try to stop the cows coming toward them
payload.explanation: Moving to the fence edge and exiting if necessary is the safest response to cows with calves.

payload.snippet: Lily discovers a hedgehog curled up in a pile of leaves she was about to rake away.
options: gently puts the leaves back and tells an adult so they can move the pile safely later
pulls the hedgehog out of the leaves to look at it up close
pours water on the leaves to wake the hedgehog up
removes all the leaves anyway since the hedgehog can find another place
payload.explanation: Hedgehogs hibernate and nest in leaves — protecting the pile and seeking adult help is kind and correct.

payload.snippet: Zoe is at the pet shop when a hamster in a tank bites her finger as she reaches in.
options: removes her finger calmly and asks the shop assistant for help
jabs her finger back in and tries again immediately
drops the tank lid to stop the hamster from getting out
shouts loudly and tells everyone in the shop the hamster is dangerous
payload.explanation: Calmly removing the finger and getting help is the right response — bites can happen when animals feel threatened.

payload.snippet: Sam is walking near a pond when he hears a loud hissing sound from some tall reeds nearby.
options: stops immediately and steps back from the reeds cautiously
pushes the reeds aside to find out what is making the noise
throws a stone into the reeds to scare whatever is there away
calls out loudly to see if a person made the noise
payload.explanation: Stopping and stepping back is the correct caution response when you hear an unexpected animal sound from cover.

payload.snippet: Finn sees a wasp flying around his food at a picnic table.
options: covers the food and moves calmly away from the wasp
swats at the wasp hard with a newspaper
blows air at the wasp repeatedly to drive it away
tries to squash the wasp under his cup
payload.explanation: Covering food and moving calmly is the safest response — wasps only sting when threatened.

payload.snippet: Ruby is visiting a farm when she finds a newborn lamb that seems to have wandered away from its mother.
options: tells the farmer immediately and stays nearby without touching the lamb
picks the lamb up and tries to return it to the flock herself
bottle-feeds the lamb with water from her drinks bottle
calls the lamb's name to see if its mother comes running
payload.explanation: Telling the farmer immediately is the right action — farmers know how to reunite separated lambs safely.

payload.snippet: Owen is on holiday when he notices a jellyfish on the beach near where children are playing.
options: tells a lifeguard or beach supervisor about the jellyfish straightaway
picks up the jellyfish to move it away from the children
throws sand on the jellyfish to bury it quickly
tells the children it is dead and completely safe to touch
payload.explanation: Telling a lifeguard ensures the correct hazard warning is given and no one is injured.

payload.snippet: Sophie finds a mouse in the kitchen of her house that is running along the back of the cupboards.
options: tells a parent or adult who can contact pest control
tries to catch the mouse using a bowl from the kitchen
pours bleach near the cupboards to drive it away
feeds the mouse to encourage it to stay in one place
payload.explanation: Telling an adult who can contact pest control is the responsible and humane action.

payload.snippet: Jake is in the garden when a bee lands on his arm and stays there without stinging.
options: stays completely still and waits patiently for the bee to fly away on its own
shakes his arm hard to make the bee fly off immediately
tries to flick the bee off quickly with his other hand
calls for help loudly even though the bee is not stinging him
payload.explanation: Staying still is the safest response — bees are harmless when resting and will leave on their own.

payload.snippet: Chloe sees a seagull trapped in a plastic net near the seafront and it cannot free itself.
options: finds a nearby adult and tells them so a wildlife rescue can be called
tries to cut the net herself using scissors from a nearby shop
shouts at the seagull to encourage it to struggle free faster
picks the seagull up to try to unwrap the net herself
payload.explanation: Finding an adult and calling a wildlife rescue is the safest and most effective action.

payload.snippet: Ethan sees a large dog tied up outside a shop that starts growling as he walks past.
options: crosses to the other side of the pavement giving the dog plenty of space
stops and stares at the dog trying to decide if it is dangerous
tries to calm the dog by reaching out his hand for it to sniff
makes loud noises to see whether the growling gets worse or stops
payload.explanation: Crossing to give the dog space is the safe and sensible response to a growling restrained dog.

payload.snippet: Isla finds a slow worm in her garden curled up under a piece of wood.
options: gently replaces the wood and leaves the slow worm alone
picks it up thinking it is a worm and it will not mind
shows all her friends by lifting the wood repeatedly
pours water on it to make it move so she can see it better
payload.explanation: Slow worms are protected reptiles — leaving them undisturbed under their refuge is the correct and legal response.

payload.snippet: Leo is building a tall tower but it falls over every time he adds a new layer.
options: makes the base much wider and uses heavier blocks at the bottom
keeps building it taller until it somehow stays up on its own
uses tape to stick the blocks together so they cannot fall
gives up and knocks down everyone else's tower in frustration
payload.explanation: A wider, heavier base is the engineering solution to a toppling tower.

payload.snippet: Mia wants to build a birdhouse but has never used a hammer or nails before.
options: asks an adult to supervise and teach her before she begins
hammers nails in by herself without any guidance or safety check
uses the hammer as a bat to play a game instead
draws a birdhouse on cardboard since it is much safer and easier
payload.explanation: Getting adult supervision when using tools for the first time is both safe and a great way to learn.

payload.snippet: Kai's team is building a model bridge and his partner wants to do it completely differently from him.
options: discusses the two ideas and tries combining the best parts of each
ignores his partner and builds his own version on the side
gives in completely and lets his partner do it all themselves
argues until the teacher makes them split into separate teams
payload.explanation: Discussing and combining ideas produces a better result and teaches collaboration.

payload.snippet: Nina is following instructions to build a shelf but finds the booklet is in another language.
options: looks up pictures in the booklet and figures out the steps from the diagrams
throws the instructions away and guesses every single step
gives up and asks her parents to pay someone else to do it
calls the customer service number on the booklet for help
payload.explanation: Using the diagrams when the written instructions are unclear is a smart problem-solving approach.

payload.snippet: Tom has cut a plank of wood two centimetres too short for his project and cannot undo the cut.
options: measures and cuts another piece to the correct length instead
glues the two cut pieces back together and hopes it holds
tries to stretch the wood to the right length by pulling hard
uses the short piece anyway and pretends the measurements were flexible
payload.explanation: Cutting a new piece to the right length is the correct response to a measurement error.

payload.snippet: Ava is building a model using air-drying clay but it has cracked in several places while still soft.
options: smooths more water and clay over the cracks gently with her fingers
leaves the model as it is hoping the cracks close up when it dries
throws the cracked clay away and starts from scratch entirely
bakes the clay in the oven to see if it helps
payload.explanation: Smoothing water and clay into soft cracks repairs them before drying is complete.

payload.snippet: Ben is helping paint a fence when the paint keeps dripping down onto the path below.
options: puts newspaper or a dust sheet down on the path below first
paints faster so less paint has time to drip onto the path
wipes each drip as it forms which takes a very long time
stops painting the bottom third of the fence where drips mostly occur
payload.explanation: Laying a dust sheet or newspaper prevents paint dripping onto surfaces below.

payload.snippet: Grace discovers her team built the wrong wall in the wrong place during a school project.
options: tells the teacher and asks whether the wall can be moved or changed
says nothing and hopes the teacher does not notice during marking
tears the wall down and rebuilds it without telling anyone what happened
convinces her team the wrong position was actually the plan all along
payload.explanation: Telling the teacher promptly allows the problem to be fixed properly.

payload.snippet: Max is mixing cement for a small garden project but it is coming out too runny and liquid.
options: adds more dry cement powder to thicken the mixture to the right consistency
keeps adding water to the mix hoping the runny cement will firm up
leaves the liquid cement to dry and uses it next time
pours the runny cement out and starts the whole mixture from scratch
payload.explanation: Adding more dry powder is the correct way to thicken an overly runny cement mix.

payload.snippet: Lily is building a den in the garden and wants to use a large sheet of glass she found in the shed.
options: leaves the glass in the shed and finds a safe alternative material
carries the glass outside carefully and leans it against the fence
drills holes in the glass herself to attach it to the structure
smashes the glass into smaller pieces since it is too big to use as is
payload.explanation: Glass is a dangerous building material for a den — finding a safe alternative is the right decision.

payload.snippet: Zoe notices a very big crack forming in the wall of the outdoor classroom at school.
options: tells a teacher about the crack immediately
puts a poster over the crack so it cannot be seen by anyone
pokes a stick into the crack to see how deep it goes
uses filler from the art room to seal the crack herself
payload.explanation: Reporting a structural crack to a teacher immediately is the safe and correct action.

payload.snippet: Sam's team is building a model tower in class and his teammate keeps adding pieces that make it less stable.
options: explains politely to his teammate why those pieces are weakening the structure
takes the pieces off silently while his teammate is not watching
lets the tower fall over so the teacher sees what his teammate did wrong
tells the teacher his teammate is ruining the project
payload.explanation: Explaining politely why certain pieces weaken the design is the collaborative and educational approach.

payload.snippet: Finn is helping his dad build a garden shed when he sees his dad start to skip an important step in the instructions.
options: mentions it to his dad calmly and asks if they should follow the step
stays silent since it is his dad's shed and his dad knows best
follows the instructions himself on the next panel without telling his dad
reads out all the skipped steps loudly until his dad agrees to do them
payload.explanation: Mentioning the skipped step calmly allows his dad to decide with full information.

payload.snippet: Ruby is painting a mural on a school wall and runs out of the specific red paint halfway through.
options: tells the art teacher and asks what to do before continuing
mixes other colours together hoping to create a matching red shade
leaves the mural unfinished since she cannot continue without that colour
uses a completely different colour for the remaining section of the mural
payload.explanation: Telling the teacher ensures the correct paint can be obtained before the mural is compromised.

payload.snippet: Owen is assembling flat-pack furniture and has several screws left over after finishing.
options: checks the instructions to see whether the extra screws are spares or were forgotten
assumes leftover screws are just extras and leaves the furniture as it is
unscrews everything and starts completely from scratch to find where they go
throws the leftover screws away since the furniture seems solid enough
payload.explanation: Checking the instructions is the only reliable way to know whether remaining screws are spares or missing.

payload.snippet: Sophie needs to cut a piece of wood for her project but the only saw available is a large sharp one.
options: asks a supervising adult to cut the wood for her using the large saw
cuts the wood herself since the project needs to be done soon
uses a blunt kitchen knife which is safer than the large sharp saw
finds a different piece of wood that does not need to be cut
payload.explanation: Asking an adult to operate a large sharp saw is the correct safety decision.

payload.snippet: Jake is working on a group construction project when one team member does no work and keeps distracting the others.
options: calmly asks the team member to take on a specific part of the task
does all the work himself while complaining to the rest of the team
tells the teacher immediately without first trying to involve the team member
stops working himself since it is unfair that only some people are contributing
payload.explanation: Assigning the team member a specific role is the constructive solution before escalating to the teacher.

payload.snippet: Chloe is building a model volcano and the baking soda and vinegar reaction is much less dramatic than expected.
options: checks the amounts in the recipe and adjusts the quantities
adds washing-up liquid and food dye hoping to make it more dramatic
declares the experiment a complete failure and refuses to present it
waits longer for the reaction to intensify but adds nothing new
payload.explanation: Checking and adjusting the quantities based on the recipe is the scientific approach.

payload.snippet: Ethan is designing a building on a computer program and accidentally deletes a large section of his work.
options: uses the undo function to recover the deleted section
