payload.snippet: Maya is auditioning for a solo role in the school musical and discovers the night before that the key of her prepared song is too high for her voice today.
options: She practises transposing the song down two semitones and confirms the new key with the accompanist before the audition.
She performs the song in the original key and apologises for any strained notes.
She chooses a completely different song the night before to avoid the problem.
She asks the panel if she can perform without accompaniment in a comfortable key.
payload.explanation: Transposing and confirming with the accompanist is the professional solution to a key problem before an audition.

payload.snippet: Tom is in a drumming workshop when he plays a complex rhythm that accidentally throws the whole group out of time.
options: He stops, listens to re-find the group's pulse, and re-enters on the downbeat.
He plays louder to reassert the correct rhythm over the confused group.
He keeps playing his rhythm hoping the group will follow him back into time.
He puts his sticks down and lets the group find the pulse without him.
payload.explanation: Stop, listen, and re-enter on the downbeat is the correct way to recover from a rhythm error in group drumming.

payload.snippet: Anna notices that the sheet music stand she is using at home keeps toppling forward because a leg is loose.
options: She tightens the leg before placing the sheet music on it.
She leans the stand against the wall and props the music with a book.
She places a heavy dictionary on the base to stop it falling forward.
She balances the sheet music on top of the piano instead and ignores the stand.
payload.explanation: Tightening the loose leg before use prevents the stand from toppling during practice.

payload.snippet: Oliver's school band is preparing for a competition and the lead guitarist breaks a string two days before the performance.
options: He orders a replacement string set immediately and allows time to restring and stretch the strings before the competition.
He borrows a classmate's guitar for the competition and returns it after.
He superglues the broken string back in place to last for the two days.
He performs the piece with five strings, adjusting fingering to work around the missing string.
payload.explanation: Ordering a replacement set and allowing stretch time ensures the guitar is in tune for competition day.

payload.snippet: Clara is practising a complicated piece and keeps stopping at the same difficult passage every time.
options: She marks the start of the difficult passage, practises only that section slowly until it is reliable, then gradually increases the tempo.
She plays the whole piece repeatedly from the beginning, hoping the difficult passage gets easier through repetition.
She skips the difficult passage entirely and learns the rest of the piece perfectly first.
She asks her teacher to simplify the difficult passage so she can perform it comfortably.
payload.explanation: Isolating, slowing, and incrementally speeding up a difficult passage is the most efficient practice method.

payload.snippet: Tom is playing football when he twists his ankle going for a tackle and hears a slight pop. He can still walk but it hurts.
options: He leaves the field, sits out the rest of the game, and shows the ankle to a parent or coach.
He runs it off because walking on it means it is probably just a sprain.
He keeps playing because his team needs him for the last ten minutes.
He asks his teammate to help him hop along the sideline to stay in the game.
payload.explanation: A pop and pain after a twisted ankle needs rest and adult assessment — playing on risks further injury.

payload.snippet: Lily is swimming in a race when she swallows a mouthful of chlorinated pool water and starts coughing in the middle of her lane.
options: She moves to the side of the pool, holds the lane rope, and coughs until clear before continuing.
She keeps swimming through the coughing so she does not lose her position in the race.
She signals to the lifeguard immediately to say she is choking.
She turns onto her back and floats while she waits for the coughing to stop.
payload.explanation: Moving to the side prevents panic and allows safe coughing without the risk of submerging.

payload.snippet: Sam is batting in cricket when the ball strikes his unprotected finger directly and it bends backwards sharply.
options: He leaves the field, ice is applied to the finger, and an adult checks whether it is broken.
He shakes his hand, checks he can move the finger, and goes back to batting.
He wraps it in a spare sock from his kit bag and keeps batting.
He asks a teammate to keep score so he can stay at the crease and just call for someone to field for him.
payload.explanation: A finger bent backwards by impact needs ice and adult assessment — continuing to bat risks a worse injury.

payload.snippet: Anna is in a gymnastics class when she attempts a cartwheel and lands awkwardly on her wrist, which immediately starts to swell.
options: She tells the coach straight away and keeps the wrist still until it can be assessed.
She flexes the wrist repeatedly to check whether she can still move it.
She asks to try the cartwheel one more time in case the landing was just a fluke.
She puts her wrist under cold water and waits until the end of the class to tell anyone.
payload.explanation: Swelling after impact needs to be kept still and assessed by an adult immediately.

payload.snippet: Jack is playing rugby and gets a bad knock to the head. He feels a bit dizzy but his team still has ten minutes left.
options: He tells the referee he feels dizzy and comes off the field immediately under concussion protocol.
He carries on because dizziness usually clears after a minute or two of play.
He asks to be moved to a lighter position where he will not get hit again.
He sits at the side but does not tell anyone, planning to go back on when the dizziness passes.
payload.explanation: Any dizziness after a head knock means leaving the field immediately under concussion protocol — no exceptions.

payload.snippet: Maya is running a cross-country race in hot weather when she starts feeling sick and her vision goes slightly blurry halfway round the course.
options: She slows to a walk, moves to the side of the course, and signals to a marshal for help.
She pushes through the discomfort because she is nearly halfway and slowing down now would cost her the race.
She splashes water from her bottle on her face and runs harder to generate more airflow.
She sits on the ground in the sun and waits for a teammate to pass.
payload.explanation: Nausea and blurry vision during exercise in heat are warning signs — stop, signal for help, get out of the sun.

payload.snippet: Oliver is playing in a school basketball match when a teammate is talking over the coach's half-time instructions and distracting the rest of the team.
options: He quietly nudges the teammate and nods toward the coach so they refocus.
He speaks over both of them to restore order and deliver the instructions himself.
He tells the coach loudly that his teammate is not listening.
He ignores the situation and listens to the coach on his own.
payload.explanation: A quiet non-verbal signal is the least disruptive way to redirect a teammate without embarrassing them.

payload.snippet: Clara is at swimming training when she realises the swimmer in the next lane has drifted slightly and they accidentally collide heads mid-length.
options: She stops and checks if the other swimmer is okay before continuing.
She pauses for a second and then carries on with her length.
She taps on the lane rope to show she saw the collision and keeps swimming.
She completes her length and raises the collision with the coach afterwards.
payload.explanation: Stopping to check if another person is hurt takes priority over continuing training.

payload.snippet: Ben is competing in a long jump competition when he notices the sand in the landing pit has dried out and hardened on the surface.
options: He tells the official so the pit can be raked and dampened before he jumps.
He lands as lightly as possible and adjusts his technique to avoid compressing the hardened surface.
He skips the landing pit and jumps onto the grass strip beside it instead.
He takes his jump and accepts that a hard landing surface is part of competing.
payload.explanation: Reporting a hazardous landing surface to an official is the correct pre-competition safety check.

payload.snippet: Maya is a goalkeeper who has let in three quick goals and is visibly upset, crouching at the back of the net.
options: The team captain jogs back and gives her an encouraging word before the restart.
The team captain calls from the halfway line to remind her of the defensive formation.
The team captain asks the coach to substitute the goalkeeper before confidence drops further.
The team captain gathers the outfield players for a huddle without including the goalkeeper.
payload.explanation: An in-person encouraging word from a captain is the fastest way to support a rattled goalkeeper.

payload.snippet: Tom is playing tennis when his opponent calls a ball out that Tom is certain was clearly in, and the opponent refuses to replay the point.
options: Tom accepts the call since there is no independent official and plays the next point.
Tom argues his case loudly until his opponent agrees to replay the point.
Tom calls the next close ball of his opponent's out to restore balance.
Tom stops playing and asks a bystander to adjudicate on the disputed point.
payload.explanation: In self-officiated tennis, accepting a disputed call and playing on is the standard sportsmanship expectation.

payload.snippet: Anna is warming up for a race when she notices her left hamstring feels unusually tight and slightly painful when she stretches it.
options: She tells the coach before the race so they can decide together whether to run or withdraw.
She warms up more intensely to loosen the muscle before the race starts.
She says nothing and runs the race as planned, monitoring the pain level.
She withdraws immediately without consulting the coach because any pain before a race means injury risk.
payload.explanation: A pre-race pain signal needs a coach's assessment — running through it risks a full hamstring tear.

payload.snippet: Jake is playing football when a player on the other team gets injured in a challenge and falls to the ground. The ball is loose and Jake could score easily.
options: He kicks the ball out of play so the injured player can receive attention.
He scores the goal and then checks on the injured player.
He waits for the referee to stop play before acting on the ball.
He plays on as the referee has not blown the whistle.
payload.explanation: Kicking the ball out when a player is injured is the standard fair-play convention in football.

payload.snippet: Clara is cycling in a junior road race when she punctures a tyre at a corner, causing her to slide sideways into the roadside barrier. She is bruised but upright.
options: She stays with the bike on the verge, signals to the race marshal, and waits for the support vehicle.
She changes the inner tube herself from her kit bag so she can rejoin the race.
She freewheels on the flat tyre to the nearest checkpoint rather than stopping.
She walks the bike to the finish line carrying it over her shoulder.
payload.explanation: After a crash in a road race, staying visible, signalling the marshal, and waiting for support is the correct safety procedure.

payload.snippet: Oliver is a young tennis coach when a pupil throws his racket in frustration after missing a shot.
options: He stops the session, calmly explains that throwing equipment is dangerous and unacceptable, and resumes once the pupil has settled.
He ignores the throw and moves quickly to the next drill so the pupil's frustration has an outlet.
He ends the session immediately and sends the pupil home.
He asks the pupil to run laps around the court as a consequence for the racket throw.
payload.explanation: Addressing dangerous equipment behaviour calmly and directly before resuming is the correct coaching response.

payload.snippet: Maya is at a swimming competition when she wins a race but then realises she may have swum in the wrong lane on the final length due to misreading the turn.
options: She reports her concern to the officials immediately and accepts whatever ruling they make.
She says nothing, as she is not certain she was in the wrong lane.
She checks with her competitor from the adjacent lane before deciding whether to inform officials.
She waits to see if the officials noticed before deciding whether to raise it herself.
payload.explanation: Self-reporting a potential technical infringement is the correct sportsmanship response — do not wait for the officials to catch it.

payload.snippet: Ben is a young football referee officiating his first match when two players from opposite teams clash and then start arguing aggressively, face to face.
options: He blows his whistle firmly, steps between them, and speaks calmly to each player separately.
He lets the players resolve it themselves and only intervenes if it becomes physical.
He calls both teams' captains over and asks them to separate the players.
He issues a red card to both players immediately to show authority.
payload.explanation: Stepping physically between arguing players and separating them for calm individual conversation de-escalates the situation.

payload.snippet: Anna is in a swimming relay team when the handover touch she gave to the next swimmer comes slightly early, possibly an illegal exchange.
options: She immediately alerts the team captain and they report the possible infringement to the official together.
She says nothing and waits to see if the timekeepers flag the exchange.
She tells only her coach privately so the coach can decide whether to report it.
She waits until after the results are announced to mention the early touch to officials.
payload.explanation: Self-reporting a possible relay infringement immediately is the sportsmanlike action — not waiting for detection.

payload.snippet: Jake is playing in a junior cricket match when rain starts and the outfield becomes wet and slippery. He has the ball and his run-up feels dangerous on the wet crease.
options: He tells the umpire immediately that the run-up is unsafe.
He bowls at reduced pace and adjusts his run-up length to manage the risk.
He bowls normally and hopes the wet conditions do not cause a slip.
He asks the opposing captain to agree to stop play until the crease dries.
payload.explanation: Unsafe playing conditions must be reported to the umpire — it is not the bowler's job to manage the risk alone.

payload.snippet: Clara is coaching a junior athletics session when a child collapses on the track mid-sprint and lies still.
options: She calls 999 immediately, checks for breathing, begins CPR if needed, and sends another adult to meet the ambulance.
She runs to the child, checks their pulse, and calls the child's parents before calling 999.
She drags the child off the track and elevates their legs while she calls the ambulance.
She waits for a minute to see if the child regains consciousness before calling for help.
payload.explanation: A collapsed unresponsive child on a sports field is a 999 emergency — check breathing and begin CPR immediately.

payload.snippet: Maya visits the library and finds the book she wants is already borrowed by someone else.
options: She asks the librarian to place a reservation so she is notified when it is returned.
She removes the borrower's record tag so the system thinks it is available.
She waits by the shelf every day until it appears.
She asks her friend who has a library card to reserve it under their name instead.
payload.explanation: A reservation is the correct and fair way to queue for a borrowed book.

payload.snippet: Tom is reading quietly when a younger child keeps interrupting him to ask what words mean.
options: He patiently answers twice, then suggests the child ask a librarian or use the children's dictionary on the shelf nearby.
He tells the child to go away and find someone else.
He ignores every question and refuses to look up.
He keeps answering every question himself for as long as the child asks.
payload.explanation: Helping briefly and then directing the child to an appropriate resource is kind and practical.

payload.snippet: Clara returns a book and notices the librarian has not scanned it back in correctly and the record still shows it as borrowed to her.
options: She points out the error politely so the librarian can correct it on the system.
She leaves without saying anything and hopes the system fixes itself.
She emails the library later that evening to report it.
She checks the system herself on the public terminal and marks it returned.
payload.explanation: Pointing out the error immediately ensures the record is corrected before a fine is generated.

payload.snippet: Oliver is doing homework in the library when his group of friends arrive and want to chat loudly.
options: He asks them to sit down and keep their voices to a whisper, explaining the library rules.
He gives up on his homework and joins the chat.
He moves to a different table without saying anything to his friends.
He tells the librarian his friends are being disruptive.
payload.explanation: Reminding friends of the rules directly is the first step before escalating to staff.

payload.snippet: Anna's library card is expired. She tries to borrow a book and the system declines it.
options: She speaks to the librarian about renewing her membership before attempting to borrow.
She borrows under her sibling's card without asking the sibling.
She tucks the book inside her bag to read at home and return later.
She asks the librarian to override the system just this once.
payload.explanation: Renewing membership is the correct step when a card expires.

payload.snippet: Jake wants to use the study room but it has been booked by another group. The booking ends in ten minutes.
options: He waits nearby and politely asks the group when they finish whether the room is free for the next hour.
He knocks loudly on the room door and asks the group to hurry up.
He asks the librarian to end the booking early since it is nearly over.
He sits in the corner of the room even though it is not his booking.
payload.explanation: Waiting patiently and asking politely is the correct way to access a shared resource.

payload.snippet: Maya discovers a library computer has been left logged into another user's account.
options: She logs the account out without using it and lets the librarian know.
She uses the computer without logging out the other user.
She reads the open files on the screen out of curiosity.
She logs out the user and logs in with a fake name.
payload.explanation: Logging out someone else's account and notifying staff protects the other user's privacy.

payload.snippet: Tom is reading a library e-book on his card when the borrowing period expires and it is automatically returned, mid-chapter.
options: He waits a short time and re-borrows the title if it is still available, or places a reservation.
He contacts the library IT team to restore his access to the book he was mid-way through.
He borrows the physical copy and skips to the chapter he was reading.
He downloads the e-book illegally to finish it without interruption.
payload.explanation: Re-borrowing or reserving is the correct response to an auto-returned e-book.

payload.snippet: Clara is at the library for a children's reading session when a child next to her starts crying because they cannot find their favourite book on the shelf.
options: She helps the child look for a short time and then suggests they both ask the librarian together.
She tells the child the book must be lost and they should choose a different one.
She goes to the shelf herself and brings back the first book she finds.
She ignores the child and focuses on her own reading.
payload.explanation: Helping briefly and then involving the librarian is the kindest and most effective response.

payload.snippet: Oliver borrows a library book and a page falls out when he opens it at home. He did not notice it in the library.
options: He keeps the page safely and returns both the book and the loose page to the library, explaining what happened.
He tapes the page back in himself with sticky tape.
He returns the book without the page and hopes nobody notices.
He keeps the loose page as a bookmark.
payload.explanation: Returning the book with the loose page and explaining how it happened is the honest response.

payload.snippet: Anna is in the quiet study section when her computer's audio plays unexpectedly through the speakers instead of her headphones.
options: She mutes the computer immediately and checks her headphone connection before continuing.
She quickly closes the video and acts as though it did not happen.
She puts her hand over the speaker until the video ends.
She apologises loudly to the room for the disturbance.
payload.explanation: Muting immediately and correcting the headphone connection is the right practical response.

payload.snippet: Jake sees a shelf of books that has been partially reorganised but left in the wrong section.
options: He mentions it to the librarian so the books can be reshelf correctly.
He reorganises the books himself according to his own logic.
He leaves the books as he found them since it is not his responsibility.
He takes the books that interest him regardless of the wrong section.
payload.explanation: Notifying the librarian ensures books are correctly shelved so others can find them.

payload.snippet: Maya is taking notes from a reference book that cannot be borrowed. She is running out of time before the library closes.
options: She photographs the relevant pages with her phone for her own personal notes, or asks the librarian about the photocopying service.
She borrows the reference book by hiding it in her bag.
She tears the pages out and returns the book.
She asks a friend to pretend they have a different need so she can borrow it.
payload.explanation: Photography for personal notes or using the photocopy service are correct alternatives to borrowing a reference book.

payload.snippet: Tom is walking past the returns slot when a book jams halfway in. He can see it is not fully registered as returned.
options: He alerts the librarian so the book can be retrieved and scanned properly.
He pushes the book hard until it forces through the slot.
He pulls the book back out and borrows it himself since it is not registered.
He walks away since the problem is not his fault.
payload.explanation: Alerting staff to a jammed return slot ensures the borrower is not charged for an unreturned book.

payload.snippet: Clara is using the library printing service when she accidentally prints twenty copies of the wrong document.
options: She apologises to the librarian, pays for the printed pages, and reprints the correct document.
She takes all twenty copies and recycles them at home to avoid paying.
She tells the librarian the printer malfunctioned.
She leaves the twenty copies on the printer tray and prints the correct document on top.
payload.explanation: Owning the mistake and paying for the unintended print job is the honest response.

payload.snippet: Oliver has overdue library books but cannot afford the fines right now.
options: He returns the books, explains his situation to the librarian, and asks whether a payment plan is possible.
He keeps the books until he can pay everything at once.
He returns the books and disputes the fine saying he never received a reminder.
He asks his parent to claim the books are lost so the fine is wiped.
payload.explanation: Returning the books and honestly discussing the situation is better than continuing to accrue fines.

payload.snippet: Anna wants to read an academic journal article available online through the library's database but keeps getting an access error.
options: She asks the librarian to help resolve the access issue rather than finding an unofficial copy online.
She finds a pirated copy of the article on a file-sharing site.
She emails the journal directly and asks them to send her a copy.
She gives up and uses an unrelated article instead.
payload.explanation: The librarian can often resolve database access issues — seeking unofficial copies is a copyright breach.

payload.snippet: Jake is studying in the library when he notices someone has written answers in pencil in the margins of a study guide the library owns.
options: He brings it to the librarian's attention so they can erase the annotations.
He erases the annotations himself and returns the book to the shelf.
He uses the pencilled answers for his own study and says nothing.
He takes a photo of the answers and shares them in his study group chat.
payload.explanation: Notifying the librarian ensures the book is properly restored for future users.

payload.snippet: Maya tries to renew a borrowed book online but the system says it cannot be renewed because someone else has placed a reservation.
options: She returns the book by the original due date so the reserved copy is available for the next borrower.
She keeps the book and returns it when she is finished, ignoring the reservation.
She asks the librarian to cancel the other person's reservation.
She copies the relevant chapters before returning the book.
payload.explanation: When a reservation prevents renewal, the book must be returned on time for the waiting borrower.

payload.snippet: Tom is using the library's 3D printer for a school project when another student says they booked the next slot and Tom is running over time.
options: He stops his print job at a natural pause point, apologises, and arranges with the librarian to complete the job later.
He tells the student they must wait since he arrived first.
He finishes quickly and hopes the time overrun is not noticed.
He asks the librarian to let him continue since his project is more important.
payload.explanation: Respecting booked time slots for shared equipment and arranging a follow-up with staff is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Maya is at her dental check-up when the dentist finds a small cavity that needs filling. Maya is nervous because she has never had a filling before.
options: She asks the dentist to explain what will happen during the filling before they begin.
She tells the dentist not to bother and she will just brush more carefully.
She pretends to agree but plans to cancel the follow-up appointment.
She asks her mum to decide whether to have the filling without listening to the explanation.
payload.explanation: Asking for an explanation helps reduce anxiety and helps you make an informed decision.

payload.snippet: Tom has a wobbly tooth that has been loose for two weeks but has not fallen out. His friend says he should tie a string to it and pull.
options: He waits for the tooth to fall out naturally or asks the dentist at his next check-up.
He ties the string method as his friend suggested.
He stops eating on that side and hopes it falls out in his sleep.
He uses his fingers to force it out since it is nearly ready.
payload.explanation: A nearly-ready tooth will fall out naturally — forcing it risks damaging the gum or root.

payload.snippet: Clara has a dental appointment but feels really unwell with a sore throat and a fever that morning.
options: She calls the dental practice to reschedule, explaining she is unwell.
She goes anyway since she does not want to wait for another appointment.
She goes and does not mention she feels unwell.
She sends her older brother in her place.
payload.explanation: Attending a dental appointment while unwell with a fever risks spreading illness to other patients and staff.

payload.snippet: Oliver is at the dentist when the dentist says she is going to use a new type of filling material for the first time on him.
options: He asks whether this material is safe and what the differences are from the usual type.
He agrees without asking any questions because the dentist must know best.
He refuses to have the new material and insists on the old type.
He says yes but texts his mum from the chair to ask her opinion mid-procedure.
payload.explanation: Asking about a new procedure or material is your right as a patient and helps you give informed consent.

payload.snippet: Anna's school has a dental hygiene talk and the hygienist recommends an electric toothbrush. Anna's family cannot afford one.
options: She asks the hygienist whether a manual toothbrush with the right technique is just as effective.
She tells everyone at school her parents are too cheap to buy an electric brush.
She takes a disposable toothbrush from the display stand without asking.
She stops brushing as well since she cannot achieve the same clean.
payload.explanation: Asking about technique with a manual toothbrush is practical and evidence-based — correct technique matters more than brush type.

payload.snippet: Jake is having a tooth extracted when he suddenly feels pain and raises his hand to signal discomfort.
options: The dentist stops immediately and asks what Jake is feeling before continuing.
The dentist acknowledges the hand signal but continues since the procedure is almost done.
The dentist stops and immediately gives more anaesthetic without asking where it hurts.
The dentist tells Jake to keep his hand down as it makes the procedure harder.
payload.explanation: A hand signal indicating pain means the dentist must stop and assess before proceeding — continuing is not acceptable.

payload.snippet: Maya is brushing her teeth and notices a small lump on her gum that has not been there before.
options: She tells her parent and asks to see the dentist soon to have it checked.
She ignores it because it does not hurt.
She pokes it repeatedly to see if it gets bigger.
She searches online for what it could be and self-diagnoses.
payload.explanation: New lumps in the mouth should be checked by a dentist promptly — ignoring or self-diagnosing can delay necessary treatment.

payload.snippet: Tom is at the dentist for a routine clean when the hygienist says his gum health has improved significantly since his last visit.
options: He asks what has changed about his brushing technique or diet that has made the difference, to understand what is working.
He assumes it is just random chance and continues exactly as before.
He tells the hygienist he has not changed anything and does not think it is related to him.
He asks the hygienist to write on his record that it improved so his parents stop reminding him to floss.
payload.explanation: Understanding what has worked helps reinforce good habits and maintain the improvement.

payload.snippet: Clara watches her dentist take an X-ray of her teeth without explaining why. Clara is not sure what an X-ray shows and whether it is necessary.
options: She asks the dentist what the X-ray is for and whether it is a routine part of her check-up.
She says nothing since the dentist must have a good reason.
She refuses the X-ray until the dentist writes down that it was her idea.
She asks her parent to step in and question the dentist on her behalf.
payload.explanation: Patients have the right to understand why any procedure is being performed — asking is appropriate and normal.

payload.snippet: Oliver keeps forgetting to floss even though the hygienist reminds him every visit. He genuinely wants to improve but always forgets at home.
options: He asks the hygienist for a practical suggestion, such as keeping floss near something he does every day.
He tells the hygienist he flosses regularly to avoid another lecture.
He buys expensive floss hoping that will motivate him to use it.
He decides flossing is not necessary since his teeth are not sore.
payload.explanation: Asking for a practical habit tip is more effective than intention alone — habit-stacking (attaching a new habit to an existing one) is a well-supported approach.

payload.snippet: Anna needs a dental procedure that requires local anaesthetic. She has never had an injection in her gum before and is very frightened.
options: She tells the dentist she is nervous about the injection and asks what it will feel like.
She tells the dentist she does not need anaesthetic since she wants to get it over with quickly.
She closes her eyes and pretends she is somewhere else without telling the dentist she is frightened.
She asks if the procedure can be done without anaesthetic to avoid the needle.
payload.explanation: Telling the dentist you are nervous about an injection allows them to explain and use methods to reduce discomfort.

payload.snippet: Jake is at the dentist when the receptionist asks for his date of birth and address to update the records. Jake does not know his full postcode.
options: He gives the information he knows and asks the receptionist to confirm the rest with his parent.
He guesses the postcode and hopes it is correct.
He gives a wrong date of birth since he is embarrassed not to know.
He refuses to give any personal information.
payload.explanation: Providing accurate patient information helps the practice contact you and match your records correctly.

payload.snippet: Maya is visiting a new dentist for the first time. The new dentist's approach feels different and less gentle than her old one.
options: She lets the dentist know her previous experience was gentler and asks whether the same outcome can be achieved more gently.
She suffers through without saying anything because she does not want to seem difficult.
She leaves mid-appointment and refuses to continue.
She asks her parent to complain on her behalf after the appointment.
payload.explanation: Communicating your preferences and previous experience directly is a patient right — the dentist can often adjust their approach.

payload.snippet: Tom sees a list of dental treatment costs at reception and realises the filling he needs is more expensive than he expected. His family has a limited budget.
options: He asks the receptionist whether the practice offers a payment plan or whether the treatment might be available under NHS rates.
He cancels the treatment appointment rather than have a conversation about cost.
He asks for a private quote from three different dental practices before making any decisions.
He tells his parent to pay whatever it costs since it is his health.
payload.explanation: Asking about payment plans or NHS eligibility before cancelling treatment is the right practical step when cost is a concern.

payload.snippet: Clara has been advised to wear a retainer after orthodontic treatment. After a week she stops wearing it because it is uncomfortable.
options: She calls the orthodontist and tells them the retainer is uncomfortable, asking whether it needs adjusting.
She stops wearing it entirely since no one will check.
She bends the retainer slightly herself to make it fit better.
She tells the orthodontist she is wearing it as instructed when asked at her review.
payload.explanation: Discomfort with a retainer often means it needs adjusting — reporting it prevents teeth from moving back.

payload.snippet: Oliver is at his dental check-up and the dentist recommends a treatment he has read negative reviews about online.
options: He tells the dentist he has read some concerns and asks for the evidence basis for the recommendation.
He refuses the treatment immediately based on the online reviews.
He accepts the treatment but researches an alternative dentist afterwards.
He asks his mum to read the reviews and decide on his behalf.
payload.explanation: Discussing concerns with your dentist and asking for their evidence basis allows you to make an informed decision rather than acting on unverified reviews.

payload.snippet: Anna notices after her check-up that the dentist has put notes on her record that she has not seen before. She wants to know what is written.
options: She politely asks the dentist or receptionist what was noted from her appointment.
She tries to read the screen upside down without asking.
She asks a friend who works there to look at her notes unofficially.
She decides it is none of her business.
payload.explanation: Patients have the right to ask about and access their own medical records — asking directly is the correct approach.

payload.snippet: Jake is due a wisdom tooth extraction. The oral surgeon recommends removing all four at once under general anaesthetic, but his dentist had suggested waiting to see if they cause problems.
options: He asks both practitioners to explain their reasoning so he can understand the different approaches before making a decision.
He goes with the surgeon's advice since they are the specialist.
He chooses his dentist's view since they have known him longer.
He postpones any decision indefinitely to avoid having to choose.
payload.explanation: When two clinicians give different advice, understanding each practitioner's reasoning allows an informed patient decision.

payload.snippet: Maya drinks fizzy drinks every day. At her check-up the dentist points out early enamel erosion linked to acid exposure.
options: She asks the dentist what specific changes to her diet or drinking habits would have the biggest impact on slowing the erosion.
She resolves to cut out all sugar entirely from her diet.
She tells the dentist she will try to cut down but does not ask what is most important.
She decides to start using a straw and assumes that is sufficient.
payload.explanation: Asking for specific, high-impact dietary advice focuses your effort on the most effective change.

payload.snippet: Tom has a check-up and the dentist says everything looks fine. However, he has noticed that one tooth sometimes aches when he eats something cold.
options: He mentions the cold sensitivity even though the dentist did not bring it up.
He says nothing since the dentist said everything is fine.
He assumes it is just normal and reduces how much cold food he eats.
He waits until the next appointment to mention it if it happens again.
payload.explanation: Cold sensitivity that your dentist has not noticed should be raised — it may indicate an issue not yet visible on examination.

payload.snippet: Clara is invited to her best friend's birthday party on the same day as a family event her parents have already planned.
options: She tells her friend honestly and apologises, and suggests they celebrate together another day.
She tells her parents the party is more important and refuses to attend the family event.
She attends both for a short time without telling either group she is splitting her time.
She simply does not reply to the party invitation to avoid disappointing anyone.
payload.explanation: Honest communication with your friend and offering an alternative celebration is the respectful response to a scheduling clash.

payload.snippet: Oliver is organising a birthday party and one guest has a severe nut allergy. The birthday cake his mum has already ordered contains nuts.
options: He tells his mum about the allergy and asks whether the cake can be exchanged or whether an allergy-safe alternative can be found for that guest.
He tells the guest they can just avoid the cake.
He does not mention the allergy since the guest should tell hosts themselves.
He cancels the party to avoid the risk.
payload.explanation: Flagging a known allergy to the organising adult is a safety responsibility — telling the guest to avoid the food is not a safe solution.

payload.snippet: Anna is at a friend's birthday party when she notices a younger child in the garden is playing near a gate that is not properly latched and leads to the road.
options: She tells an adult at the party immediately.
She calls the child away from the gate herself and continues playing.
She closes the gate herself and tells the child to be careful.
She watches the child to make sure they do not open the gate.
payload.explanation: A road safety hazard involving a young child must be reported to an adult — watching or managing it yourself is not sufficient.

payload.snippet: Jake's birthday party invitation says to arrive at 3pm. He arrives at 2:45 and the hosts are still setting up.
options: He offers to help set up and waits cheerfully.
He asks why the decorations are not ready yet.
He demands his friend comes outside to play immediately.
He goes home and comes back at 3pm on the dot.
payload.explanation: Offering to help when you arrive early is considerate — the host is still preparing.

payload.snippet: Maya's birthday present budget is very small this year. Her friend's party invitation mentions a specific expensive gift on the wishlist.
options: She buys a thoughtful affordable alternative and writes a warm card explaining her choice.
She does not attend the party since she cannot afford the requested gift.
She asks another guest to combine on the expensive gift and contributes only what she can.
She gives nothing but attends the party.
payload.explanation: A thoughtful affordable gift with a warm card is a perfectly appropriate alternative to a wishlist item beyond your budget.

payload.snippet: Tom receives a birthday gift in the wrong size from a relative who lives far away and cannot easily exchange it.
options: He writes a thank-you note expressing genuine gratitude for the thought and asks his parent whether an exchange is worth pursuing.
He contacts the relative directly to say the size is wrong and ask for a replacement.
He gives the item away without telling the relative.
He says nothing to his parent and keeps the ill-fitting item in the drawer.
payload.explanation: Gratitude first, then a practical conversation with a parent about exchange — contacting the giver directly about a size issue can feel ungrateful.

payload.snippet: Clara is at a birthday party where one activity involves fast running. A guest has a bandaged sprained ankle from earlier in the week.
options: She suggests to the host that the activity could be adapted so the injured guest can take part.
She tells the injured guest they should just watch that game.
She asks the host to cancel the running activity entirely.
She ignores the situation and plays the game as planned.
payload.explanation: Suggesting an adaptation is more inclusive than exclusion or cancellation.

payload.snippet: Oliver's birthday party is at a trampoline park. One friend arrives who is too tall for the recommended height limit by a small amount.
options: He tells a member of trampoline park staff and asks for guidance.
He tells his friend it should be fine since the limit is just a guideline.
He pays extra for a different area of the park where the limit does not apply.
He tells his friend to crouch when passing the staff member.
payload.explanation: Height and weight limits at activity venues are safety guidelines — staff must be consulted, not bypassed.

payload.snippet: Anna is blowing out her birthday candles when she accidentally spits on the cake.
options: She laughs it off, apologises to the guests, and asks if anyone minds before cutting the cake.
She cuts the cake immediately before anyone notices.
She pretends it did not happen.
She asks her mum to order a new cake.
payload.explanation: Acknowledging what happened and checking in with guests before serving is the honest and considerate response.

payload.snippet: Jake's parents have thrown him a surprise party, but he had already guessed it was happening. He acts completely surprised.
options: He keeps up the act warmly to honour the effort his parents put in.
He tells his parents immediately that he already knew.
He acts surprised for the first few minutes but then admits he guessed.
He tells his friends at the party that he had figured it out.
payload.explanation: Honouring a surprise party even when you know about it is a kindness — your parents' effort deserves a genuine-feeling reaction.

payload.snippet: Maya is having her birthday dinner at a restaurant when she realises one friend in the group has been left out of the conversation for most of the meal.
options: She steers the conversation to include her friend and asks them a question to bring them in.
She waits to mention it to the friend privately after dinner.
She asks everyone to stop talking so her friend can speak.
She ignores it since it is her birthday and she cannot manage everyone.
payload.explanation: Gently steering the conversation to include a quiet guest is the kind and practical response.

payload.snippet: Tom's birthday falls on a school day. He wants to bring cupcakes for his class but the school has a no-food-sharing policy.
options: He asks his teacher in advance whether an exception can be made or whether there is an alternative way to celebrate.
He brings the cupcakes anyway since it is a special occasion.
He distributes them quietly at break time where teachers cannot see.
He gives up on the idea without asking.
payload.explanation: Checking school policy before bringing food prevents embarrassment and respects the rules — asking for an exception is fine.

payload.snippet: Clara is at a party where a game results in one child winning every round and the others getting increasingly frustrated.
options: She suggests changing to a different game that gives everyone more of a chance.
She tells the winning child to let others win.
She tells the frustrated children to stop being sore losers.
She quits the game herself to make a point.
payload.explanation: Suggesting a game change is a constructive way to address growing frustration at a party.

payload.snippet: Oliver receives birthday money from a relative and his parents say he must save half. He disagrees.
options: He listens to their reasoning and accepts the decision, even if he is disappointed.
He spends the money before his parents find out.
He argues until his parents back down.
He hides some of it to spend later.
payload.explanation: Accepting parental financial guidance, even when you disagree, is part of responsible growing up.

payload.snippet: Anna is planning her birthday party when she realises the date clashes with a religious holiday that means one of her closest friends cannot attend.
options: She checks with her friend and moves the party date if possible, or finds a way to celebrate separately with that friend.
She keeps the date since she has already sent invitations.
She tells her friend they can celebrate together another time without rescheduling.
She moves the party date without checking whether the new date works for others.
payload.explanation: Checking with the affected friend before rescheduling shows consideration — keeping the date or assuming another time will work both miss the mark.

payload.snippet: Jake is at a friend's party when a game goes wrong and a friend is accidentally hit by a thrown object and starts crying.
options: He stops the game and checks on his friend, and tells an adult if the friend is hurt.
He continues the game since it was an accident and his friend will be fine.
He apologises once and carries on playing.
He blames the child who threw the object.
payload.explanation: Stopping play to check on someone who is hurt is the immediate right response.

payload.snippet: Maya has been planning her birthday for weeks when she discovers her best friend has arranged a birthday party on the same date for a shared friendship group.
options: She speaks to her friend directly and kindly to discuss whether either party can be rescheduled.
She moves her party date without telling her friend.
She sends a competing party invitation on the same day.
She cancels her own party because her friend got there first.
payload.explanation: A direct, kind conversation is the right way to resolve a scheduling conflict between friends.

payload.snippet: Tom's birthday wish is to go to a theme park, but the entry cost would stretch the family budget uncomfortably.
options: He accepts his parents' suggestion of a more affordable alternative and thanks them for making the effort.
He tells his parents he will not have a birthday this year if they cannot afford the theme park.
He asks all his relatives to contribute to the entry cost without his parents knowing.
He sulks until his parents agree to find the money.
payload.explanation: Accepting a thoughtful affordable alternative and expressing gratitude is the mature and considerate response.

payload.snippet: Clara brings a birthday gift to a friend's party and then discovers when she arrives that it is actually not a gift-giving party.
options: She puts the gift aside and gives it to her friend privately after the party.
She gives the gift publicly and apologises for not knowing the convention.
She takes the gift home without explaining.
She asks the host whether it is okay to give the gift.
payload.explanation: Giving the gift privately avoids embarrassing either the friend or the other guests who did not bring gifts.

payload.snippet: Oliver's birthday party has a theme and one friend arrives without dressing up. Other children comment on it.
options: He welcomes his friend warmly and tells the group the theme is optional.
He tells his friend they should have dressed up.
He lends his friend a costume piece from the dress-up box.
He says nothing and lets his other guests continue commenting.
payload.explanation: Welcoming a guest and publicly relieving the pressure is the kind and hosting-appropriate response.

payload.snippet: Maya and her family arrive at the campsite after dark. Her dad is struggling to put up the tent in the dim light.
options: She holds the torch steadily to give him a clear view of what he is doing.
She plays with the torch beam to entertain herself.
She holds the torch but keeps moving it to look around.
She tells her dad to wait until morning to put the tent up.
payload.explanation: Holding the torch steadily where it is needed is a practical and helpful contribution.

payload.snippet: Tom is camping when he notices the campfire smoke keeps blowing into the food preparation area because of the wind direction.
options: He tells the campsite warden and asks whether the fire can be moved or the food area set up on the other side.
He fans the smoke away himself while everyone cooks.
He tells everyone to hold their breath while preparing food.
He puts the fire out since it is causing problems.
payload.explanation: Identifying the cause and asking for an appropriate fix is the correct practical response.

payload.snippet: Clara is packing away the campsite when she finds a used battery on the ground near the fire pit.
options: She picks it up carefully and places it in a separate waste bag to be recycled at an appropriate facility.
She throws it into the fire pit to get rid of it.
She leaves it since she did not drop it.
She puts it in the general rubbish bag.
payload.explanation: Batteries contain harmful chemicals — they must not go in general rubbish or be burned.

payload.snippet: Oliver is on a camping trip when he wakes up needing the toilet but the shared toilet block is a five-minute walk away and it is raining.
options: He gets dressed, puts on his rain jacket, and makes the walk.
He uses a corner of the campsite rather than walk in the rain.
He holds it until morning and hopes for the best.
He wakes his tent-mate to go with him.
payload.explanation: Using the designated toilet facilities, even inconveniently, is the respectful and hygienic choice.

payload.snippet: Anna is camping with her class when a classmate who is usually confident begins shaking and says she does not want to sleep in the tent because she is scared.
options: She sits with her classmate, listens without teasing, and suggests they tell a teacher so they can decide together what to do.
She tells her classmate to be brave since it is only one night.
She tells the rest of the group so everyone can help.
She offers to swap sleeping spots since she is less scared.
payload.explanation: Listening without teasing and involving a teacher to find a solution is the caring and practical response.

payload.snippet: Jake is helping cook on a camp stove when the flame goes out unexpectedly. He can smell gas.
options: He moves away from the stove immediately, does not relight it, and tells the adult in charge.
He tries to relight the stove straight away since the food is still cooking.
He checks under the stove to see what happened.
He opens the gas canister to check whether gas is flowing.
payload.explanation: A gas smell after flame-out is a safety emergency — do not relight and tell an adult immediately.

payload.snippet: Maya's sleeping bag gets wet from condensation during the night. She is cold and uncomfortable.
options: She tells her parent at first light and asks for a spare blanket or dry layer while the sleeping bag is aired.
She puts the sleeping bag in the direct sun without telling anyone, hoping it dries before tonight.
She says nothing and tries to sleep through the next night in the damp bag.
She turns the bag inside out and gets back in straight away.
payload.explanation: Reporting the wet bag and asking for a dry alternative ensures you stay warm — putting a damp bag in direct sun without adult awareness is not a reliable fix.

payload.snippet: Tom is walking a trail at the campsite when a sign says the path ahead is temporarily closed for conservation work.
options: He turns back and follows the alternative route marked on his map.
He continues on the closed path since he can see it is usable.
He looks for a way around the barriers.
He asks a passing walker to accompany him past the sign.
payload.explanation: Conservation closures must be respected — the path closure is for ecological, not purely physical, reasons.

payload.snippet: Clara is collecting firewood when she notices the wood pile contains several pieces with a bright orange fungal growth on them.
options: She tells the adult in charge and does not use the affected wood.
She uses the wood since fire will kill the fungus.
She uses the unaffected pieces from the same pile since the fungus only covers some of them.
She removes the fungal pieces and uses the rest without telling anyone.
payload.explanation: Infected or fungus-covered wood should be reported — burning it spreads spores and is not a safe solution.

payload.snippet: Oliver is at a family campsite when he notices a younger child from another pitch is eating berries they have picked from a bush near the treeline.
options: He tells a nearby adult from the child's family immediately.
He tells the child the berries might be poisonous.
He asks the child to show him the bush so he can check what kind they are.
He takes the berries away from the child.
payload.explanation: A young child eating unidentified berries is a safety emergency — the nearest responsible adult must be alerted immediately.

payload.snippet: Anna has forgotten her sunscreen on a sunny camping trip. There is one other bottle in the group.
options: She asks if she can borrow some, uses a small amount, and makes sure there is enough left for others.
She uses as much of the shared bottle as she normally would.
She stays in the shade all day without telling anyone why.
She asks her parent to drive to a shop during the trip to buy more.
payload.explanation: Using a sensible amount of shared resources and leaving enough for others is the considerate approach.

payload.snippet: Jake finds a bird that appears injured on the path near the campsite.
options: He keeps his distance, marks the spot, and tells the campsite warden.
He tries to pick up the bird and carry it to a safer place.
He stands guard over the bird until it recovers.
He leaves it and continues his walk without telling anyone.
payload.explanation: Injured wildlife should be reported to the warden — handling it may injure the bird further and handling wild birds is not safe.

payload.snippet: Maya's family is barbecuing when the charcoal takes a long time to light. Her brother suggests using petrol to speed it up.
options: She says she does not think that is safe and suggests asking a parent before trying anything.
She goes along with the idea since her brother is older.
She tries it herself since petrol is faster.
She lights more firelighters instead without saying anything.
payload.explanation: Petrol near a barbecue is a serious fire and explosion risk — stopping to ask an adult is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Tom wakes up and finds water pooling inside the bottom of the tent after heavy rain.
options: He wakes his parent, moves his sleeping bag and belongings off the wet groundsheet, and waits for adult guidance on next steps.
He tries to re-pitch the tent himself in the rain.
He soaks up the water with his sleeping bag.
He moves to the car without telling his parent.
payload.explanation: Waking the adult and moving belongings away from the water while waiting for guidance is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Clara is on a guided nature walk when the guide asks the group not to touch any plants they do not recognise.
options: She follows the instruction and asks the guide about any plant that interests her.
She touches a leaf of a plant she thinks she knows.
She asks another child what a plant is before touching it.
She waits until the guide's back is turned before examining an interesting plant.
payload.explanation: Following the guide's instruction and asking if curious is the safe and respectful approach.

payload.snippet: Oliver is at a campsite with rules about quiet time after 10pm. His family's neighbours are still playing music at 11pm.
options: His parent speaks politely to the neighbouring campers to let them know about the quiet time rule.
He goes and tells the neighbours himself to be quiet.
He turns up his own music to make a point.
He calls the campsite warden without first speaking to the neighbours.
payload.explanation: A polite word from an adult to the neighbouring campers is the proportionate first step — escalating to the warden comes if that fails.

payload.snippet: Anna's group loses signal on their phones during a walk and the map app stops loading.
options: She tells the group leader and suggests they follow the last saved map direction until signal is restored.
She keeps walking in the direction she thinks is correct.
She climbs a nearby hill to try to get a signal.
She tells the group they are lost and should call for help.
payload.explanation: Telling the group leader and using the last known information calmly is the correct response when technology fails on a walk.

payload.snippet: Jake notices the campfire has been left with glowing embers when everyone goes to sleep.
options: He wakes a parent and tells them the fire is not fully out.
He pours water on it himself.
He puts soil on top and goes back to sleep.
He leaves it since glowing embers are normal.
payload.explanation: An unextinguished campfire must be fully put out — waking an adult to do this correctly is the safe approach.

payload.snippet: Maya finds a tick attached to her leg during a camping trip.
options: She tells an adult immediately without trying to remove it herself.
She pulls it off with her fingers.
She burns it off with a match.
She covers it with Vaseline and waits.
payload.explanation: Ticks must be removed correctly with a special tool — improper removal increases infection risk.

payload.snippet: Tom's camping group is crossing a shallow stream when one child slips and gets completely soaked.
options: He helps the child to the bank and calls the group leader immediately.
He laughs and helps the child out without telling anyone.
He tells the child to walk quickly so they dry off faster.
He continues the walk and leaves the group leader to notice.
payload.explanation: A soaked child in outdoor conditions needs adult attention immediately for warmth and safety assessment.

payload.snippet: Clara is tidying her room when she finds a broken glass she did not know about under the bed.
options: She leaves it where it is and tells a parent immediately so they can clear it up safely.
She tries to pick it up with her hands.
She sweeps it away with her foot.
She covers it with a sock and ignores it.
payload.explanation: Broken glass is a safety hazard — an adult must be told so it can be cleared up correctly.

payload.snippet: Oliver is cleaning his room when he finds a library book that has been missing for a week.
options: He puts it aside to return to the library and checks whether any fine has accumulated.
He hides it under a new pile of clothes.
He returns it without telling his parent about the fine.
He leaves it where he found it since he has already given up on finding it.
payload.explanation: Finding an overdue library book means returning it promptly and being honest about any fine.

payload.snippet: Anna is asked to tidy her room before her friend arrives in an hour. The room is very messy.
options: She prioritises the areas her friend will see and sorts items quickly, leaving a deeper tidy for later.
She pushes everything under the bed and into the wardrobe.
She tells her friend her room is clean and blocks the door.
She cancels the visit since the room is too messy to fix in time.
payload.explanation: Prioritising key areas and planning a fuller tidy later is a practical and honest approach.

payload.snippet: Jake is organising his desk when he finds some homework he forgot to hand in last week.
options: He tells his teacher the next day, explains it was lost in a messy room, and hands it in.
He throws it away since it is too late to hand in.
He puts a different date on it and hands it in quietly.
He hides it again and hopes the teacher forgot to chase it.
payload.explanation: Being honest about late work — even when it is your own fault — is better than deception or avoidance.

payload.snippet: Maya is decluttering her room when she finds toys she no longer uses that are still in good condition.
options: She asks her parent if they can be donated to a charity or passed on to younger children.
She throws them in the bin since she does not want them anymore.
She keeps them all since she might want them later.
She sells them at school without telling her parent.
payload.explanation: Donating or passing on still-usable toys is a good way to declutter and help others.

payload.snippet: Tom's room has a very strong smell. He cannot find the source after a quick look.
options: He does a more thorough search including under the bed and behind the wardrobe.
He opens the window and ignores the smell.
He sprays air freshener and considers it handled.
He tells his parent the room smells but it is not his fault.
payload.explanation: A persistent smell requires a proper search — masking it with freshener does not solve the problem.

payload.snippet: Clara is cleaning her room with her music on loud when her sibling knocks and asks her to turn it down.
options: She turns it down or uses headphones and continues tidying.
She ignores the knocking.
She turns it up louder to show it is her room.
She opens the door and argues.
payload.explanation: Considering others in a shared home by adjusting your volume is considerate.

payload.snippet: Oliver is supposed to tidy his room but instead organises one small drawer for twenty minutes and declares the room tidy.
options: He recognises he is avoiding the harder work and makes a proper start on the rest of the room.
He tells his parent the room is done.
He takes a break and promises to do more later.
He tidies only the areas his parent checks.
payload.explanation: Avoiding the harder parts of a task while appearing productive is not the same as completing the task.

payload.snippet: Anna is cleaning her room and finds a friend's belonging she borrowed three months ago and forgot about.
options: She contacts her friend, apologises, and arranges to return it soon.
She keeps it since the friend has probably forgotten.
She hides it more carefully so the friend cannot ask for it.
She returns it without apologising.
payload.explanation: Returning a borrowed item promptly and apologising for the delay is the honest and respectful response.

payload.snippet: Jake tidies his room very quickly before a chore check and hides several items in his wardrobe without organising them.
options: He acknowledges to himself that the wardrobe still needs sorting and plans to do it properly when he has more time.
He tells his parent the room is fully tidy.
He locks the wardrobe so no one can check.
He forgets about the wardrobe and never returns to it.
payload.explanation: Acknowledging that a hidden mess is not truly tidy — and planning to address it — is honest self-awareness.

payload.snippet: Maya is asked to help clean a shared room but her sibling refuses to help and leaves Maya to do everything.
options: She does her share of the shared space and tells a parent that her sibling is not participating.
She refuses to clean anything until her sibling helps.
She does the whole room herself and says nothing.
She makes her sibling's area even messier in protest.
payload.explanation: Doing your share and involving a parent to address unequal participation is the fair response.

payload.snippet: Tom finds a bag of coins while tidying that he does not recognise. He thinks they might belong to his sibling.
options: He puts them somewhere safe and asks his sibling if they are theirs.
He keeps them since he found them in his room.
He puts them in his piggy bank before asking.
He spends them and hopes his sibling does not ask.
payload.explanation: Finding items that might belong to someone else requires checking before claiming them.

payload.snippet: Clara realises she has been putting off tidying her room for two weeks and it has become overwhelming.
options: She breaks the task into small sections — one area at a time — and starts with the easiest part.
She gives up since it is too much to do.
She asks her parent to do it for her.
She tidies the entire room in one go even if it takes the whole day.
payload.explanation: Breaking an overwhelming task into manageable sections is a practical and effective strategy.

payload.snippet: Oliver is tidying his room when he finds a gift he was given but never used and does not like.
options: He puts it away neatly and considers whether it could be donated without hurting the giver's feelings.
He throws it in the bin.
He gives it to a friend directly without asking his parent.
He leaves it out where the giver can see he has used it when they visit.
payload.explanation: Donating an unused gift thoughtfully — and with parental guidance — is kinder than throwing it away.

payload.snippet: Anna is cleaning and finds a note from a friend that she had kept but now wants to throw away.
options: She decides whether it holds personal value before putting it in the bin.
She leaves all notes everywhere in case they matter later.
She keeps every note without reading them.
She shows the note to her sibling before deciding.
payload.explanation: Deciding what has personal value before discarding notes is a good habit when decluttering.

payload.snippet: Jake is asked to tidy his room by a specific time. He does not finish in time.
options: He tells his parent honestly that he ran out of time and asks for a short extension.
He pretends he is finished when his parent checks.
He hides the remaining mess under the bed.
He blames his sibling for distracting him.
payload.explanation: Honest communication about not finishing — rather than hiding the mess — is the mature response.

payload.snippet: Maya finds her sister's toy in her room and realises she had borrowed it and forgotten to return it.
options: She returns it and apologises.
She puts it in the charity bag since she does not use it.
She denies knowing anything about it if asked.
She puts it back in her room but in a hidden place.
payload.explanation: Returning what you borrowed and apologising for not returning it sooner is the right thing to do.

payload.snippet: Tom is cleaning and finds some money on the floor — he is not sure if it is his.
options: He puts it in a safe place and asks the family if anyone is missing money.
He keeps it since he found it in his own room.
He puts it in a family pot without asking.
He spends it and tells no one.
payload.explanation: Even money found in your own room could belong to a visitor or sibling — checking first is honest.

payload.snippet: Clara is supposed to clean her room but asks her younger sibling to do it for her in exchange for a sweet.
options: She reconsiders and does her own room — it is her responsibility.
She lets the younger sibling do it and gives them the sweet.
She lets the sibling start and then takes over when her parent comes.
She pays the sibling but tells her parent she cleaned it herself.
payload.explanation: Your own chores are your own responsibility — using a younger sibling as a substitute is not fair.

payload.snippet: Oliver does a thorough tidy of his room and is proud of the result. His parent asks him to do it again the following week.
options: He maintains the standard he reached and starts the next week's tidy from a much easier starting point.
He is annoyed since it was already clean.
He tidies only the parts that got messy again.
He refuses since he just did it.
payload.explanation: Maintaining a clean room makes each subsequent tidy much easier.

payload.snippet: Clara is doing a homework project and realises she has copied a whole paragraph from a website without changing anything.
options: She rewrites the paragraph in her own words and cites the website as a source.
She submits the paragraph as written since she found the information herself.
She changes a few words so it looks different.
She deletes the paragraph and leaves that section blank.
payload.explanation: Rewriting in your own words and citing the source avoids plagiarism — minor word changes do not.

payload.snippet: Oliver has three pieces of homework due the same day. He leaves them all to the night before.
options: He works out which will take longest and starts with that one, completing as much as possible before bed.
He picks the easiest one and submits only that, hoping teachers forget the others.
He copies his friend's answers for the two he runs out of time for.
He stays up all night to finish everything.
payload.explanation: Prioritising by effort required and working through as much as possible is more effective than avoidance or copying.

payload.snippet: Anna is asked to research a topic for homework and the first website she finds has information that contradicts her textbook.
options: She checks two or three additional sources to see which version is supported by most reliable evidence.
She uses the website since it came up first in the search.
She uses the textbook since teachers provided it.
She includes both versions and lets the teacher decide which is correct.
payload.explanation: Cross-checking multiple sources is the correct research method when information conflicts.

payload.snippet: Jake has been given a reading homework but discovers he has left his reading book at school. The assignment is due tomorrow.
options: He emails his teacher that evening to explain and asks if there is a digital version available, or if he can complete it the next day.
He invents a summary of what he thinks the pages probably contain.
He copies a review of the book from online and submits it.
He tells the teacher he finished the reading, having not done it.
payload.explanation: Honest communication about a missing resource — with a request for an alternative or extension — is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Maya is given a maths homework sheet but half the questions seem to relate to content her class has not yet been taught.
options: She completes the questions she can, leaves the others blank, and notes for her teacher that she was not sure about those sections.
She guesses the answers for the unfamiliar questions.
She copies answers from an online homework helper site.
She asks her parent to complete the unfamiliar sections.
payload.explanation: Completing what you can and flagging confusion honestly is the correct response to homework beyond your current understanding.

payload.snippet: Tom has a homework deadline at 8am and at 7:30am he spots a significant error in his submitted work.
options: He sends a quick correction to his teacher explaining the error before the deadline if possible.
He says nothing and hopes the teacher marks it as correct.
He resubmits a new version without informing the teacher.
He deletes the submission and resubmits as if the error never existed.
payload.explanation: Proactively notifying a teacher of a spotted error — before or just after a deadline — demonstrates honesty and responsibility.

payload.snippet: Clara is given a homework extension by her teacher. She uses the extra time to do a much more thorough job than she would have done originally.
options: She submits the improved work and thanks the teacher for the extension.
She does only slightly more than she originally submitted.
She submits the same work she would have done anyway.
She asks for another extension since she wants to improve it further.
payload.explanation: Using extra time productively and acknowledging the teacher's flexibility is the mature and respectful response.

payload.snippet: Oliver's parent offers to check his homework and suggests significant changes to the answers.
options: He considers the suggestions but makes sure the submitted work reflects his own understanding rather than his parent's answers.
He copies all his parent's suggestions directly since they must be correct.
He ignores the suggestions to avoid getting help.
He thanks his parent but does not change anything regardless of whether the suggestions are useful.
payload.explanation: Using suggestions to understand — and then writing in your own words — is the right use of parental help.

payload.snippet: Anna has been ill for a week and comes back to school with several pieces of missed homework to catch up on alongside current work.
options: She talks to each teacher about what she missed and agrees a realistic catch-up schedule.
She does as much as she can without talking to teachers and hopes no one notices the gaps.
She prioritises only the subjects she likes and ignores the rest.
She asks her friends to summarise the missed content for her to save time.
payload.explanation: Communicating with teachers about illness-related missed work and agreeing a structured catch-up is the professional and effective approach.

payload.snippet: Jake is given a creative writing homework and is completely stuck on ideas.
options: He uses a simple brainstorm method — jotting random words and images until something sparks — before starting to write.
He submits a very short piece because he had no ideas.
He copies the plot of a book he has read recently.
He asks a parent or sibling to come up with the story idea for him.
payload.explanation: A brainstorm gives you a starting point even when you feel blank — using someone else's idea is not your own creative work.

payload.snippet: Maya has a long-term project due in three weeks. She plans to start in the final few days.
options: She reconsiders and sets a plan to do a small amount each day so she is not overwhelmed at the end.
She sticks to her original plan since the deadline is still far away.
She asks her teacher to extend the deadline in advance just in case.
She asks a friend to share their completed project so she can see how to structure it.
payload.explanation: Starting a long-term project in stages from the beginning produces better work and avoids last-minute stress.

payload.snippet: Tom receives back a graded homework with a low mark and comments he does not understand.
options: He asks the teacher after class to explain the comments so he knows how to improve.
He ignores the comments and moves on.
He argues with the teacher about the mark.
He asks his parent to email the teacher about the mark.
payload.explanation: Asking a teacher to explain feedback — rather than arguing or ignoring it — is the most useful response to a low mark.

payload.snippet: Clara is doing group homework online when she notices one member has been contributing very little while others do the majority of the work.
options: She mentions it to the group first, and if it continues, she tells the teacher about the contribution imbalance.
She does all the work herself to avoid the problem.
She removes the low-contributing member from the group without speaking to them.
She complains to the teacher immediately without speaking to the group first.
payload.explanation: Raising the issue within the group first — and escalating to the teacher if it continues — is the correct sequence.

payload.snippet: Oliver has a homework task that requires internet research but his home broadband is broken.
options: He visits the local library or uses his school's homework club to complete the task.
He submits the homework without the research section.
He uses his mobile data even though it will use up his allowance.
He tells the teacher he had no internet and hopes for an extension.
payload.explanation: Finding an alternative access point for research is more resourceful than skipping the task or requesting an extension without trying.

payload.snippet: Anna is checking her completed homework when she realises a question she answered confidently may actually have a different correct answer.
options: She rechecks the answer using another source before submitting.
She submits her original answer since she is probably right.
She asks a friend which answer they got and copies their version.
She removes the answer and leaves it blank to be safe.
payload.explanation: Rechecking a doubted answer with a reliable source before submission is good academic practice.

payload.snippet: Jake finishes his homework very quickly and thinks it might be too short.
options: He rereads the question to check whether he has met all the requirements and adds more if needed.
He submits it since he has answered the question.
He adds padding to make it look longer without adding content.
He asks a parent to write an extra paragraph for him.
payload.explanation: Checking the task requirements before submitting ensures you have not missed something — padding without content does not improve quality.

payload.snippet: Maya discovers that a classmate has been copying from her homework in several different subjects without her knowledge.
options: She tells a teacher privately rather than confronting the classmate alone.
She confronts the classmate in front of others.
She says nothing since it benefits her classmate and does not hurt her.
She deliberately puts wrong answers in future homework to stop the copying.
payload.explanation: Telling a teacher privately is the correct response — deliberate wrong answers could harm your own marks, and confrontation without teacher involvement escalates conflict.

payload.snippet: Tom is assigned a homework task he finds genuinely interesting and wants to spend a lot of extra time on it.
options: He completes the required task well and then develops his extra interest independently as a side project.
He submits an enormous extended version and asks his teacher for extra credit.
He focuses so much on the extended version that he neglects other homework.
He submits only his extended version without completing the core task.
payload.explanation: Completing the core task first and pursuing extra interest separately ensures no other responsibilities are neglected.
