She adds boiling water to the whole pond to melt the ice fast.
payload.explanation: Gentle hot water melts a breathing hole without shocking the fish.

payload.snippet: Tom is walking home through heavy snowfall when he realises he has taken a wrong turn and does not recognise the street.
options: He stops, stays calm, and calls home for directions.
He keeps walking quickly in the same direction hoping to find a landmark.
He knocks on a random door and asks to wait inside until the snow stops.
He retraces his steps at a run before his footprints fill in.
payload.explanation: Stopping and calling home is the safe response when lost in bad weather.

payload.snippet: The forecast warns of a severe blizzard tomorrow and grandma lives alone on a rural road.
options: The family drives to collect her and bring her to stay for the duration.
They call her daily and trust the council to check on her.
They send her a supply kit by courier and hope it arrives in time.
They wait until the blizzard starts to assess how bad it really is.
payload.explanation: Collecting a vulnerable person before a blizzard is the safest precaution.

payload.snippet: Oliver has been wearing wet gloves all afternoon and his hands are very cold, red, and painful.
options: He goes inside, removes the gloves, and warms his hands gently with warm water.
He keeps the wet gloves on because removing them would be colder.
He holds his hands over a direct flame to get the heat back quickly.
He runs his hands under the cold tap to wake the feeling up.
payload.explanation: Removing wet gloves and using warm (not hot) water is the correct cold-hand treatment.

payload.snippet: A blizzard starts while Clara's family is on a motorway far from any exit.
options: Dad slows right down, puts hazard lights on, and follows the vehicle ahead carefully.
Dad pulls fully off the road and turns the engine off to save fuel.
Dad accelerates to reach the next exit before the snow gets worse.
Dad reverses along the hard shoulder to the exit they already passed.
payload.explanation: Slowing, using hazards, and following the car ahead are correct blizzard-driving rules.

payload.snippet: Tom and his friends have been cycling in the summer heat for three hours without a break when one friend suddenly stops, says he feels sick and confused, and his skin feels very hot and dry.
options: Tom gets him into shade immediately, calls 999, and uses water to cool the back of his neck while they wait.
Tom pours cold water over his friend's head and tells him to lie in the sun to stay awake.
Tom gives him an energy drink and asks him to eat something quickly to raise his blood sugar.
Tom sits him upright against his bike, fans him with a map, and calls his parents.
payload.explanation: Hot dry skin with confusion signals heat stroke — 999, shade, and cool water to the neck are urgent.

payload.snippet: Anna is at an outdoor music festival when a friend who has been in the sun all day collapses. The friend is conscious but very pale, sweating heavily, and says her vision is going blurry.
options: Anna calls for the medical tent team, moves her friend into shade, lays her down with legs raised, and gives her water in small sips.
Anna fans her friend briskly, gives her all her remaining water, and calls her parents.
Anna walks her friend slowly to the medical tent, supporting her weight on one side.
Anna pours her friend's water bottle over her face and head to cool her down quickly.
payload.explanation: Pale sweating dizziness is heat exhaustion — lay down with legs raised, shade, small sips, and call medical staff.

payload.snippet: Jake is helping his neighbour paint the garden fence in direct sun when he notices the neighbour has stopped moving, is sitting slumped in the chair, and does not respond to his name.
options: Jake shouts for help, calls 999, tilts the neighbour's head back to open the airway, and checks for breathing.
Jake pats the neighbour's cheeks firmly and asks if he is okay before deciding what to do.
Jake runs inside the house to get water and a cool towel for the neighbour.
Jake calls the neighbour's wife first because she will know what medication he takes.
payload.explanation: Unresponsive means 999 first, then airway-check — not fetching water or calling family.

payload.snippet: Clara's family has parked their car and gone for a walk, accidentally leaving the windows up and her younger brother asleep in the back seat on a day that is now thirty-four degrees.
options: She tells her parents immediately, who run back and open the car doors at once and cool her brother with water.
She knocks on the window to wake her brother so he can attract attention.
She waits at the car while her parents carry on walking as her brother is asleep and calm.
She calls the ice cream van to park next to the car so the cold side keeps it cooler.
payload.explanation: A child locked in a hot car is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate adult return and ventilation.

payload.snippet: Oliver is mowing the lawn in the summer heat and finds a young hedgehog lying still on its side in the open grass during daylight hours.
options: He leaves it in place, stops mowing that patch, places a box loosely over it, and calls a wildlife rescue line for advice.
He picks it up, brings it inside to a warm spot, and gives it bread and milk.
He moves it to a hedgerow with his gloved hands and checks on it later that evening.
He leaves it completely alone and resumes mowing around it carefully.
payload.explanation: Hedgehogs active in daylight and lying still are likely injured or ill — wildlife rescue advice is needed.

payload.snippet: Maya is in charge of five younger children at a summer party in the garden when she notices dark clouds rolling in rapidly and hears distant thunder.
options: She calmly leads all children inside the house and informs the hosting adult immediately.
She lets the children finish the current game and then brings them inside at its natural end.
She moves the children to a large tree at the garden edge for natural shelter.
She counts the seconds between lightning and thunder to judge if it is close enough to worry about.
payload.explanation: Thunder means lightning is present — all outdoor supervision responsibilities require immediate indoor evacuation.

payload.snippet: Ben is at the beach building sandcastles when his younger cousin digs a deep narrow trench nearby and then climbs inside to hide. The trench walls suddenly collapse inward covering the cousin's legs and waist.
options: Ben calls loudly for adults, kneels at the edge without going in, and begins carefully removing sand from around his cousin's waist while adults run over.
Ben jumps into the trench to pull his cousin free as quickly as possible.
Ben runs to the sea to get a bucket of water to make the sand softer and easier to remove.
Ben tells his cousin to push with his hands to free himself from the collapsed walls.
payload.explanation: Sand collapses can be deadly — calling adults, staying out of the trench, and careful sand removal are correct.

payload.snippet: The family's outdoor paddling pool has been sitting uncovered in the sun for five days and has developed green algae on the base.
options: Mum empties it completely, scrubs it with a diluted disinfectant, and rinses it thoroughly before refilling.
Mum adds extra pool chlorine tablets and lets the children play while the chemicals work.
Mum lets the sun kill the algae for another day as UV is a natural disinfectant.
Mum skims the visible algae off the top with a net and refills with clean water to dilute it.
payload.explanation: Algae in paddling pools require emptying, disinfection, and full rinse before refilling — not chemical top-ups.

payload.snippet: Tom is helping at the community summer fete when an elderly volunteer faint in the drinks queue on what is the hottest day of the year.
options: He lowers her gently to the ground, elevates her legs, calls for the first-aider, and keeps her cool with a wet cloth on her forehead.
He helps her to a chair and gets her a glass of cold water to drink straight away.
He fans her face vigorously and asks nearby people to help him walk her to the shade.
He lays her flat on her back, puts her arms by her sides, and calls for an ambulance.
payload.explanation: Fainting in heat requires: down to the ground, legs raised, first-aider called, cool compress — not sitting up.

payload.snippet: Anna is walking her dog at noon when it lies down suddenly on the path and refuses to move, panting rapidly.
options: She picks the dog up if she can, or sits with it in any available shade, pours water over its paws and head, and calls the vet.
She waits for the dog to recover and then continues the walk at a slower pace.
She tries to encourage it with a treat and walks it to the nearest water fountain.
She puts the lead down and jogs ahead to find the nearest shaded bench for it.
payload.explanation: A dog collapsing mid-walk in heat is a medical emergency — shade, cooling, and a vet call are urgent.

payload.snippet: Jake finds a dead bird near the garden bird bath on a very hot day and wonders if it was the water.
options: He empties and scrubs the bird bath and refills it with fresh cool water, then washes his hands thoroughly.
He covers the bird bath so other birds cannot drink from it until he checks.
He tips extra water in to dilute any contamination that might be in the bath.
He leaves everything as it is to avoid disturbing the scene before he does more research.
payload.explanation: Stagnant bird bath water breeds bacteria — cleaning and refilling prevents further harm to garden birds.

payload.snippet: Clara's younger sibling plays barefoot on the hot patio and comes inside crying with a blister forming on one foot.
options: Clara runs cool water over the blister gently, covers it with a clean dressing, and tells a parent.
Clara pops the blister with a clean pin and covers it with a plaster.
Clara applies butter from the kitchen to soothe the hot skin on the foot.
Clara puts ice from the freezer directly on the blister to cool it down fast.
payload.explanation: Cool water, not ice or butter, soothes a heat blister; do not pop it — cover and tell an adult.

payload.snippet: Ben's family is camping when they find an abandoned campfire left by a previous group that is still smouldering the next morning.
options: Dad douses it with water, stirs the ashes with a stick until no steam rises, and reports it to the campsite warden.
Dad covers the smouldering area with soil to smother it and leaves it to cool.
Dad leaves it alone as smouldering fires burn themselves out without causing a wildfire.
Dad uses a bucket of sand from the campfire kit to cover the hot embers.
payload.explanation: Full water dousing, stirring to ash, steam check, and reporting are the correct abandoned campfire steps.

payload.snippet: The class is on a summer trip to a nature reserve when a student is stung on the neck by an unknown insect and the sting site swells rapidly to twice the size of a normal sting.
options: The teacher calls 999, keeps the student calm and still, asks if she has an EpiPen, and loosens anything tight around the neck.
The teacher applies antihistamine cream from the first-aid kit and gives the student water.
The teacher takes a photo to show the doctor later and monitors the swelling carefully.
The teacher calls the school office for advice and asks a parent helper to drive the student to a walk-in centre.
payload.explanation: Rapid large-area swelling near the airway after a sting warrants 999 and airway monitoring — not cream or driving.

payload.snippet: Oliver is at an outdoor film screening when the grass fire alarm sounds. He can smell smoke but cannot see any flames from his position.
options: He gathers the people near him and walks calmly toward the nearest exit markers.
He waits to see flames before reacting so he does not cause unnecessary panic.
He climbs onto his picnic chair to look for the smoke source and assess the risk.
He asks the people around him to vote on whether to stay or go.
payload.explanation: Smoke without visible flames is still a fire alarm — immediate calm evacuation is always correct.

payload.snippet: Jake is mowing the sports-field grass when the mower kicks out a stone that shatters the glass panel of the groundskeeper's shed twelve metres away. No one is hurt but the broken glass has scattered across the footpath children use to reach the cricket nets.
options: He stops the mower, marks both ends of the glass-covered path with cones, and reports the damage and the hazard to the groundskeeper before resuming.
He sweeps the visible pieces off the path with his boot and carries on mowing.
He puts a sign saying 'watch your step' at one end of the path and continues his schedule.
He completes the mowing first so the field is safe and then reports the shed damage.
payload.explanation: Marking the glass hazard and reporting it before resuming work is the correct duty-of-care response.

payload.snippet: Clara is at an outdoor summer market when she notices an unattended backpack sitting under a stall table that no vendor or visitor has approached in over fifteen minutes.
options: She informs the nearest market steward or security officer immediately without touching the bag.
She opens the bag carefully to check if it belongs to anyone or contains anything harmful.
She picks it up and hands it to the nearest stall holder so it does not block the path.
She waits another fifteen minutes to see if an owner returns before doing anything.
payload.explanation: Unattended bags in a public place should be reported to security without being touched.

payload.snippet: Ben's younger sibling is playing in the paddling pool when she slips climbing out and scrapes her chin on the plastic edge, producing a small but freely bleeding cut.
options: Ben lifts her out, applies gentle pressure with a clean cloth, and tells a parent immediately.
Ben pours pool water over the cut to rinse it and tells her to press the edge herself.
Ben goes to get a plaster and leaves his sibling sitting on the wet pool edge alone.
Ben applies pressure with his hand and asks a neighbour to call an ambulance right away.
payload.explanation: Gentle pressure with a clean cloth controls small bleeding while an adult is summoned.

payload.snippet: Maya is helping organise a summer charity run when a participant returns early and reports a runner is lying by the path two kilometres out, conscious and confused, and very pale.
options: Maya calls 999 immediately, sends a marshal in a buggy to the location with a first-aid kit, and stops further runners from being dispatched until the situation is clear.
Maya asks the returned participant to run back to help while she finishes her route-marshal duties.
Maya drives the route herself to locate the runner and assess what first aid is needed.
Maya tells the race director and waits for his decision before acting.
payload.explanation: A collapsed runner with confusion is a 999-level emergency requiring immediate first-aid dispatch and a race pause.

payload.snippet: Oliver is doing a summer litter-pick in the park when he finds a used syringe half-hidden in a patch of grass near the children's play area.
options: He marks the spot with a stick, keeps others away, and calls the local council's sharps-collection line.
He picks it up carefully with a plastic bag over his hand and puts it in the nearest bin.
He uses tongs from his kit to move it into the hedgerow where children will not find it.
He photographs it and posts it to the council's social media page asking for urgent collection.
payload.explanation: Discarded syringes must be reported to a professional sharps-collection service — never handle them yourself.

payload.snippet: Tom is delivering newspapers on his bike when a flash downpour starts. He has twelve more streets to cover and the papers are in an open basket getting drenched.
options: He pulls under the nearest shelter, wraps the remaining papers in the plastic liners from the delivered ones, and continues delivering once the worst passes.
He delivers as fast as he can and apologises to each customer about the wet papers.
He abandons the remaining papers at a community noticeboard and heads home.
He phones the newsagent to ask whether he should continue or return with the wet papers.
payload.explanation: Protecting remaining stock and waiting for the worst to pass keeps the papers readable and the job done.

payload.snippet: Anna is leading a group of eight-year-olds on a nature walk when steady rain turns to a severe downpour with thunder. They are in an open field with no building in sight.
options: She moves the group to the lowest point in the field away from isolated trees and has them crouch low in a spread-out cluster, not touching each other.
She takes the group to the tall hedgerow at the field edge for maximum shelter.
She runs the group to the nearest large isolated oak tree to shelter underneath.
She tells the children to stand flat against each other under her waterproof cape.
payload.explanation: In an open field during lightning: avoid trees, move to low ground, spread out and crouch — tall objects attract strikes.

payload.snippet: Jake is camping when overnight rain makes the tent floor wet. He realises water is seeping in under the groundsheet and has soaked his sleeping bag.
options: He moves his sleeping bag to the dry end, uses clothes to soak up water at the entry point, and the next morning re-pitches the tent on higher ground.
He opens the tent door to let the water flow out through the front and then closes it.
He puts stones around the tent base to divert the water and stays in the wet sleeping bag.
He gets up and sits in the car for the rest of the night so the sleeping bag can dry.
payload.explanation: Stopping the water source, using clothes as temporary absorbent, and re-pitching higher prevents recurrence.

payload.snippet: Maya's grandmother's house has a flat roof extension and heavy rain is pouring through a section of ceiling in the kitchen. A patch of plaster is bulging visibly with trapped water above it.
options: Maya tells her grandmother not to go in the kitchen, places a bucket under the bulge, and calls a family member with the photos she takes.
Maya pushes a skewer through the bulge so the water drains through a small hole rather than in a burst.
Maya stacks towels on the counter under the bulge and goes to get a ladder to inspect the roof.
Maya tells her grandmother to phone the council for emergency repairs right away.
payload.explanation: Staying out, catching the water, and calling family for help is the correct response to an indoor ceiling flood.

payload.snippet: Oliver is playing in the garden when he finds his baby sibling has climbed out through the open back door and is sitting in a puddle in the rain in only a nappy.
options: He brings his sibling inside immediately, wraps them in a warm towel, and calls a parent.
He covers his sibling with a large leaf and runs inside to get a parent before picking them up.
He gives his sibling a drink of water to warm them up and calls for a parent to come outside.
He stays with the sibling in the garden and waits for a parent to notice they are missing.
payload.explanation: Wet babies lose heat fast — bringing the baby in and warming them before calling a parent is correct.

payload.snippet: Clara is in charge of a junior after-school film club in a temporary outdoor shelter when the weather forecast changes to a severe weather warning with risk of structural damage from wind and rain.
options: She calmly ends the session early, ensures every child is collected by a known adult, and stays with any remaining children inside the school building until all are accounted for.
She checks the shelter's stability and continues the session as the warning says risk not certainty.
She sends all children home on their own immediately so they reach safety before the storm arrives.
She calls a parent vote by text message on whether to continue or end the session.
payload.explanation: A structural-risk severe weather warning ends outdoor/temporary-shelter supervision — all children inside with known adults.

payload.snippet: Ben is fishing by a river when he notices the water level is rising rapidly and the bank he is sitting on is starting to feel soft and unstable underfoot.
options: He picks up his equipment and moves immediately to higher ground well back from the bank.
He casts further into the river to get ahead of the rising water before leaving.
He calls the Environment Agency to report the rising level before moving position.
He sits on a dry patch of bank three metres from the water and monitors the level.
payload.explanation: Rapidly rising water on a soft bank is a flash-flood warning — immediate retreat to high ground.

payload.snippet: Tom is supervising younger children at an indoor soft-play centre when the ceiling starts dripping and several large patches of water form on the play equipment after a burst pipe above.
options: He removes all children from the wet play areas immediately, reports to staff at the reception desk, and keeps children in the dry seating area.
He tells children to avoid the dripping patches and continues supervising their play.
He puts his coat over the wettest patch of equipment so the children can keep playing.
He takes the children outside while the roof leak is fixed by staff.
payload.explanation: Wet soft play equipment is a slip and electrical hazard — clear children immediately and report to staff.

payload.snippet: Anna's class is doing an outdoor science experiment recording rainfall over twenty-four hours when overnight heavy rain fills their rain gauge to overflowing, losing the true reading.
options: She notes the gauge overflowed, records the overflow as the minimum figure, and suggests repeating the experiment with a larger gauge or more frequent readings.
She estimates the extra rainfall from a neighbouring weather website and adds it to the reading.
She asks the class to accept the gauge maximum as the official reading for the experiment.
She empties the gauge and repeats only the final four hours of the experiment.
payload.explanation: Scientific integrity requires flagging measurement failure, noting the minimum bound, and improving methodology — not estimating or ignoring the error.

payload.snippet: Oliver walks into the school library and notices water pouring through a ceiling tile above a shelf of fragile reference books. Two books are already wet.
options: He moves the wet books to a dry surface, puts a bin under the drip, alerts the librarian, and helps lay the books flat open to dry.
He stacks the wet books tightly together to protect their spines while they dry.
He puts the wet books outside on the windowsill so the wind helps them dry faster.
He reports the leak to the office and leaves the books in place so the librarian can assess them.
payload.explanation: Moving wet books flat to dry and catching the drip limits damage while professional help is arranged.

payload.snippet: Maya is returning from a camping trip when a rainstorm floods the road she planned to drive home on. Her map shows an alternative route but it crosses a ford that may also be flooded.
options: The driver turns around and follows a diversion on higher ground roads, avoiding both the flooded road and the uncertain ford.
The driver tests the ford slowly in four-wheel drive to check whether it is passable.
The driver waits at the flooded road for thirty minutes to see if the level drops.
The driver takes the shortcut across a ploughed field beside the road to bypass the flood.
payload.explanation: Flooded roads and uncertain fords should both be avoided — a longer high-ground diversion is the only safe choice.

payload.snippet: Jake is standing at a bus stop in heavy rain when he notices a young woman who is soaking wet and shivering has been standing there for over half an hour and is not checking a phone or looking for a bus.
options: He asks if she is okay and whether she needs any help.
He moves to the other end of the bus shelter to give her space and privacy.
He calls 999 because she might be in some kind of danger.
He gives her his umbrella and walks away so she does not feel embarrassed.
payload.explanation: Checking in with someone visibly distressed in a public space is a compassionate and proportionate response.

payload.snippet: Clara is at a sports tournament being held on outdoor courts when the rain makes the surface dangerously slippery and a player slips and falls hard, winding herself badly.
options: Clara calls for the match referee to pause play, stays with the player, and supports her to sit up gently once she is breathing normally again.
Clara helps the player to her feet immediately and walks her to the sideline.
Clara pours water on the court surface where the player slipped to wash the mud away.
Clara shouts to the other players to keep playing while she checks on the fallen player.
payload.explanation: Pausing play for safety and supporting a winded player calmly are the correct match-official and bystander responses.

payload.snippet: Ben is walking home in rain when he trips on a broken paving slab and grazes both palms on the wet ground. His hands are bleeding and dirty.
options: He cleans his hands as best he can with the water bottle in his bag, holds a clean tissue over the worst graze, and walks the rest of the way home to clean it properly.
He puts his hands in a puddle of rainwater to wash the grazes with fresh clean water.
He wraps his school scarf tightly around both hands and runs the rest of the way home.
He knocks on the nearest house and asks the occupant for antiseptic cream.
payload.explanation: Bottled water and a clean tissue are the best immediate first-aid tools when grazes occur outdoors.

payload.snippet: Tom is helping his dad unload shopping from the car in heavy rain when one carrier bag splits, spilling a dozen loose eggs across the wet driveway.
options: Tom gathers the unbroken eggs by hand into another bag and leaves the broken ones for his dad to clean once they are inside.
Tom picks all the eggs up as fast as he can, cracked and whole, and carries them to the kitchen.
Tom stamps on the remaining cracked eggs to prevent them being stepped on later.
Tom takes off his coat to carry all the eggs at once so they stay drier.
payload.explanation: Salvaging unbroken eggs and leaving the messy cleanup for later is the sensible priority in the rain.

payload.snippet: It has been raining for three days and the small stream at the bottom of the park has flooded over the path. Anna wants to cross to reach the picnic area on the other side.
options: Anna warns others not to cross and takes the long route around the park instead.
Anna wades through the flooded section as it only looks ankle deep.
Anna places stepping stones in the flood to create a path for other walkers.
Anna calls the park authorities and waits by the flooded area for them to arrive.
payload.explanation: Flooded paths can hide deep water or strong currents — go around and warn others.

payload.snippet: Jake's new umbrella has a metal handle and he is walking near a road as a thunderstorm begins.
options: He puts the umbrella down and takes shelter in the nearest shop doorway.
He holds the umbrella higher to keep more rain off during the lightning.
He keeps the umbrella up but holds it by the fabric dome instead of the metal handle.
He hands the umbrella to a passing adult and runs under a tree for cover.
payload.explanation: Metal umbrella handles conduct electricity in a thunderstorm — sheltering indoors is the only safe option.

payload.snippet: Oliver is doing a summer litter-pick in the park when he finds a used syringe half-hidden in a patch of grass near the children's play area.
options: He marks the spot with a stick, keeps others away, and calls the local council's sharps-collection line.
He picks it up carefully with a plastic bag over his hand and puts it in the nearest bin.
He uses tongs from his kit to move it into the hedgerow where children will not find it.
He photographs it and posts it to the council's social media page asking for urgent collection.
payload.explanation: Discarded syringes must be reported to a professional sharps-collection service — never handle them yourself.

payload.snippet: Clara is at a sports tournament being held on outdoor courts when the rain makes the surface dangerously slippery and a player slips and falls hard, winding herself badly.
options: Clara calls for the match referee to pause play, stays with the player, and supports her to sit up gently once she is breathing normally again.
Clara helps the player to her feet immediately and walks her to the sideline.
Clara pours water on the court surface where the player slipped to wash the mud away.
Clara shouts to the other players to keep playing while she checks on the fallen player.
payload.explanation: Pausing play for safety and supporting a winded player calmly are the correct match-official and bystander responses.

payload.snippet: Maya is returning from a camping trip when a rainstorm floods the road she planned to drive home on. Her map shows an alternative route but it crosses a ford that may also be flooded.
options: The driver turns around and follows a diversion on higher ground roads, avoiding both the flooded road and the uncertain ford.
The driver tests the ford slowly in four-wheel drive to check whether it is passable.
The driver waits at the flooded road for thirty minutes to see if the level drops.
The driver takes the shortcut across a ploughed field beside the road to bypass the flood.
payload.explanation: Flooded roads and uncertain fords should both be avoided — a longer high-ground diversion is the only safe choice.

payload.snippet: Tom is supervising his younger siblings on the playground when he notices the bolts on the bottom of the slide ladder have come loose and the whole structure wobbles when touched.
options: He tells his siblings to stay off the slide, marks the area with his bag, and tells the nearest adult immediately.
He tightens the bolts himself with a coin from his pocket and tests the structure carefully.
He helps his siblings down the slide one at a time watching closely for any wobble.
He tells his siblings to use it but to hold the sides very tightly at all times.
payload.explanation: A structurally unsafe piece of equipment must be kept clear and reported — never attempt DIY repairs.

payload.snippet: Anna is at the park with a group of friends when one friend tries to show off by standing up on the moving roundabout and loses his balance, hitting the ground hard and holding his wrist.
options: She calls for an adult, keeps her friend still, and checks if he can move his wrist without rushing him.
She helps him to his feet and asks him to flex his wrist to check it is just a sprain.
She continues turning the roundabout slowly while she assesses the injury.
She asks the group to form a circle around him so she can assess the injury privately.
payload.explanation: After a fall with a wrist impact, keeping the person still and calling for an adult is correct — do not force movement.

payload.snippet: Jake is playing in the park when a stranger approaches the playground and starts asking the children where their parents are and offering to show them something on his phone.
options: Jake moves toward the group of children near the main gate and calls out for the adults sitting on the nearby benches.
Jake tells the stranger that the adults are watching and asks him what he wants to show them.
Jake runs to the opposite corner of the park and hopes the adults notice the stranger.
Jake asks the stranger politely to leave before running to get an adult.
payload.explanation: Moving children to safety and alerting adults without confronting the stranger is the correct safeguarding response.

payload.snippet: Clara has been playing on the zip wire for twenty minutes when a younger child with a disability comes over and asks for a go but cannot reach the handle by themselves.
options: Clara helps the child reach the handle and stays nearby while they have a go.
Clara tells the child the zip wire is for older children and suggests the swings instead.
Clara asks her friends to watch so they are ready if the child falls.
Clara lifts the child onto the zip wire and pushes them gently to get them started.
payload.explanation: Helping the child access the equipment safely and supervising closely is inclusive and kind.

payload.snippet: Oliver is running across a wet wooden bridge in the playground when he slips and lands on his back, knocking the wind out of him. He cannot breathe for about ten seconds.
options: He stays still until his breathing comes back, then sits up slowly and tells an adult.
He gets straight back up and carries on playing so his friends do not worry.
He asks a friend to perform the Heimlich manoeuvre on him right away.
He panics and tries to breathe faster to replace the air he lost quickly.
payload.explanation: Getting winded needs calm stillness until breathing returns — then tell an adult to confirm you are okay.

payload.snippet: Maya watches as two older children start throwing woodchip pieces at each other from the play area and one piece hits a toddler in the face nearby.
options: She immediately picks up the toddler and checks their face, then calls for the nearest adult.
She shouts at the older children to stop and then assesses the toddler herself.
She moves the toddler away and watches to see if the children stop on their own.
She photographs the older children and sends the photo to the park's Facebook page.
payload.explanation: Protecting the vulnerable child first and calling an adult are the correct immediate priorities.

payload.snippet: Ben is playing on the high climbing net when he hears a ripping sound and notices the net has torn loose from one of its fixings directly above where younger children are climbing below.
options: He calls down to the children to move away from the net immediately and shouts for an adult.
He climbs down and tries to reattach the net to the fixing with a knot.
He tells the children to avoid that section but finishes his climb first.
He climbs to the broken fixing and holds it in place until an adult arrives.
payload.explanation: Warning children below and calling an adult without touching a broken piece of equipment is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Anna is playing in the park when she sees a toddler fall face-first off a low step and not move for several seconds. The toddler's parent runs over but is panicking.
options: Anna stays calm, tells the parent the toddler needs to be checked gently, and offers to call 999 if the parent is too distressed to dial.
Anna picks up the toddler and places her on the nearby bench so the parent can see her better.
Anna asks the parent to turn the toddler over quickly to check her face.
Anna runs to the café in the park to call for a first aider instead.
payload.explanation: A child not moving after a fall needs gentle assessment — staying calm and offering to call 999 supports the distressed parent.

payload.snippet: Jake is at the skate park attached to the playground when he sees a younger child on a scooter heading straight toward the deep bowl section without a helmet or any protective gear.
options: He stands at the edge of the bowl to block the child's path and asks the child to stop.
He shouts a warning and steps back so the child can make their own choice.
He lets the child go as the bowl is only two metres deep and they will be fine.
He chases the child and grabs their scooter to stop them, causing the child to fall sideways.
payload.explanation: Physically blocking the route is the fastest safe way to prevent a helmetless child entering a deep skate bowl.

payload.snippet: Clara is in a playground next to a main road when a ball goes over the fence and lands on the pavement on the other side.
options: She asks an adult to retrieve the ball rather than climbing the fence herself.
She climbs the fence quickly and picks up the ball before any cars come.
She asks a friend to hold her legs while she leans over the fence to grab it.
She leaves the ball and tells the owner to ask their parents to get it later.
payload.explanation: Retrieving a ball near a main road is a task for an adult, not a child alone.

payload.snippet: Oliver notices a child on the seesaw who has been bumping the seat hard on the ground repeatedly and now shows a graze on their coccyx area and is starting to cry.
options: He offers to help the child to the bench and tells the playground supervisor what happened.
He asks the child to sit on the seesaw more gently from now on and checks on them later.
He tells the child that hurting themselves was their own fault for bumping the seesaw.
He finishes his current game before checking on the child.
payload.explanation: Helping an injured child to safety and reporting to the supervisor is the correct caring response.

payload.snippet: Maya is on the trampoline in the park when she bounces into the air and lands awkwardly on her ankle, which twists under her. She can feel it swelling already.
options: She sits on the edge of the trampoline, avoids putting weight on the ankle, and calls for an adult.
She bounces gently a few more times to loosen the joint and see if it improves.
She gets off the trampoline and walks around on it to test whether it is a sprain.
She lies flat on the trampoline to rest and waits for the swelling to go down.
payload.explanation: A swelling ankle after a twist needs to be rested immediately and shown to an adult.

payload.snippet: Ben is playing in the park on a hot day when he notices another child who has been sitting alone on a bench in full sun for a long time and is very red in the face and not moving much.
options: He goes over to check on the child, asks if they are okay, and calls for an adult if the child seems unwell.
He offers his water bottle to the child from across the path.
He tells a nearby adult that the child looks hot and then leaves them to it.
He asks his friends if they know the child before approaching.
payload.explanation: Directly checking on a child showing signs of heat exhaustion and calling for help is the caring and correct response.

payload.snippet: Anna is helping run a holiday club in a playground when a thunderstorm begins. She counts five children spread across different pieces of equipment.
options: She calls all five children in by name, counts them, and leads them as a group to the nearest indoor building.
She shouts for all children to go inside and then runs in herself before they all arrive.
She uses the buddy system and pairs children to run to cover in twos.
She takes the three closest children inside first and then runs back for the remaining two.
payload.explanation: All children must be counted and moved as one group to indoor safety during a lightning risk.

payload.snippet: Jake finds a wallet on the ground near the park entrance with cards and cash inside it.
options: He hands it in to the park warden's office without looking through the contents.
He looks through it to find the owner's name and then calls out across the park.
He puts it in his bag to hand to his parents who can deal with it at home.
He leaves it on the nearby bench where the owner is more likely to find it.
payload.explanation: Handing a found wallet to a park warden intact is the correct lost-property procedure.

payload.snippet: Ben is at an outdoor playground when he sees a water feature has a pump making a loud grinding noise and has a visible electrical cable lying across the wet ground near the splash area where young children are playing.
options: He moves all children away from the wet area immediately, calls for the park warden, and makes sure no one touches the cable or the water until the warden arrives.
He asks a child to hold the cable off the ground so it does not touch the water.
He switches the pump off at the power button on the unit to remove the electrical hazard.
He tells children to step over the cable carefully and continues watching the area.
payload.explanation: A wet cable near an electrical pump with children present is a live electrical hazard — clear the area immediately and call a warden.

payload.snippet: Jake finds a wallet on the ground near the park entrance with cards and cash inside it.
options: He hands it in to the park warden's office without looking through the contents.
He looks through it to find the owner's name and then calls out across the park.
He puts it in his bag to hand to his parents who can deal with it at home.
He leaves it on the nearby bench where the owner is more likely to find it.
payload.explanation: Handing a found wallet to a park warden intact is the correct lost-property procedure.

payload.snippet: Maya is on the trampoline in the park when she bounces and lands awkwardly on her ankle, which twists under her. She can feel it swelling already.
options: She sits on the edge of the trampoline, avoids putting weight on the ankle, and calls for an adult.
She bounces gently a few more times to loosen the joint and see if it improves.
She gets off the trampoline and walks around to test whether it is a sprain.
She lies flat on the trampoline to rest and waits for the swelling to go down.
payload.explanation: A swelling ankle after a twist needs to be rested immediately and shown to an adult.

payload.snippet: Oliver notices a child on the seesaw who has been bumping the seat hard on the ground and now shows a graze and is starting to cry.
options: He offers to help the child to the bench and tells the playground supervisor what happened.
He asks the child to sit on the seesaw more gently from now on and checks on them later.
He tells the child that hurting themselves was their own fault for bumping the seesaw.
He finishes his current game before checking on the child.
payload.explanation: Helping an injured child to safety and reporting to the supervisor is the correct caring response.

payload.snippet: Clara is in a playground next to a main road when a ball goes over the fence and lands on the pavement on the other side.
options: She asks an adult to retrieve the ball rather than climbing the fence herself.
She climbs the fence quickly and picks up the ball before any cars come.
She asks a friend to hold her legs while she leans over the fence to grab it.
She leaves the ball and tells the owner to ask their parents to get it later.
payload.explanation: Retrieving a ball near a main road is a task for an adult, not a child alone.

payload.snippet: Tom is leading an after-school art club when he notices a student mixing two chemicals from the school's printmaking supplies together in a jar. The mixture immediately starts fizzing and producing a sharp smell.
options: He evacuates everyone from the room, opens windows if safe to do so, and calls for the science or health and safety lead immediately.
He takes the jar from the student and pours the mixture down the sink right away.
He puts the jar outside the classroom window and carries on with the session.
He asks the student what they mixed and looks up the chemicals on his phone.
payload.explanation: Unknown chemical reactions in a classroom require evacuation and specialist response — do not handle the mixture.

payload.snippet: Anna is photographing her art project for a portfolio submission when she realises the photos are needed in an hour and her camera memory card is corrupted, losing all the images she had already taken.
options: She sets up the lighting as best she can, re-photographs all available work quickly, and notifies the submission coordinator about the technical issue.
She borrows a classmate's photos of a similar project to submit in place of her own.
She submits the portfolio without photos and explains what happened in a cover note.
She asks the art teacher to give her extra time by claiming a personal illness caused the delay.
payload.explanation: Re-photographing and transparently communicating the technical problem is the honest and practical response.

payload.snippet: Jake is screen-printing t-shirts for a school fundraiser when the squeegee handle breaks mid-run, leaving twenty incomplete prints with wet ink on them.
options: He lays all twenty prints flat to protect the wet ink, asks the teacher for a replacement squeegee, and then completes the prints once he has one.
He uses his hand to complete the remaining prints, spreading the ink as evenly as he can.
He abandons the batch and starts over when the new squeegee arrives.
He completes the prints using the broken handle by pressing harder with both thumbs.
payload.explanation: Protecting wet prints and waiting for the right tool ensures all twenty are completed correctly.

payload.snippet: Clara is working on a clay kiln project and notices a classmate has placed a sealed hollow clay form in the kiln before firing — it has no air holes.
options: She tells the teacher before the kiln is switched on, because a sealed hollow form can explode in the kiln.
She pokes an air hole in the piece herself to solve the problem quickly.
She tells the classmate quietly and lets them decide whether to remove the piece.
She removes the piece herself while the classmate is not looking to prevent an argument.
payload.explanation: Sealed hollow clay explodes in a kiln — tell the teacher before firing so the piece can be corrected or removed.

payload.snippet: Oliver is painting a large landscape outdoors when a gust of wind blows his wet canvas face-first onto the grass, embedding grass and dirt into the paint surface.
options: He carefully removes the largest debris with a palette knife, lets it dry, and then assesses whether to incorporate the texture or scrape and repaint.
He wipes the canvas clean with a wet cloth while the paint is still wet.
He discards the canvas and starts fresh, as the grass-embedded surface cannot be recovered.
He adds more paint immediately on top of the contamination to cover it up.
payload.explanation: Letting an accidental texture dry and then deciding how to respond is the correct approach for wet canvas damage.

payload.snippet: Maya is doing a photography project in a public space when a member of public approaches and objects to being in the background of her shots and asks her to delete any images with him in them.
options: She apologises, confirms whether he is identifiable in any images, deletes those where he clearly appears, and thanks him for letting her know.
She explains she has the legal right to photograph in a public space and does not need to delete anything.
She agrees to crop him out of the images but keeps the originals for her portfolio.
She moves to a different location immediately without showing him which images have him in them.
payload.explanation: Respecting an objection to being photographed and deleting identifiable images is the ethical and courteous response.

payload.snippet: Ben is building a papier mâché balloon sculpture for a school exhibition when he notices the balloon inside has deflated before the final layers have dried, causing the shape to sag and deform.
options: He inflates a new balloon inside carefully through a small opening and reinforces the structure with fresh layers.
He fills the sagging form with expanding foam to restore the shape quickly.
He props the sculpture with rolled paper from the inside to maintain the shape while it dries.
He accepts the sagged shape as a creative outcome and redesigns the piece around the new form.
payload.explanation: Re-inflating carefully and adding fresh layers is the correct repair for a deflated papier mâché armature.

payload.snippet: Anna is using a band saw for a woodcarving sculpture in design technology when the blade starts vibrating noticeably more than usual and the cut becomes irregular.
options: She switches the machine off immediately and tells the teacher before resuming.
She slows her feed rate and presses the wood more firmly against the fence to reduce vibration.
She checks the blade tension herself by flicking it and adjusting the tension knob.
She finishes the current cut quickly and then reports the vibration at the end of the lesson.
payload.explanation: Unusual machine vibration means stop immediately and report — do not try to compensate with technique.

payload.snippet: Jake is working on a multi-media project that uses copyright music as its soundtrack. His teacher has asked him to find a legal audio track for the school presentation.
options: He searches for Creative Commons or royalty-free music sites and finds a track with the right licence for school use.
He downloads his favourite song from a streaming service as the quality is much better.
He records himself humming the tune of the song he wants so it technically is not the original.
He uses the copyrighted track and credits the artist in his presentation notes.
payload.explanation: Creative Commons and royalty-free sources provide legal music for school presentations — crediting a copyrighted track does not make it legal.

payload.snippet: Clara is applying gold leaf to a final piece using size adhesive when she reaches the last section and realises she does not have enough gold leaf to complete it. The adhesive is already applied and will become too dry to work with if she does not act in the next thirty minutes.
options: She asks the teacher if there are more gold leaf sheets, and if not, adapts the design by incorporating a different metallic finish for the final section.
She applies a second layer of size over the tacky section to buy more time while she finds gold leaf.
She cuts the remaining sheets into very small pieces and tries to tile the whole area with minimal overlap.
She leaves the adhesive section ungilded and presents the piece as an intentional incomplete artwork.
payload.explanation: Asking for more materials first and adapting creatively if none are available is the professional response to a supply shortfall mid-process.

payload.snippet: Oliver is leading an art workshop when he notices that one of the participants is becoming increasingly distressed while painting — the subject matter on their canvas is getting darker and more disturbing with each layer.
options: He checks in gently with the participant after the session, notes his concern, and mentions it to the session coordinator or safeguarding lead.
He stops the participant mid-session and asks what the dark images mean.
He moves the participant to a different table and gives them a different subject to paint.
He monitors the participant without raising the concern, as art is a personal expression.
payload.explanation: Unusual distress signals in creative work warrant a gentle post-session check-in and safeguarding notification — not mid-session confrontation or ignoring the signal.

payload.snippet: Maya is doing an outdoor mural commission on a community wall when she realises the wall surface is still wet from recent rain and the exterior paint she is using is refusing to adhere properly.
options: She waits for the wall surface to dry fully before continuing, even if it means returning on a different day.
She applies the paint more thickly to compensate for the poor adhesion on the wet surface.
She uses a hair dryer to dry the wall surface section by section as she paints.
She adds water to the paint to thin it so it absorbs better into the damp wall.
payload.explanation: Exterior paint applied to a wet surface will peel — waiting for full drying is the only correct approach for a permanent commission.

payload.snippet: Ben is running a screen-printing business from home and discovers that the chemicals he uses to reclaim screens are classified as hazardous waste that cannot be poured down the drain.
options: He contacts the local council to find out the correct hazardous waste disposal procedure and makes arrangements accordingly.
He dilutes the chemicals heavily with water before pouring them down the drain to reduce concentration.
He pours the chemicals into sealed containers and puts them in the regular household waste collection.
He asks a neighbouring print studio if they can take his waste chemicals when they dispose of theirs.
payload.explanation: Hazardous chemicals must be disposed of through the correct council channels — diluting or hiding them in household waste is illegal.

payload.snippet: Anna is photographing a classmate for a portrait project. Reviewing the images later she realises one shows the classmate in an unflattering and vulnerable moment they were unaware of.
options: She does not use the image in any form and deletes it, then tells her classmate she has done so.
She uses the image in her portfolio as it shows genuine emotion and is artistically strong.
She crops the image heavily so the moment is less obvious and uses it in her private portfolio.
She asks her classmate which images they are happy with and lets them choose from the full set.
payload.explanation: Photographing someone in an unaware vulnerable moment and using it without consent is an ethical violation — delete and inform.

payload.snippet: Jake is painting a community portrait project when he realises the preliminary sketch he transferred onto the canvas has an anatomical error — the proportions of one figure's arms are clearly wrong after scaling up.
options: He corrects the drawing with charcoal over the transferred lines before applying any paint.
He paints the first layers and hopes the painting will draw attention away from the arm proportions.
He adds extra objects to the composition near the figure to obscure the arm area.
He re-scales the entire canvas transfer to get the proportions right before painting.
payload.explanation: Correcting a proportional error in charcoal before painting is the most efficient and cleanest fix.

payload.snippet: Jake is working on a commission for a local authority public sculpture. During fabrication he discovers the structural steel was a lighter gauge than the specification, meaning the finished piece may not be safe for public interaction.
options: He stops fabrication, documents the discrepancy, contacts the supplier and the commissioning authority, and will not proceed until correctly specified materials are provided and an engineer signs off.
He reinforces the lighter steel by welding additional internal supports so the piece meets the load requirement.
He proceeds with fabrication and discloses the material substitution in the installation documentation.
He contacts the commissioning authority but continues fabrication to avoid missing the installation deadline.
payload.explanation: A safety-critical material substitution in public art requires a full stop, documented disclosure, and engineering sign-off before proceeding.

payload.snippet: Anna is finalising a documentary photography project about a vulnerable community when she realises one of her most powerful images inadvertently identifies a person who had only consented to appear in anonymous form.
options: She excludes the image from all exhibitions and publications, contacts the subject to inform them, and re-examines all other images for similar consent issues before publishing.
She crops the image to obscure the identifying features and uses it in the exhibition.
She uses the image only in her private portfolio since it will not be seen publicly.
She includes the image and credits the subject by their chosen alias to satisfy the consent requirement.
payload.explanation: Consent to appear anonymously must be fully honoured — exclude, inform the subject, and audit all remaining images.

payload.snippet: Oliver is running a community print workshop when a participant with severe colour blindness arrives and struggles to distinguish between the colours needed for the layered registration process.
options: He modifies the registration markers to high-contrast black-and-white patterns and provides verbal guidance for each layer.
He assigns another participant to guide the colour-blind person through the session.
He suggests the participant do a mono-colour single-layer print instead.
He provides a printed colour chart and asks the participant to reference it for each step.
payload.explanation: Adapting the environment with high-contrast markers gives the participant full independent access to the process.

payload.snippet: Maya is exhibiting at a major graduate show when she learns the day before opening that the lighting rig above her work is flickering, which may trigger photosensitive epilepsy in visitors.
options: She reports it to the gallery's technical team immediately and requests the flickering light be replaced or her piece be moved before opening.
She places a warning sign in front of her piece and leaves the decision to visitors.
She tells the gallery team at the opening so they are aware during the show.
She turns off the light above her piece and uses natural light from the window instead.
payload.explanation: A flicker that may trigger epilepsy is a safeguarding issue requiring a technical fix or relocation before public access — a warning sign is insufficient.

payload.snippet: Ben is working on a multi-media project that uses copyright music as its soundtrack. His teacher has asked him to find a legal audio track for the school presentation.
options: He searches for Creative Commons or royalty-free music sites and finds a track with the right licence for school use.
He downloads his favourite song from a streaming service as the quality is much better.
He records himself humming the tune of the song he wants so it technically is not the original.
He uses the copyrighted track and credits the artist in his presentation notes.
payload.explanation: Creative Commons and royalty-free sources provide legal music for school presentations — crediting a copyrighted track does not make it legal.

payload.snippet: Tom is performing his first public piano recital when he notices halfway through the piece that the piano's sustain pedal is not working, significantly changing the sound of the music.
options: He adapts his finger technique to hold notes longer manually and completes the performance professionally.
He stops, announces the problem to the audience, and asks for the piece to restart.
He plays so fast that the missing sustain is not noticeable to the audience.
He leaves the stage and asks the teacher to play instead.
payload.explanation: A professional adapts to equipment failure mid-performance rather than stopping — the audience barely knows the intended sound.

payload.snippet: Anna is leading a junior music group when one child becomes distressed and starts crying during a free improvisation exercise. When asked, the child says the sound reminds them of something sad.
options: She gently redirects the group to a different, brighter activity and checks in with the distressed child quietly afterwards.
She asks the child to share what memory the music triggered with the whole group.
She stops the improvisation entirely and ends the session early to protect the child.
She continues the improvisation and asks the group to play more cheerfully.
payload.explanation: Gently redirecting and checking in privately respects the child's feelings without making them the centre of attention.

payload.snippet: Jake is playing the acoustic guitar at a community event when he hears a faint buzzing from the guitar body every time he plays a specific note.
options: He identifies which fret is causing the buzz, avoids that position where possible, and reports the issue to be fixed after the event.
He presses down harder on that note to eliminate the buzz regardless of how much it hurts his fingertip.
He stops playing and announces there is a problem with his guitar to the audience.
He detunes the affected string slightly so the note is not played in that position.
payload.explanation: Identifying and working around a buzz mid-performance, then reporting it afterwards, is the professional approach.

payload.snippet: Clara is a student music teacher running her first lesson when the pupil refuses to put down their phone and keeps playing games during the lesson.
options: She calmly asks the phone to be placed face-down on the piano, explains why focus is needed, and continues the lesson.
She takes the phone from the pupil and locks it in the piano bench for the lesson.
She gives the pupil a five-minute free time on the phone at the end if they focus now.
She texts the pupil's parents during the lesson to inform them of the behaviour.
payload.explanation: A calm direct request with a brief explanation is the appropriate first response to distracted behaviour in a lesson.

payload.snippet: Oliver is the lead singer in a band and the bassist shows up to rehearsal visibly upset and not focused, making repeated mistakes throughout the session.
options: He pauses the rehearsal, checks in with the bassist one-to-one, and adjusts the session to run-through pieces the bassist knows well today.
He tells the bassist that personal problems should stay at the door and continues.
He asks the bassist to sit out this rehearsal and watch instead.
He replaces the bassist with a stand-in for the rehearsal and says nothing more about it.
payload.explanation: Checking in and adjusting the session shows care and keeps the rehearsal productive despite a difficult day.

payload.snippet: Maya is practising for her grade five violin exam when she pulls a muscle in her bow arm and it is sore and swollen the day before the examination.
options: She rests the arm completely, applies ice, and calls the examination board to ask about a medical postponement if it does not improve overnight.
She practises at half speed to keep her skills sharp without straining the arm further.
She performs the exam the next day and relies on adrenaline to push through the pain.
She cancels the exam immediately and rebooks without asking about a medical postponement option.
payload.explanation: Rest, ice, and asking about medical postponement are the correct responses to a pre-exam injury — practising through injury worsens it.

payload.snippet: Ben is running a community choir when two members with strong voices are persistently singing louder than everyone else and drowning out the sopranos.
options: He addresses the group as a whole about balance, using a general note rather than singling the two members out, then follows up individually if the imbalance continues.
He moves the two loud members to the back of the choir so their volume is absorbed by the group.
He asks the other members to project more to compensate for the imbalance.
He tells the two members directly in front of the whole choir that they need to reduce their volume.
payload.explanation: A general note addresses the issue without humiliating individuals — individual follow-up is reserved if the problem continues.

payload.snippet: Anna is teaching a music lesson when she notices that one pupil is consistently producing a strained sound on the flute and appears to be in mild discomfort around the jaw.
options: She stops the pupil, gently corrects the embouchure, and asks if the pupil has been experiencing jaw pain.
She continues the lesson and notes to mention the embouchure at the end.
She asks the pupil to rest while the others continue, to avoid reinforcing a bad habit.
She passes the pupil on to a specialist teacher without discussing it first.
payload.explanation: Immediately correcting a technically poor embouchure prevents physical injury and bad habits from developing.

payload.snippet: Jake finds a rare vintage guitar at a car boot sale for ten pounds. When he gets it home he realises it may be a historically significant instrument worth considerably more.
options: He has it assessed by a reputable musical instrument dealer before doing anything else.
He sells it online immediately for fifty pounds to make a quick profit before someone claims it.
He takes it apart to check for hidden serial numbers that might confirm its value.
He uses it for daily practice because it sounds exceptional and he owns it legally.
payload.explanation: Getting a professional assessment before any sale, modification, or extended use is the responsible step with a potentially valuable instrument.

payload.snippet: Clara is rehearsing for a school concert when the accompanist makes repeated errors in the same place, and the rehearsal time is running short.
options: She adjusts the tempo slightly to give the accompanist more time in the difficult passage and continues without making the errors a big deal.
She asks the accompanist to practise the section alone at home and moves on without them for now.
She plays through the section herself on the piano to show the accompanist how it should sound.
She tells the music teacher that the accompanist is not ready for the concert.
payload.explanation: Adjusting tempo to support a struggling accompanist during limited rehearsal time is collaborative and constructive.

payload.snippet: Oliver is recording a demo at a home studio when he notices that the recording contains a clearly audible click at the beginning of every bar, which he eventually traces to the CPU fan on his laptop.
options: He moves the laptop further from the microphone and uses a noise gate plugin before recording the final takes.
He re-records everything at twice the speed so the fan noise is less noticeable per second.
He accepts the clicks as background ambience and submits the demo as is.
He edits out every click manually in the waveform editor before submission.
payload.explanation: Physical separation and a noise gate address the source and the symptom of laptop fan interference in recording.

payload.snippet: Maya is in a music exam when she realises thirty seconds in that she has memorised the wrong piece and is playing a different one than the examiner is following.
options: She stops, tells the examiner politely, and asks to restart with the correct piece.
She continues playing the piece she knows and hopes the examiner will mark her on what she plays.
She tries to transition from her memorised piece to the correct one mid-performance.
She plays the wrong piece to the end and then explains the mistake in her written feedback form.
payload.explanation: Stopping and asking to restart is the only correct response when you realise you are playing the wrong piece in a formal examination.

payload.snippet: Ben is performing at an open-mic night when a drunk heckler in the audience interrupts his song twice.
options: He pauses briefly, says something lighthearted, and resumes performing without engaging in a back-and-forth.
He stops the song and asks the venue staff to remove the heckler before he will continue.
He responds directly to the heckler with a cutting remark to assert control of the room.
He plays louder to drown out the heckler for the remainder of his set.
payload.explanation: A brief lighthearted response followed by resuming the performance keeps control of the room without escalating.

payload.snippet: Anna is teaching a pupil who is technically talented but refuses to practise scales, claiming they are boring and pointless.
options: She explains the specific technique each scale builds and ties it to a passage in a piece the pupil loves.
She removes scales from the lesson until the pupil agrees to practise them at home.
She tells the pupil that scales are required for their grade exam and leaves it at that.
She finds a different teacher who uses a methodology without technical exercises.
payload.explanation: Connecting scales to music the pupil loves makes the purpose concrete and motivates practice.

payload.snippet: Jake is part of a school band that is supposed to perform at an assembly in an hour when the keyboard player does not arrive and is not answering their phone.
options: He informs the music teacher immediately and they together decide whether to perform without keyboard or replace with a simpler arrangement.
He starts trying to learn the keyboard part himself on his instrument in the remaining time.
He tells the rest of the band the performance is cancelled and they should go back to class.
He calls all the keyboard player's friends in the school to track them down.
payload.explanation: Immediate teacher notification when a performer goes missing allows a decision to be made with enough time to adapt.

payload.snippet: Clara overhears two members of her choir gossiping about a third member's voice quality in a way that would be hurtful if overheard.
options: She speaks to the two members privately and asks them to keep choir feedback constructive and within the group's values.
She tells the choir director so the two members can be formally warned.
She stands near the person being gossiped about to make sure they do not overhear.
She says nothing because gossip is not her responsibility to manage.
payload.explanation: Addressing gossip privately and reinforcing group values is the proportionate first response before escalating to a director.

payload.snippet: Oliver is playing in an exam when he notices a parallel melody piece that sounds very similar to a copyrighted pop song he has been asked to arrange for a competition.
options: He checks the competition rules about copyright, substitutes the problematic passage with an original bridge, and discloses the similarity to the competition organiser.
He submits the arrangement and notes in the submission form that it was inspired by the pop song.
He changes the key and rhythm of the similar passage so it no longer sounds obviously related.
He withdraws the arrangement entirely and submits a completely different piece instead.
payload.explanation: Copyright in competition arrangements requires rule-checking, modification, and organiser disclosure — not relying on inspiration as a defence.

payload.snippet: Maya is a student composer who submits a piece for a local prize and wins, but later discovers she accidentally included eight bars that are near-identical to a published work she had studied closely.
options: She contacts the prize organisers immediately, discloses the similarity, and offers to withdraw if the committee deems it appropriate.
She keeps the prize and resolves to be more careful in future compositions.
She contacts only the original composer to apologise rather than the prize organisers.
She revises the work and resubmits the corrected version without mentioning the original submission.
payload.explanation: Accidental musical plagiarism in a prize entry requires immediate disclosure to the organisers — keeping the prize while knowing about the similarity is dishonest.

payload.snippet: Ben is asked to play the organ at a friend's wedding service. During the ceremony he loses his place in the hymn and plays three bars of silence while flicking through his score.
options: He finds his place and re-enters on the next strong beat as smoothly as possible.
He plays whatever notes come to mind to fill the silence while he searches the score.
He stops playing and signals to the congregation to continue unaccompanied.
He closes the score and plays the melody from memory, hoping his version is close enough.
payload.explanation: Finding your place and re-entering on a strong beat is the most seamless recovery from a lost page mid-ceremony.

payload.snippet: Anna discovers that her music-streaming playlist used for a warm-up class contains a track with explicit lyrics she was not aware of, and the class includes young children.
options: She skips the track immediately, apologises to any parents present, and audits her playlist before the next session.
She turns the volume down so the lyrics are less intelligible and finishes the warm-up.
She keeps the track running and tells the children not to listen to the words.
She ends the warm-up early to avoid playing any more of the unreviewed playlist.
payload.explanation: Skipping immediately, apologising, and auditing the playlist before next use is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Tom is refereeing a youth football match when both team coaches simultaneously start shouting contradictory instructions to their players from the sideline, making it impossible for the players to hear each other or focus.
options: He stops play, walks to the touchline, and calmly reminds both coaches of the sideline conduct expectations before restarting.
He ignores the shouting and lets the coaches manage their own sidelines during play.
He issues both coaches a yellow card from the touch line without stopping play.
He asks the team captains to go and tell their coaches to be quiet.
payload.explanation: Stopping play and directly addressing the coaches is the only way to restore a focused playing environment.

payload.snippet: Anna is a sports coach when one of her athletes discloses that a coach at their previous club used to make them train through pain they had reported, leading to a stress fracture that took six months to heal.
options: She listens fully, thanks the athlete for sharing, and explains that her approach here is always to refer to the medical team when an athlete reports pain.
She reassures the athlete that she is different and moves on to the training session.
She contacts the previous club to inform them of the disclosure.
She asks the athlete to write down the details and submit them to the club as a formal complaint.
payload.explanation: Listening, validating, and explaining the current safe practice address both the athlete's concern and the culture going forward.

payload.snippet: Jake is a young cricket player on a school tour abroad when a teammate who has been struggling with the trip says he wants to go home early and stops speaking to others in the group.
options: Jake tells the tour manager privately about the teammate's withdrawal, while continuing to include the teammate in normal group activities.
Jake reassures the teammate himself and promises to keep it private without telling any adults.
Jake posts in the group chat asking everyone to be nice to the teammate who is having a hard time.
Jake gives the teammate some space for the rest of the tour and checks in again on the last day.
payload.explanation: Reporting withdrawal to the tour manager ensures adult support while private inclusion maintains dignity.

payload.snippet: Clara is a gymnastics coach when a gymnast achieves a personal best vault on a surface she used without permission because the official surface was occupied. The unofficial surface has no edge safety mat.
options: She praises the vault performance and separately addresses the safety boundary that was crossed — using any equipment without permission or proper safety matting is non-negotiable.
She validates the personal best fully and notes the safety issue in her session plan for later.
She tells the gymnast the vault does not count because it was on the wrong surface.
She completes the session normally and adds safety rules to the next session's briefing instead.
payload.explanation: Performance and safety must both be addressed — one does not override the other.

payload.snippet: Oliver is the team manager for a junior rugby club when he discovers that one of the volunteer coaches has been giving under-sixteen players supplements he describes as 'protein boosters' without parental consent or medical advice.
options: He removes the coach from all contact with players immediately, informs the parents of all players who may have received supplements, and reports the incident to the national governing body's safeguarding team.
He speaks to the coach privately and warns him never to give supplements again.
He contacts the supplement supplier to confirm the product is safe for minors before deciding on next steps.
He sends a general note to parents about club supplement policy without identifying the specific incident.
payload.explanation: Unsolicited supplement use with minors is a safeguarding matter requiring immediate removal, parent notification, and NGB reporting.

payload.snippet: Maya is a PE teacher when a student refuses to participate in the swimming lesson because they are embarrassed about wearing a swimsuit in front of their classmates.
options: She speaks to the student privately, acknowledges the concern without judgment, and explores whether a different swimwear option or a private changing arrangement would help.
She marks the student as absent for the lesson and does not raise the issue further.
She asks the class to focus on their own swimming so the student has less pressure.
She tells the student that swimming is mandatory and they must participate regardless.
payload.explanation: Addressing body image concerns privately and adapting where possible is the inclusive and respectful response.

payload.snippet: Ben is a sports journalist attending an international athletics event when he witnesses a competitor collapse just after crossing the finish line in first place. Medical staff rush onto the track.
options: He continues reporting the event but contacts his editor immediately to flag the developing situation rather than assuming the collapse is minor.
He approaches the medical team to ask for an update on the athlete's condition for his report.
He publishes a brief update on social media stating the athlete has collapsed before any medical information is confirmed.
He waits until after the medal ceremony to mention the collapse in his full match report.
payload.explanation: A journalist should flag a developing medical situation to their editor immediately without speculating on severity or seeking medical information at the scene.

payload.snippet: Anna is the manager of a junior sports team when she learns that a parent has been sending intimidating messages to a teenage player on the opposing team after a cup match because they disagreed with a foul call.
options: She contacts the parent immediately to make clear this behaviour is unacceptable, informs the league's disciplinary officer, and checks on the wellbeing of the targeted player.
She contacts the other team's manager to apologise and hopes the issue resolves informally.
She warns the parent at the next training session in front of other parents to set a clear example.
She waits to see whether the targeted player or their parents make a formal complaint before acting.
payload.explanation: Parent online intimidation of a player requires immediate parental contact, league disciplinary reporting, and player welfare check — not waiting for a complaint.

payload.snippet: Jake is a swimming club coach when he notices one of his fastest swimmers has lost a significant amount of weight in a short period and is performing worse despite increasing training. The swimmer has become withdrawn.
options: He speaks to the swimmer privately after training, checks in on their wellbeing without mentioning weight directly, and follows the club's safeguarding protocol to report his concern.
He reduces the swimmer's training load and monitors their performance over the next month.
He asks other swimmers if they have noticed anything different about their teammate.
He contacts the swimmer's parents to discuss the weight loss before following any formal protocol.
payload.explanation: Performance decline combined with weight loss and withdrawal signals a potential eating disorder — safeguarding protocol, not parent contact by the coach, is the correct response.
