payload.snippet: Oliver is given a homework task on a topic he knows very well and thinks the work is too easy.
options: He completes the task thoroughly and then, if he wants more challenge, asks his teacher if there is extension work available.
He submits minimal work since he already knows the content.
He rewrites the homework as a much harder version and submits that instead.
He tells the teacher the work is too easy and asks to be excused from it.
payload.explanation: Completing the set task thoroughly and asking for extension work is the right approach to easy homework.

payload.snippet: Anna is completing online homework when she discovers the answer to a question is available as the first result on a search engine. She is tempted to just copy it.
options: She uses the search result to understand the concept and then writes the answer in her own words.
She copies the answer directly since it is publicly available.
She copies it and changes a few words.
She does not search at all and guesses instead.
payload.explanation: Understanding first and writing in your own words is the correct use of online resources — direct copying is plagiarism.

payload.snippet: Jake's school has a no-phone policy but he uses his phone to take a photo of the homework assignment written on the whiteboard. A teacher confiscates the phone.
options: He explains calmly why he used the phone and accepts the consequence while asking if there is an alternative way to record the assignment.
He argues that using the phone for school purposes should be an exception.
He denies using it for the assignment and claims it was already in his hand.
He refuses to hand over the phone since it contains a photo he needs.
payload.explanation: Accepting the consequence while calmly explaining the context and asking about alternatives is the appropriate response to breaking a school rule for a practical reason.

payload.snippet: Maya is given a homework task she knows is exactly the same as one she completed last year. She still has the old version.
options: She completes the task fresh to test whether her understanding has improved since last year.
She submits the old version with only her name changed.
She uses the old version as a reference but writes a completely new version.
She tells the teacher the task has already been done and asks for a different one.
payload.explanation: Redoing old material tests genuine learning — submitting the old version is dishonest regardless of whether the task has changed.

payload.snippet: Tom is working on a take-home test and his parent offers to give him the answers to the questions he is stuck on.
options: He thanks his parent but explains it is a test and he needs to answer it himself.
He accepts the help since his parent is at home and the test does not say no adults.
He accepts help on the hardest question only.
He lets his parent look at his answers and confirm them before submitting.
payload.explanation: A take-home test is an individual assessment — any parental input on answers undermines the purpose regardless of the setting.

payload.snippet: Clara discovers halfway through a long-term project that her initial research was based on a flawed premise and a significant part of the work is therefore incorrect.
options: She revises her understanding, restarts the incorrect sections, and — if the deadline needs to be extended — asks the teacher honestly for one.
She submits the flawed version since restarting is too much work.
She corrects only the parts most likely to be marked.
She asks a classmate how they approached it and adapts their structure to fit her topic.
payload.explanation: Restarting flawed work — and seeking an extension if genuinely needed — is better than submitting incorrect work or copying another student's structure.

payload.snippet: Oliver is given homework in a subject he finds very difficult and his parent suggests a private tutor.
options: He tries the homework independently first and identifies specific areas where he struggles, so that any tutoring is targeted.
He waits for the tutor before attempting the homework.
He tells his parent the tutor is unnecessary since he just needs more time.
He asks his parent to complete the difficult sections while he does the easier ones.
payload.explanation: Attempting the work independently first reveals specific gaps — targeted tutoring is more effective than blanket help.

payload.snippet: Anna is completing an individual research essay when she and a classmate independently reach very similar conclusions using different sources.
options: She checks that her essay reflects her own reasoning and sources without duplicating the classmate's wording, and submits her own work.
She asks the classmate to change their conclusion so the essays differ.
She changes her conclusion to be deliberately different from the classmate's.
She tells the teacher they arrived at the same conclusion to avoid any suspicion.
payload.explanation: Similar independent conclusions are academically normal if the work is genuinely your own — changing your honest conclusion to appear different is academically dishonest.

payload.snippet: Jake receives a very positive mark for homework that he feels he did not fully understand when completing. He got lucky with his answers.
options: He goes back over the material to ensure he actually understands the topic, regardless of the mark.
He moves on since the mark shows he understood it.
He tells his teacher he does not understand the material even though his work was marked correct.
He submits a question to the teacher asking if he was right for the right reasons.
payload.explanation: A correct answer without understanding leaves a knowledge gap — reviewing the material ensures the learning is solid.

payload.snippet: Maya is given a homework assignment to interview a family member about a historical event. She does not feel comfortable asking anyone in her family.
options: She explains this to her teacher and asks whether she can interview a willing neighbour, older community member, or use an archived oral history instead.
She invents responses and attributes them to a made-up family member.
She submits the assignment without the interview section.
She asks a classmate to share the interview they did with their family.
payload.explanation: Explaining a genuine personal constraint and proposing an alternative is the honest and constructive response to a homework task that does not fit your situation.

payload.snippet: Tom is given a science experiment homework that requires a specific material he does not have at home.
options: He asks his teacher before the deadline whether the material can be substituted or whether the school can supply it.
He uses a different material and does not disclose the substitution.
He submits results he predicts the experiment would show without doing it.
He skips the experiment section and submits only the theory.
payload.explanation: Asking the teacher in advance about a missing material allows for a sanctioned substitution or supply — substituting without disclosure or skipping is not transparent.

payload.snippet: Clara is working on a creative homework project when she realises her idea is very similar to a project she submitted last year.
options: She develops the idea in a different direction so the work is genuinely new.
She submits the same core idea since it is a different year.
She changes only the presentation format and reuses the content.
She tells the teacher the idea was inspired by her previous project.
payload.explanation: Genuinely developing a new angle on a previous idea is required — recycling old work as new is academically dishonest.

payload.snippet: Oliver is completing a science homework that requires him to record an experiment result. His experiment did not go as expected and the result disproves his hypothesis.
options: He records the actual result honestly and discusses in his write-up why it may have differed from his prediction.
He adjusts the result to match his hypothesis since the experiment probably went wrong.
He omits the result section and focuses on the theory.
He repeats the experiment until he gets the result he expected.
payload.explanation: Recording an unexpected result and analysing it is scientifically correct — fabricating or omitting results is scientific dishonesty.

payload.snippet: Anna receives homework that requires her to practise a skill by doing twenty repetitions, but after ten she feels confident in the skill.
options: She completes all twenty as requested, since the teacher set the number for a reason.
She stops at ten since she has understood the skill.
She does fifteen as a compromise.
She tells the teacher she understood it after ten and did not need to do more.
payload.explanation: Following the full homework task as set shows respect for the teacher's pedagogical reasoning — deciding when you have done enough is the student's assumption to make.

payload.snippet: Jake is given a homework task to practise a skill using a specific method the class has been taught. He finds a different method online that he thinks is better.
options: He uses the method the teacher set for the homework, and if interested, shows the teacher the alternative method he found.
He uses the alternative method since it is better.
He uses both methods and presents both to cover all bases.
He argues with the teacher that their method is outdated.
payload.explanation: Practising the taught method is the homework objective — sharing the alternative method with the teacher is an appropriate way to explore further.

payload.snippet: Anna starts at a new school mid-year and the existing class seems to have very established social groups already.
options: She identifies shared-interest activities like clubs or sport teams as the most natural route into a social group.
She waits for someone to invite her into a group rather than seeking entry herself.
She tries to insert herself into the closest group regardless of shared interests.
She gives up on making friends in the first month and focuses only on academic work.
payload.explanation: Interest-based entry points — clubs, teams, activities — are more natural and effective than cold social insertion.

payload.snippet: Jake is befriending a new student when he discovers the student has been spreading rumours about a mutual friend. He is unsure if the rumours are true.
options: He addresses it directly with the new student, telling them the rumours are affecting someone he cares about and asking them to stop.
He spreads counter-rumours to undermine the new student's credibility.
He distances himself from both without saying why.
He immediately tells the mutual friend what the new student has been saying.
payload.explanation: Addressing rumour-spreading directly and early is more productive than counter-measures or triangulation.

payload.snippet: Maya is forming a friendship with a new classmate who has different values on an issue Maya feels strongly about.
options: She decides whether the difference is a dealbreaker or something she can respectfully disagree on, and discusses it honestly with the new friend.
She changes her own position to match the new friend's to avoid conflict.
She decides they cannot be friends because of the value difference.
She avoids all topics where their views might differ.
payload.explanation: Deciding whether a value difference is a dealbreaker — rather than suppressing or avoiding it — is a more honest basis for friendship.

payload.snippet: Tom's new friend group includes someone who consistently makes unkind comments disguised as jokes.
options: He tells that person privately that the comments bother him, even if they are meant as jokes.
He laughs along since everyone else does.
He leaves the friend group rather than raising it.
He complains to others in the group about the person behind their back.
payload.explanation: Telling someone privately that their jokes are hurtful is more likely to change the behaviour than avoidance or indirect complaints.

payload.snippet: Clara has been making a new friend online through a gaming platform. The friend is asking to meet in person.
options: She tells a parent about the friendship and the request, and does not agree to meet without her parent's knowledge and involvement.
She agrees to meet at a public place since the person seems friendly.
She refuses and immediately blocks the person since any online friend asking to meet is suspicious.
She asks her friend what they look like before deciding whether to tell her parent.
payload.explanation: Online friendships moving to in-person require parental knowledge and involvement — neither reflexive trust nor reflexive blocking is the right response.

payload.snippet: Oliver's new friend circle has one person who always tries to steer activities away from things Oliver enjoys. Oliver is not sure if it is personal.
options: He raises it privately with the friend who seems to be steering things and asks if they can include everyone's preferences.
He stops suggesting his own preferences to keep the peace.
He organises a separate activity for the friends he gets on better with.
He tells the others in the group what he has noticed.
payload.explanation: Raising an observed pattern directly and kindly with the person involved is more effective than adapting around it or involving others.

payload.snippet: Anna meets a new friend who is significantly older than her and wants to spend a lot of time one-on-one.
options: She tells a trusted adult about the new friendship and follows their guidance on appropriate time together.
She keeps the friendship private since adults would not understand.
She refuses to spend any time with the older friend since age gaps are always a bad sign.
She meets the friend in public places without telling her parent.
payload.explanation: Significant age gaps in new friendships benefit from adult knowledge and guidance — secrecy or reflexive avoidance are both the wrong responses.

payload.snippet: Jake's new friend confides that they are being bullied by another student. Jake witnessed some of it.
options: He encourages his friend to report it to a trusted adult, and offers to support them or corroborate what he saw if they are comfortable.
He tells the bully to stop directly, without involving adults.
He reports it himself without telling his friend first.
He listens but says there is nothing he can do since he was not the target.
payload.explanation: Encouraging the friend to report, and offering support, respects their agency while ensuring the issue gets addressed.

payload.snippet: Maya joins a new class activity and befriends someone who her existing friends warn her about, saying the person has a bad reputation.
options: She forms her own opinion based on her direct experience of the person, while staying alert to whether the warnings reflect anything she actually observes.
She immediately drops the new friendship out of loyalty to her existing friends.
She ignores the warnings entirely since her existing friends must be biased.
She tells the new friend what the warnings were about.
payload.explanation: Forming your own opinion while staying observant is more fair and accurate than either blind loyalty or blind trust.

payload.snippet: Tom's new friend seems to have different social energy — they need more quiet time and pull back from plans more than Tom does.
options: He talks to his friend about their different needs and finds an arrangement that works for both.
He pushes his friend to be more social since that is what he prefers.
He decides they are incompatible and stops making plans.
He adjusts entirely to his friend's pace without mentioning his own needs.
payload.explanation: Discussing different social energy needs openly and finding a middle ground respects both friends.

payload.snippet: Clara meets a new potential friend who immediately asks for personal contact details during their first conversation.
options: She shares details only on platforms she is comfortable with and uses her usual privacy settings.
She shares all her details since the person seems friendly and trustworthy.
She refuses to share any contact information and ends the conversation.
She shares details and then reports the request to a parent.
payload.explanation: Sharing contact details selectively and with your usual privacy settings is the balanced response to a first-meeting request.

payload.snippet: Oliver is forming a new friendship when he realises his new friend has been talking about him to others more than he is comfortable with.
options: He tells his friend directly that he would prefer they keep their conversations more private.
He stops sharing anything personal with the friend.
He tells the same things to more people to neutralise the impact.
He ends the friendship without explaining why.
payload.explanation: A direct, calm conversation about privacy expectations is the most constructive response to oversharing.

payload.snippet: Anna is the only person from her background in a new friend group and sometimes feels her perspective is not fully understood.
options: She shares her perspective when relevant and, when misunderstood, takes a moment to explain calmly.
She says nothing to avoid making the group uncomfortable.
She leaves the group since she feels she does not belong.
She brings up every instance of misunderstanding publicly.
payload.explanation: Sharing and explaining your perspective when relevant — without demanding constant accommodation — is the most sustainable approach.

payload.snippet: Jake becomes close to a new friend very quickly and then has a significant falling out over something minor.
options: He reflects on whether the intensity of the friendship developed faster than the trust it needed, and has an honest conversation with the friend about what happened.
He ends the friendship since clearly it was not meant to be.
He tells all their mutual friends about the falling out to get support.
He pretends nothing happened to restore the friendship quickly.
payload.explanation: Reflecting on the pace of a friendship's development — and having an honest conversation — is more productive than abandonment or pretence.

payload.snippet: Maya discovers that a new friend has only been spending time with her because they want access to Maya's larger social circle.
options: She tells the friend she has noticed the pattern and asks directly whether they are genuinely interested in being friends.
She immediately cuts off the friend and warns her other friends.
She uses the friend in return since the friendship is transactional anyway.
She says nothing but stops making herself available.
payload.explanation: A direct honest question gives the friend a chance to be genuine — silent withdrawal or retaliation are less constructive.

payload.snippet: Priya moves to a new city and on her first day at school nobody sits with her at lunch, but then a girl named Suki smiles and waves her over.
options: Priya walks to Suki's table and says hello
Priya stares at her food and says nothing
Priya pretends she is not hungry and goes outside
Priya sits alone at a different table
payload.explanation: Accepting a friendly invitation takes courage but leads to new friendships.

payload.snippet: At swimming lessons, Leo realises he forgot his goggles and the boy next to him, Finn, has a spare pair in his bag and notices Leo looking worried.
options: Finn offers to lend Leo his spare goggles
Finn puts both pairs in his bag and says nothing
Finn tells the coach Leo is not prepared
Finn leaves his bag on the bench
payload.explanation: Sharing equipment is a kind way to help someone feel welcome.

payload.snippet: Roxy arrives at a birthday party where she knows only the birthday girl, and the other guests are already playing a game together in a tight circle.
options: Roxy asks if she can join the game
Roxy stands outside the circle and feels too shy to speak
Roxy pulls out her phone and ignores everyone
Roxy tells the birthday girl the party is boring
payload.explanation: Asking to join is the fastest way to become part of the group.

payload.snippet: Jake and his new classmate Omar both reach for the last red pencil at the art table at exactly the same moment and then look at each other.
options: They agree to share the pencil and take turns
Jake grabs it first and puts it in his drawer
Omar says finders keepers and walks off
Both pull hard until the pencil breaks
payload.explanation: Sharing a resource fairly turns a potential argument into a friendly moment.

payload.snippet: Danielle's new neighbour Chloe is practicing riding her bicycle and keeps wobbling; Danielle used to struggle with that too and watches from her front step.
options: Danielle goes over and offers to run beside Chloe while she practices
Danielle laughs at Chloe wobbling
Danielle goes back inside so Chloe is not embarrassed
Danielle shouts encouragement from her doorstep
payload.explanation: Offering practical help based on shared experience builds friendship quickly.

payload.snippet: Anna is at a theme park when she realises her phone is missing. She last remembers having it at a ride with a locker system.
options: She returns to the ride, checks the locker system, and then goes to the theme park's lost property office.
She reports it stolen to the park security before checking whether she left it in the locker.
She posts on social media that she lost her phone at the theme park.
She starts walking back to where she remembers using it last without telling anyone where she is going.
payload.explanation: Checking the locker system first — before reporting theft — is the correct sequence, since most 'lost' phones at rides are left in lockers.

payload.snippet: Jake loses a valuable sports trophy he borrowed from his school to show family, and cannot find it despite searching at home.
options: He informs the school honestly, explains the situation, and discusses replacement or compensation.
He waits to see if it turns up before saying anything to the school.
He purchases a similar trophy to replace it without telling the school what happened.
He reports it as stolen to avoid being blamed.
payload.explanation: Honest early disclosure to the school — including offering compensation — is more trustworthy than delaying, substituting, or fabricating a theft.

payload.snippet: Maya finds a bag in a public toilet containing what appear to be personal belongings and a small amount of cash.
options: She takes the bag to the nearest police station or hands it to a staff member at the nearest venue.
She takes the cash since the bag was abandoned.
She looks through the bag for contact details and calls the owner.
She leaves the bag where she found it since the owner may come back.
payload.explanation: A found bag with cash requires formal handling — keeping cash, self-initiated contact, or leaving it unattended are all incorrect.

payload.snippet: Tom has lost an item that is covered by his household insurance but is not sure whether making a claim is worth it given the excess.
options: He checks the policy terms, calculates whether the payout after the excess is worthwhile, and makes an accurate claim if it is.
He exaggerates the item's value on the claim to cover the excess.
He claims for several other minor losses at the same time to make the claim worthwhile.
He does not investigate the insurance option at all.
payload.explanation: An honest claim on accurate terms is the correct use of insurance — inflation or bundling multiple claims dishonestly constitutes insurance fraud.

payload.snippet: Clara loses a piece of jewellery at a friend's house and is not certain she lost it there.
options: She asks her friend if they found anything, explains what the item looks like, and accepts the outcome gracefully.
She searches her friend's house herself without asking.
She accuses her friend of taking it before checking other places.
She says nothing to her friend and replaces the item.
payload.explanation: A polite direct question to the friend — rather than searching without permission or making accusations — is the correct approach when uncertain where an item was lost.

payload.snippet: Oliver finds a bag of groceries left on a bus. They include perishable food items.
options: He leaves the bag with the bus driver and describes what is inside.
He takes the food since it will be wasted otherwise.
He leaves the bag on the seat since it is not his responsibility.
He takes the bag off the bus and looks for the owner himself.
payload.explanation: Leaving found items with the driver is the correct bus procedure — the driver can ensure it goes to lost property.

payload.snippet: Anna finds a set of keys with a car key fob but no other identifying information.
options: She hands them in to the nearest police station.
She presses the fob in the car park nearby to find the car and puts the keys on it.
She keeps them in case no one claims them.
She tries each key fob in the car park to find the matching car.
payload.explanation: Unidentifiable found keys go to the police — attempting to locate the car yourself is not the correct lost property procedure.

payload.snippet: Jake has lost his passport and has a flight in two days.
options: He applies for an emergency passport through the official government process immediately, and contacts the airline to explain the situation.
He uses an old expired passport hoping it will not be noticed.
He asks a friend who looks similar to lend him their passport.
He cancels the trip and accepts the loss.
payload.explanation: An emergency passport application is the legitimate option when a passport is lost before imminent travel — using someone else's passport is identity fraud.

payload.snippet: Maya finds a memory stick left in a library computer.
options: She removes it from the computer and hands it to the library desk.
She checks the files on the memory stick to find out who it belongs to.
She keeps it since it was abandoned.
She leaves it in the computer since the owner may return.
payload.explanation: Memory sticks left in public computers should be removed and handed to staff — checking the files violates the owner's privacy.

payload.snippet: Tom loses his student rail card and is mid-journey.
options: He speaks to the conductor honestly, explains the situation, and offers to buy a standard fare or contact the rail company about a replacement.
He hides in the toilet until the conductor passes.
He tells the conductor he left it at home and will bring it tomorrow.
He asks a friend with a similar card to send him a photo of theirs.
payload.explanation: Honest disclosure to the conductor and an offer of payment or replacement is the correct response to a lost railcard mid-journey.

payload.snippet: Clara finds a USB drive outside her workplace containing files. A folder is labelled with a company name.
options: She hands it to her manager or IT department without looking at the files.
She opens the files to identify who it belongs to.
She hands it in with a note of what files she saw when opening it.
She posts on a local community board asking if anyone lost a USB.
payload.explanation: Unidentified storage media found outside a workplace must be handled through IT — opening files is a security risk and a privacy breach.

payload.snippet: Oliver thinks an expensive item he lost has been picked up by someone he knows, based on circumstantial evidence.
options: He raises his concern directly and calmly with the person, presenting what he observed and asking for an explanation.
He tells mutual friends about his suspicion before speaking to the person.
He searches the person's belongings when they are not looking.
He reports it to the police as a theft based on his suspicion.
payload.explanation: Raising a concern directly with the person, calmly and based on observable facts, is the correct first step before any other action.

payload.snippet: Anna loses an important document that she needs for an official appointment the following week.
options: She contacts the issuing authority immediately to explain and arrange a replacement or certified copy.
She creates a photocopy of an older version and hopes it is accepted.
She attends the appointment without the document and explains on the day.
She postpones the appointment without contacting anyone.
payload.explanation: Contacting the issuing authority as soon as possible for a replacement gives the best chance of having the right document in time.

payload.snippet: Jake loses a rented bicycle in a city. He locked it but the lock was cut.
options: He reports the theft to the police, gets a crime reference number, and reports it to the hire company.
He returns the hire key and says nothing, hoping the company does not notice.
He pays for a replacement privately before the company notices.
He tells the company only if they contact him first.
payload.explanation: A bicycle theft while rented requires a police report for the crime reference number — the hire company must also be informed regardless of who contacts whom first.

payload.snippet: Maya finds a large amount of cash in an envelope on the street with no identifying information.
options: She hands it in to the nearest police station and provides her contact details as the finder.
She keeps it since there is no way to identify the owner.
She donates it to a charity since keeping it would be wrong but there is no way to return it.
She posts about it on local social media and keeps it until someone claims it.
payload.explanation: Found cash must be handed to the police — as the finder, you may be entitled to it if unclaimed after a period, but only through the official process.

payload.snippet: Grace puts her favourite bookmark inside her library book before returning it; when she opens her next book at home she realises the bookmark is gone.
options: Grace goes back to the library and asks the librarian to check the returned book
Grace buys a new bookmark and does not tell anyone
Grace accuses her brother of taking it
Grace waits until her mum offers to help
payload.explanation: Retracing the last known place of an item is the most efficient first step.

payload.snippet: Finn sets his lunch bag on the bench during football practice and when he returns to the bench after the session his bag is missing.
options: Finn asks his teammates and coach if anyone saw the bag before checking lost property
Finn assumes someone stole it and tells his teacher
Finn walks home without eating and says nothing
Finn checks lost property first before asking anyone
payload.explanation: Asking witnesses who were present is faster than checking unrelated places first.

payload.snippet: Isla loans her coloured pencils to a classmate during art class; at the end of the day she cannot find them in her desk and is not sure who borrowed them last.
options: Isla asks the last person she remembers lending them to if they returned them
Isla empties the whole classroom's pencil boxes looking for them
Isla tells her teacher a classmate stole her pencils
Isla buys new ones and decides never to lend things again
payload.explanation: Following the chain of borrowing is the logical way to find a lent item.

payload.snippet: Oscar's science project worksheet is due tomorrow and he cannot find it anywhere in his bag or room; he remembers working on it at the kitchen table yesterday.
options: Oscar searches the kitchen table area and checks if the paper slipped under furniture
Oscar tells his teacher the dog ate it
Oscar copies answers from a friend at the last minute
Oscar starts the worksheet from scratch through the night
payload.explanation: Returning to the last place you worked is the most productive search starting point.

payload.snippet: Maya wears her grandmother's ring to a family picnic; when washing her hands at the park she realises the ring is not on her finger and panics.
options: Maya retraces her steps to the tap and checks the grass nearby immediately
Maya tells everyone the ring was stolen
Maya drives home assuming she left it there
Maya waits for her parents to notice and tell them first
payload.explanation: Acting quickly while memory is fresh dramatically improves the chance of finding lost jewellery.

payload.snippet: Isla's violin bow snaps at the stick during practice. Her lesson is tomorrow and a replacement bow costs a lot of money.
options: She tells her parents immediately so they can contact the music teacher about borrowing a spare
She tries to tape the bow back together herself
She hides the bow and says she forgot her instrument
She practices with her fingers on the strings and says nothing
payload.explanation: A borrowed spare bow is the practical short-term fix; honesty avoids bigger problems.

payload.snippet: Marcus drops his tablet and the screen cracks badly. It still works but pieces of glass are showing.
options: He tells his parents straight away and stops using it until the glass is made safe
He keeps using it so the glass cut is not noticed
He covers the crack with stickers and hopes no one sees
He blames the table for being slippery
payload.explanation: Broken glass screens are a safety risk — reporting promptly protects fingers and avoids the problem growing.

payload.snippet: Amara borrows her cousin's remote-control boat for the weekend and it sinks in the pond, filling with water. The motor makes a grinding noise.
options: She retrieves it, drains the water, and tells her cousin and parents honestly what happened
She dries it quietly and returns it without mentioning the damage
She leaves it in the pond and tells her cousin she lost it
She orders a cheap replacement and swaps it without saying anything
payload.explanation: Returning borrowed property honestly, even when damaged, is the only respectful response.

payload.snippet: Will's brand-new football boot splits along the sole during his first match on a cold day. The coach is waiting for him to come back on.
options: He tells the coach his boot has split and asks to sit out until it is safe
He tapes the sole with grass and re-enters the pitch
He plays in one boot hoping no one notices
He pretends he has a cramp so he can leave without explaining
payload.explanation: A coach needs to know about equipment failure — playing on risks injury.

payload.snippet: Freya's telescope for the school astronomy project has a cracked lens. The project deadline is in three days.
options: She emails her teacher explaining the situation and asks if the school has a spare telescope she can borrow
She does the project from memory without observing
She uses her phone camera and labels the blurry photos as telescope shots
She buys a cheap replacement and does not tell her teacher
payload.explanation: Communicating a genuine equipment problem to a teacher is always the correct first step.

payload.snippet: Jonah's science fair model volcano, built over two weeks, falls off the table the night before the fair and shatters.
options: He calls a friend to help him rebuild the key parts overnight with simplified detail
He cries and refuses to attend the science fair
He blames his dog for being in the way
He takes a photo of the broken model and claims it was a deliberate art project
payload.explanation: A simplified rebuild done honestly is far better than missing the event or deceiving judges.

payload.snippet: Sofia's electric keyboard is left plugged in during a thunderstorm and the power surge kills it. Her recital is next week.
options: She tells her parents so they can check the insurance policy and contact the music teacher
She keeps pressing keys hoping it will start working
She tells the music teacher it was always faulty
She practises on a drawn keyboard diagram
payload.explanation: Power-surge damage may be covered by home insurance; reporting quickly opens that option.

payload.snippet: Tyler's skateboard deck snaps clean in half during a ramp session. Other skaters are waiting to use the ramp.
options: He moves off the ramp immediately, tells the session supervisor, and calls his parents
He tries to balance on both halves as if nothing happened
He leans the broken deck against the ramp and pretends he just finished
He borrows someone else's board without asking
payload.explanation: Clearing the ramp immediately and informing an adult is the safe and courteous response.

payload.snippet: Nia's robot kit motor burns out because she connected the wires incorrectly. The kit was a gift and she is embarrassed.
options: She tells her parents what happened and researches whether a replacement motor can be ordered
She reassembles the kit without the motor and says it was always decorative
She blames a faulty kit and asks for a full replacement
She hides the kit in her wardrobe
payload.explanation: Admitting a wiring mistake is how you learn electronics safely; replacement motors are usually affordable.

payload.snippet: Grace's pottery project cracks in the kiln at the art club. She was going to give it to her grandmother as a birthday gift.
options: She tells the art teacher and asks if she has time to make a replacement before the birthday
She glues the cracked pieces and presents it as intentional rustic art
She buys a cheap mug and claims she made it
She cancels giving Grandma a gift without explanation
payload.explanation: Honest communication with the teacher opens up a solution; trying to hide the crack is deceptive.

payload.snippet: Alex's drone crashes into a neighbour's garden and one of the rotors snaps. The drone lands in the neighbour's flower bed.
options: He knocks on the neighbour's door, apologises, retrieves the drone, and checks whether any flowers were damaged
He reaches over the fence without asking to grab the drone
He waits until dark to retrieve it
He pretends the drone was not his
payload.explanation: Introducing yourself and apologising immediately is the respectful way to handle a drone incident with neighbours.

payload.snippet: Eva's violin string snaps during a school concert and she is mid-performance.
options: She pauses, signals to the teacher watching from the wings, and waits calmly
She keeps bowing on the remaining strings playing wrong notes
She walks off stage without signalling
She starts crying loudly on stage
payload.explanation: A calm signal to a supervising adult is the professional response to an instrument failure on stage.

payload.snippet: Sam's ant farm cracks and ants begin escaping into his bedroom.
options: He places a damp cloth over the crack to slow the ants and calls Dad for help immediately
He stamps on the ants escaping
He seals the crack with chewing gum
He tells his mum the ants escaped on their own
payload.explanation: Containing the situation first, then getting adult help, is the right sequence.

payload.snippet: Lily's brand new camera drops when the strap snaps and the lens cap and filter ring crack.
options: She stops using it and shows her parents the damage so they can decide about repair
She tests the camera to see if it still works, risking further glass damage
She buys a new strap and pretends the lens crack was already there
She hides the damage and uses the camera at an angle
payload.explanation: Using a camera with a cracked lens risks further damage — an adult needs to assess it first.

payload.snippet: Ryan's mechanical pencil breaks in class during an important test and his spare pens are at home.
options: He raises his hand and quietly asks the teacher if he can borrow a pencil
He writes the whole test in his fingernail scratches on the paper
He copies from his neighbour using their pencil when they are not looking
He panics, puts his hand up, and shouts
payload.explanation: Asking the teacher quietly is the calm, correct response to a tool failing during a test.

payload.snippet: Ravi's long-board snaps in two while doing a jump at the skate park. He lands safely but his board is in pieces.
options: He picks up both pieces, leaves the ramp safely, and tells his parents it needs replacing
He tries to skate on the longer half
He leaves the broken pieces on the ramp for someone else to clear
He glues the board and goes back on the ramp the same day
payload.explanation: A snapped board is a safety hazard — both pieces must be cleared and the board not used until professionally assessed.

payload.snippet: Isla's kite string tangles badly in a tree and the spool mechanism breaks when she tries to pull it free.
options: She stops pulling, ties off the string, and asks an adult to help free it from the tree
She pulls harder and the string cuts her fingers
She leaves the whole kite in the tree and walks away
She cuts the string and abandons the spool
payload.explanation: Tugging a jammed mechanism causes injury — stopping and asking for help is always safer.

payload.snippet: Tom's science kit barometer tube cracks and the coloured liquid inside spills onto the table. He doesn't know if the liquid is safe.
options: He leaves the liquid alone, tells a parent, and reads the kit safety sheet
He wipes up the liquid with his bare hand
He drinks a small drop to check if it tastes safe
He throws the whole kit in the bin without telling anyone
payload.explanation: Unknown chemical spills require adult supervision and a check of safety instructions before clean-up.

payload.snippet: Maya's bicycle tyre explodes with a loud bang during a ride. She swerves but stays upright.
options: She pulls over safely, puts the bike down, and calls home for a pick-up
She rides slowly home on the flat tyre, damaging the rim
She tries to inflate the tyre with her mouth
She leaves the bike on the path and walks away
payload.explanation: Riding on a blown-out tyre destroys the rim — stopping immediately and calling for collection is right.

payload.snippet: Noah's RC car controller breaks mid-race and the car drives into a wall at full speed, cracking the chassis.
options: He retrieves the car, tells his dad the controller needs looking at, and stops the session for the day
He tapes the chassis and races it again
He blames the wall for being too close
He throws the car and controller away in frustration
payload.explanation: A broken controller is a safety issue for other people nearby — stopping the session is the responsible call.

payload.snippet: In a school group project, Priya does most of the research but the group votes to put Tom's name first on the title page because he presented it.
options: Priya speaks up before submission and asks that authors be listed in contribution order
Priya does future projects alone so this cannot happen again
Tom agrees but quietly changes it back later
Priya accepts it but refuses to contribute as much next time
payload.explanation: Authorship order should reflect contribution — raising it calmly before submission is the right moment.

payload.snippet: Marcus trains twice as hard as anyone else on the football team but is consistently picked last due to his smaller size.
options: The coach starts selecting based on demonstrated skill and effort, not size
Marcus quits the team
The other players tell Marcus to join a different sport
Marcus plays only in friendlies hoping never to be picked last
payload.explanation: Selection criteria should be transparent and based on relevant factors; raising the pattern with a coach is appropriate.

payload.snippet: Two students submit the same quality of maths work. One gets a commendation because the teacher knows their parent; the other receives average feedback.
options: The student who received average feedback asks the teacher for specific reasons their work didn't merit commendation
The student tells all classmates the teacher shows favouritism
The student copies the commended student's work next time
The student stops trying since effort isn't recognised
payload.explanation: Asking for specific, criteria-based feedback opens a dialogue and may reveal a genuine oversight.

payload.snippet: At a school fair, the stall rota is managed by a parent who gives their own child the most popular stall for the whole day.
options: Another parent notices and politely raises the allocation method with the organiser, suggesting a rotation
The other parents complain loudly in front of the children
The children argue over the popular stall in public
Everyone accepts the arrangement but it causes lasting resentment
payload.explanation: Raising a structural fairness issue with the organiser, not publicly, is the productive path.

payload.snippet: In a debate class, the teacher always gives one side more preparation time, meaning that side wins every debate.
options: Students ask the teacher to give both sides equal preparation time to make the debates meaningful
Students rig the debate outcomes in retaliation
Students stop preparing, knowing the outcome is predetermined
Students tell the headteacher the debate class is rigged
payload.explanation: Equal preparation time is a structural condition of fair debate — raising it directly with the teacher is correct.

payload.snippet: Zara and her friend both apply for the school council. Zara has significantly better ideas but loses because she is quieter and less popular.
options: The teachers introduce a blind policy review where ideas are read anonymously before voting
Zara refuses to accept the result
The school stops holding student council elections
Zara's friend uses Zara's ideas without crediting her
payload.explanation: Blind review processes reduce social-bias effects in selections meant to reward merit.

payload.snippet: A family has two children doing homework. One is allowed to use a quiet, tidy desk while the other must work at the noisy kitchen table.
options: The children negotiate a rota for the desk or ask a parent to find a quiet spot for both
One child always works at the desk without question
The child at the noisy table does poorer work and accepts it
The children swap without asking anyone
payload.explanation: Equal access to good study conditions directly affects academic outcomes — a rota is a fair structural fix.

payload.snippet: At a team bake sale, one student's items are priced lower because she is new and the others assume her baking isn't as good.
options: A teacher spots this and ensures all contributions are priced consistently
The new student underprices herself to try to fit in
The other students raise their own prices to compete
The new student sells nothing and feels excluded
payload.explanation: Price fairness at a shared event should be consistent regardless of the contributor's social status.

payload.snippet: A school sports day assigns running distance by gender: boys run 800m, girls run 400m.
options: A student asks whether students should be offered the choice of distance rather than being assigned by gender
Students refuse to participate in protest
Students accept the arrangement without question
Boys run the girls' distance to prove a point
payload.explanation: Offering students a choice respects individual ability and removes unfair assumptions from competition.

payload.snippet: During a class art auction, richer students buy all the best pieces cheaply and poorer students can't afford any.
options: The teacher introduces a ticket-based bidding system where every student receives the same number of tickets
The teacher cancels the auction
Rich students lend tickets to poorer students in exchange for favours
The auction proceeds unchanged and the same students dominate
payload.explanation: Equal-resource bidding systems level the playing field in economic-access situations.

payload.snippet: Two friends split the cost of a birthday gift equally but one is much wealthier. Later the wealthy friend says the poorer one should contribute more since they earned less.
options: The friends discuss what equal means to each of them and agree an amount both feel is fair
The poorer friend agrees to give more even though it is a hardship
The wealthy friend gives the gift alone and stops inviting the other friend
Both friends give nothing and the birthday is ignored
payload.explanation: Fairness in shared costs should account for means when discussing contributions between friends.

payload.snippet: In a school science experiment, only boys are assigned the hands-on experiment role while girls are asked to record results.
options: A student suggests rotating roles so everyone gets to do both tasks
Students accept the gendered roles without question
Girls refuse to record results
Boys monopolise every experiment for the rest of the term
payload.explanation: Rotating roles ensures equal practical experience regardless of gender.

payload.snippet: Ella's family has limited wi-fi bandwidth and always prioritises her older sibling's gaming, leaving Ella unable to complete online schoolwork.
options: She explains the schoolwork requirement to her parents and they agree to limit gaming during homework hours
Ella does her homework at the library every day without telling her parents why
She tells her teacher the wi-fi is too slow without explaining the real reason
She accepts the arrangement and falls behind
payload.explanation: Explaining the practical impact of a fairness issue to parents helps them make informed decisions.

payload.snippet: At a scouts meeting, leadership roles always go to the same few children because they are loudest in nominating themselves.
options: The leader introduces a nomination and draw system so every member gets a chance to lead
The loud children always lead and others never develop those skills
The quiet children stop attending
The leader picks their favourite child each time
payload.explanation: Structural rotation of leadership opportunities ensures development across the whole group.

payload.snippet: Two students receive the same punishment for different levels of involvement in an incident, even though one was merely present.
options: One student calmly explains their actual involvement to the headteacher, asking for the punishment to reflect culpability
Both students accept the same punishment in silence
The more involved student claims full responsibility to seem heroic
The less involved student accuses the other of lying
payload.explanation: Proportional consequences require accurate information — calmly presenting the facts is appropriate and fair.

payload.snippet: In a group cooking class, one student always measures and mixes while others watch. The watching students get the same grade.
options: The teacher introduces rotating roles so every student handles each part of the recipe on different days
The active student does all the work every class because she enjoys it
The watching students claim equal contribution without doing anything
The teacher grades the food quality rather than individual participation
payload.explanation: Rotating roles ensures every student develops skills, not just the most confident one.

payload.snippet: At a school quiz, teams are formed randomly and one team ends up with all the high scorers. The other teams feel the outcome is decided before the quiz begins.
options: The teacher rebalances teams by distributing known strong performers evenly
The quiz proceeds with unequal teams
Strong performers are excluded from teams to balance scores
The quiz is cancelled because teams cannot be made equal
payload.explanation: Balanced teams make competitions more meaningful for everyone — rebalancing is worth the small delay.

payload.snippet: A student helps a classmate with their maths homework every week. The classmate starts submitting better work but never acknowledges the help.
options: The helping student asks the classmate to at least tell the teacher that they studied together
The helping student stops helping without saying why
The helping student tells the teacher the classmate is cheating
The helping student does the classmate's work completely from now on
payload.explanation: Acknowledging genuine study support is an honest and fair reflection of how learning happened.

payload.snippet: A school art competition allows only one entry per student, but a teacher's child submits three pieces under different names.
options: A student politely informs the competition organiser about the multiple submissions
No one says anything and the teacher's child wins with three chances instead of one
All entries are disqualified to be safe
Students submit multiple entries themselves to compensate
payload.explanation: Equal submission rules must apply to every participant regardless of family connection to the organisers.

payload.snippet: Two students receive identical suspensions for an incident but one had significant previous behaviour notes while the other had none.
options: The headteacher reviews each case contextually and adjusts the consequences to reflect individual history
Both students receive identical consequences regardless of context
The student with more notes receives a harsher punishment with no explanation
The student with no prior notes accepts the suspension as fair
payload.explanation: Proportional disciplinary responses require context — identical misconduct by different students may warrant different responses.

payload.snippet: Priya's group has four tasks but only three people. She suggests each person picks the task they are best at and they share the fourth.
options: The group agrees and two people split the fourth task between them
One person ends up doing two full tasks without it being discussed
The group leaves the fourth task undone
They argue about the fourth task until time runs out
payload.explanation: Flexible task allocation that plays to strengths and shares overload is better than rigid equal division.

payload.snippet: Marcus's drama group must rehearse a scene but half the cast keeps missing practice. The show is in two weeks.
options: The director asks absent members directly whether they are still committed and adjusts parts if they are not
The director gives absent members' lines to whoever shows up, causing chaos
The director rehearses around the absent members hoping they remember on show night
The director cancels the show without speaking to the cast
payload.explanation: Addressing attendance problems directly and early is fairer to committed cast members than hoping the problem resolves.

payload.snippet: A group of four is doing a science experiment. Two are very confident and keep overriding the quieter members' ideas without considering them.
options: A quiet member asks the group to hear each idea before deciding which to use
The quiet members stop contributing and let the loud ones do everything
The loud members take over the whole experiment
The teacher notices and permanently separates the confident students
payload.explanation: A process step — hearing all ideas before deciding — corrects dominance without confrontation.

payload.snippet: Zara and Leo are assigned as co-captains for a team project. They disagree on every decision and the team is stuck waiting.
options: They agree that each co-captain will have final say over alternating decisions
They escalate every disagreement to the teacher
Leo makes all the decisions since he is louder
Zara resigns as co-captain rather than compromise
payload.explanation: Pre-agreeing a decision rule removes gridlock without either co-captain losing authority.

payload.snippet: The school eco-club is planning a litter-pick. One member wants to cover the whole school; others say the playground is enough.
options: They do the playground first and review whether time and energy allow more
They attempt the whole school, exhaust themselves, and finish nothing properly
They argue about the scope until the session ends
The ambitious member does the whole school alone
payload.explanation: Starting with the achievable goal and expanding if possible is better project management than overscoping.

payload.snippet: Two friends write a story together. One writes action scenes fast; the other writes character dialogue slowly but beautifully. The action writer is frustrated.
options: They play to their strengths: one writes action, one writes dialogue, then they weave it together
The action writer writes the whole story because they are faster
They slow to the dialogue writer's pace for the entire story
They submit two separate stories each claiming it is the joint one
payload.explanation: Dividing by strength and merging outputs is better than forcing a uniform pace.

payload.snippet: At a community garden project, three volunteers argue about who takes the compost-bin job because nobody wants it.
options: They agree to rotate undesirable jobs weekly so it is never the same person two sessions running
The least assertive volunteer gets stuck with the compost job every time
The compost is never turned because nobody will take the job
The project coordinator assigns the job without asking for input
payload.explanation: Rotation of undesirable roles is the fairest structural fix when nobody volunteers.

payload.snippet: A team is building a raft for a school competition. Two members want to add a sail; two think the sail will make it unstable.
options: They build a small sail with a quick-release in case it needs to be removed
The sail faction builds it full-size without a release, risking capsize
The anti-sail faction sabotages the sail build
The team votes and the losing side refuses to help any further
payload.explanation: A testable, reversible compromise satisfies both sides and lets evidence decide.

payload.snippet: A volunteer group is preparing food hampers. One person keeps adding extra items, slowing the packing line.
options: The team lead gently asks that person to stick to the agreed contents list so the line keeps moving
The team lead removes them from the line without explanation
Everyone starts adding extra items so nobody feels singled out
The packing slows and fewer families receive hampers
payload.explanation: Gentle redirection to an agreed process keeps communal work efficient and fair.

payload.snippet: Amara's coding team has three weeks to build an app. In week one they debate features rather than writing any code.
options: A team member calls a time-box: twenty minutes to decide features, then start coding
The team debates features for three weeks and submits nothing
The most experienced coder starts alone so progress happens
The teacher chooses the features for them to end the debate
payload.explanation: Time-boxing a discussion forces a decision and protects time for execution.

payload.snippet: During a tug-of-war, one team member lets go at the critical moment and the team falls. They were afraid of hurting their hands.
options: The team discusses grip technique and gloves for next time instead of blaming the person
The team shouts at the person who let go in front of everyone
The team excludes them from future physical activities
The team pretends the loss never happened and learns nothing
payload.explanation: A learning conversation after failure is more productive than blame.

payload.snippet: Three children are decorating a cake together. Two keep adding decorations to the same side.
options: One child suggests dividing the cake into sections so each person decorates their own area
All three decorate the same spot until the icing is a pile
One child takes over the whole cake
They decide individually which areas to decorate, causing an argument
payload.explanation: Spatial division of a shared object prevents accidental competition on the same area.

payload.snippet: Amara and Felix are writing a joint essay. Amara writes fast and sloppy; Felix writes slowly and perfectly. They are arguing about pace.
options: They agree Amara drafts quickly and Felix edits carefully afterwards
Amara writes the whole essay so they meet the deadline
Felix deletes Amara's sections and rewrites from scratch
They submit two separate halves with a note saying they couldn't agree
payload.explanation: Drafter-editor partnerships use both speed and precision — the right roles turn the conflict into a strength.

payload.snippet: Three children are building a cardboard rocket for a school display. One cuts, one glues, one paints. The painter finishes first and takes over gluing.
options: The painter asks if anyone needs help or starts cutting more pieces
The painter starts painting over the glued sections while they are still wet
The painter stands around doing nothing until the others finish
The painter takes the scissors from the cutter without asking
payload.explanation: When your task finishes early, offering help where needed keeps the team moving.

payload.snippet: A school quiz team has five members but only four can compete. They must choose who sits out.
options: They vote, and the person who volunteers to sit out coaches the others on weak topics
The newest member is told to sit out without discussion
Four members argue for twenty minutes about who is best while the team loses practice time
They enter five members anyway hoping nobody checks the rules
payload.explanation: Turning a limitation into a support role keeps every member contributing.

payload.snippet: A group is doing a litter pick. Two members complain the bags are too heavy and slow down.
options: They switch to smaller more frequent trips to the bin rather than overfilling bags
The two slow members are told to do a different job without being asked if they want to
Everyone carries heavy bags until someone drops theirs and litter scatters
The slow members walk ahead while the rest carry everything
payload.explanation: Adapting the method to the team's actual capacity is better than pushing through an inefficient approach.

payload.snippet: A school cooking team's timer goes off but their dish is not ready. Two people want to serve it anyway; two want to wait.
options: They check the doneness correctly — the timer is a guide, not a rule — and wait the extra time needed
The wanting-to-serve faction takes it out immediately and serves undercooked food
The waiting faction unplugs the oven in frustration
The team argues while the dish burns from being left in without attention
payload.explanation: Teams must make evidence-based decisions together, not split by preference when a safety issue is at stake.

payload.snippet: A team building a model has reached a step that requires complete silence and steady hands. One member keeps talking.
options: Another member quietly asks them to pause conversation just for this step
Everyone ignores the talking and the model collapses
The task is abandoned because the talking cannot be stopped
The talker is moved to the other side of the room without explanation
payload.explanation: A direct, specific, temporary request is the least disruptive way to manage a colleague's habit in a critical moment.

payload.snippet: Two children are rowing a boat together. They keep going in circles because they don't match their stroke speed.
options: They count aloud together so both strokes land at the same time
One child rows faster hoping the other will catch up
Both children row as hard as possible with no coordination
One child stops rowing and lets the other do all the work
payload.explanation: Synchronisation through a shared count is the classic fix for mismatched rowing.

payload.snippet: A drama group is rehearsing. One actor keeps feeding lines to others instead of letting them try to remember.
options: A castmate gently points out that prompting too early prevents everyone from learning their lines
The actor who prompts takes over all the roles to speed rehearsal
The cast gives up trying to memorise lines since they know the prompts are coming
The director bans all speaking between cast members during rehearsal
payload.explanation: Rehearsal requires the productive discomfort of trying to remember — premature prompting removes that learning.

payload.snippet: Chloe has ordered a custom birthday cake online. The baker emails to say it will be two days late, arriving on her birthday evening instead of morning.
options: She thanks the baker, adjusts the birthday meal timing, and plans a simple cake for the morning with family
She cancels the order and bakes something rushed and stressful
She emails the baker every hour asking for updates
She tells her family the birthday is ruined and refuses to celebrate
payload.explanation: A two-day delay in a non-essential item is a manageable inconvenience — adapting the plan is more proportionate than escalating.

payload.snippet: Oscar is learning to solve a Rubik's cube. After two weeks he can solve two of the six faces consistently. He expected to be faster.
options: He looks up the algorithm for the next layer and breaks learning into one new step per week
He memorises all seven algorithms in one weekend and then burns out
He decides he is bad at puzzles and gives the cube away
He watches others solving it online for hours without practising himself
payload.explanation: Structured incremental learning beats both binge-study and giving up.

payload.snippet: Amara is waiting for her best friend to come back from a month-long holiday. She misses her and the weeks feel very long.
options: She writes a list of things they'll do together and works on a hobby she enjoys in the meantime
She messages her friend every day even though roaming is expensive for the friend
She refuses to spend time with other friends until her best friend returns
She tells her friend the holiday has gone on too long
payload.explanation: Focusing on reunion plans and personal interests makes long separations more bearable.

payload.snippet: Marcus's sports physio says his injury will take six weeks to heal. He is desperate to play again but the physio warns rushing will extend recovery.
options: He follows the rehabilitation plan fully and uses the time to analyse his technique from recordings
He returns to play after four weeks because he feels fine
He argues with the physio every session about the timeline
He stops going to physio after two weeks since he feels better
payload.explanation: Premature return from sports injury is the most common reason for re-injury — the physio's timeline exists because tissue healing cannot be rushed.

payload.snippet: Priya is waiting for her art teacher to return her marked portfolio. It has been two weeks and she needs the feedback to prepare for her exam.
options: She waits one more week then politely emails asking when she can expect feedback, explaining the exam preparation context
She emails every day from the start reminding the teacher about the portfolio
She prepares for the exam without feedback hoping she has guessed her weak areas correctly
She tells other students the teacher never marks portfolios
payload.explanation: One polite follow-up after a reasonable wait, with context, is the appropriate prompt — daily reminders irritate rather than help.

payload.snippet: Jake is on a long train journey with no phone signal. The journey takes four hours.
options: He reads a book he brought for exactly this kind of situation
He opens and closes the window every ten minutes out of boredom
He asks the conductor every thirty minutes when signal will return
He turns his data off and on repeatedly hoping signal returns
payload.explanation: Planning an offline activity for known dead zones turns a signal-free zone into reading time.

payload.snippet: Ella waits eight weeks for a handmade piece of jewellery to be crafted. A week before the expected delivery, the maker emails saying it will be another two weeks.
options: She replies acknowledging the delay and asks for a confirmation message when it ships
She demands a refund citing the delay as a breach of contract
She asks for weekly progress photos
She posts a negative review before the item has been delivered
payload.explanation: Requesting a shipping confirmation is a proportionate response to a delay — cancelling before delivery is rarely warranted for handmade items.

payload.snippet: Sofia has been practising a difficult piece on the cello for six weeks. She still cannot play the hardest passage at full speed.
options: She practises the passage at half speed until it is perfect, then gradually increases the tempo
She skips the difficult passage in practice hoping it will work on performance day
She plays the whole piece at full speed repeatedly hoping the passage improves
She asks her teacher to simplify the passage for her
payload.explanation: Slow-speed perfection before incremental tempo increase is the standard technique-building method for all instruments.

payload.snippet: Ben submits a job application and hears nothing back for four weeks. The advert said decisions would be made within three weeks.
options: He sends one brief follow-up email to ask if the role is still open and when decisions are expected
He emails the company every two days after the three-week mark
He assumes he was rejected and stops applying elsewhere
He calls the company's main phone line daily
payload.explanation: One follow-up after a passed stated deadline is standard practice and often elicits a useful response.

payload.snippet: Zara wants to learn a new language. After one month of daily lessons she can only manage basic greetings.
options: She joins an online conversation group where she listens to native speakers, even understanding little
She switches app every week hoping to find a faster method
She sets an aim to be fluent in three months and is disappointed weekly
She stops lessons until she has memorised the entire vocabulary list
payload.explanation: Immersive listening builds comprehension before speaking — joining a group even before you can speak much is a recognised language acquisition method.

payload.snippet: Tyler's vegetable garden was planted in spring but a hot dry summer means the tomatoes are splitting before they fully ripen.
options: He picks them slightly early and lets them ripen on the kitchen windowsill in the warmth
He overwaters to compensate, causing root rot
He covers the whole bed with shade cloth making the plants too cold
He pulls out the plants and declares the summer a failure
payload.explanation: Countering a weather-related growing problem with an adapted harvesting strategy is standard practice for home growers.

payload.snippet: Leo is queuing for a popular new exhibition. The queue stretches around the block and the wait is estimated at ninety minutes.
options: He chats with the strangers around him and uses the time to read exhibition notes on his phone
He pushes into the queue at a point further along claiming he is with someone
He complains to museum staff that the queue is too long
He leaves and misses an exhibition he has wanted to see for months
payload.explanation: A long queue for something genuinely desired is an opportunity for social patience, not a reason to abandon the visit.

payload.snippet: Nia is learning to draw portraits. After a month her portraits still do not look like the subjects.
options: She practises individual facial features — eyes, then noses, then mouths — before combining them into full portraits
She traces photographs to get a likeness and calls it practice
She stops drawing portraits because she lacks talent
She switches to a different art style to avoid difficulty
payload.explanation: Breaking a complex skill into component practice is how all representational artists improve.

payload.snippet: Freya is waiting for planning permission to extend her family's house. The council says it takes twelve weeks. It has been eleven.
options: She uses the final week to finalise material selections so they can start immediately on approval
She calls the planning department every day in the final week
She starts preparing the foundation before permission is granted
She withdraws the application assuming it will be rejected since it took so long
payload.explanation: Using the final waiting period to prepare for an immediate start means no time is lost if permission is granted.

payload.snippet: Alex is growing bonsai for the first time. The book says the first visible shaping results take three to five years.
options: He sets a five-year journal to document growth and reads about the shaping process so he is ready when the time comes
He prunes aggressively to force faster shaping
He gives the bonsai to someone more patient
He buys a mature, shaped bonsai and calls it his project
payload.explanation: Bonsai is the quintessential patience project — journalling and studying the craft fills the wait with meaning.

payload.snippet: Ryan has applied for a scholarship. The result will be announced in twelve weeks. He checks the organisation's website daily.
options: He marks the result date in his calendar and stops checking until then
He emails the scholarship coordinator every week asking if results are ready
He tells his school he has won before the result is announced
He applies to no other funding, assuming he will win
payload.explanation: Checking a website daily for an outcome that has a known announcement date is pure anxiety — calendar marking eliminates the compulsive checking.

payload.snippet: Jonah is growing a sunflower from seed. It sprouted after ten days but has been the same height for three weeks.
options: He ensures consistent watering and sunlight and reads that slow early growth is normal as roots establish
He moves the pot to a different spot every two days to find more light
He adds fertiliser every day to accelerate growth
He pulls it up to check whether the roots are growing
payload.explanation: Root establishment looks like stasis above ground — consistent care during the slow phase supports the later rapid growth.

payload.snippet: Grace is on a waiting list for a popular after-school club. She has been waiting two terms.
options: She contacts the club leader to ask whether there are similar opportunities or a standby list for late drop-outs
She turns up at the club every week uninvited hoping to be let in
She gives up on joining and finds no alternative
She tells her friends on the waiting list to drop out so she moves up
payload.explanation: Proactively asking about standby mechanisms or alternatives is a smart way to increase the chance of access.

payload.snippet: Sam is repainting his room. He painted one coat last night. The tin says two coats are needed and the first must be fully dry.
options: He waits the specified drying time before applying the second coat, doing homework in the meantime
He applies the second coat after an hour because it feels dry to the touch
He uses a hairdryer on the first coat to speed drying
He applies three thin coats in quick succession hoping they equal two thick ones
payload.explanation: Paint drying time exists for chemical, not just physical, reasons — rushing produces peeling and uneven finish.

payload.snippet: Lily wants to release her homemade jam but the jars need to cool overnight before sealing is confirmed.
options: She waits until morning, checks the lids have all sealed, and stores them properly
She seals the jars while they are hot and puts them straight in the fridge
She gives the warm jars to friends immediately
She opens one jar that evening to check the jam set
payload.explanation: Overnight cooling of jam jars is required for a proper vacuum seal — premature interference breaks the preservation.

payload.snippet: Marcus is home alone for the first time and someone knocks at the door. He does not recognise the person through the window.
options: He does not open the door and calls his parent to let them know
He opens the door a crack to ask what they want
He shouts from the window that his parents are out
He pretends no one is home by hiding, but leaves the door unlocked
payload.explanation: Never indicate to a stranger that you are home alone — call a parent first.

payload.snippet: Priya is helping her grandmother and notices the smoke detector in the kitchen has no battery.
options: She tells her grandmother immediately so a battery can be replaced
She puts a piece of tape over the detector so it stops chirping
She decides it only matters in kitchens and the detector is not needed there
She removes the detector from the ceiling to check the model number and forgets to put it back
payload.explanation: A smoke detector without a battery is useless — replacing it immediately is a simple but potentially life-saving action.

payload.snippet: Noah is at a friend's house and sees the friend's older sibling mixing cleaning products in a bucket.
options: He tells a parent in the house that he saw the mixing happening
He stands back and watches to see what happens
He tells his friend it looks dangerous but takes no other action
He opens all the windows himself without telling an adult
payload.explanation: Mixing household chemicals can produce toxic gases — an adult must intervene immediately.

payload.snippet: Ella finds an unknown USB drive in the school car park.
options: She hands it to the school office without plugging it into any device
She plugs it into the school computer to see whose it is
She takes it home and plugs it into her own laptop
She leaves it where she found it since it is not hers
payload.explanation: Unknown USB drives can carry malware — handing them to staff unexamined is the only safe approach.

payload.snippet: Jonah is rock-climbing at an indoor wall. His belay device makes a clicking noise it never has before.
options: He stops climbing and tells the instructor before continuing
He continues climbing since the device is still holding his weight
He tightens the device's attachment himself
He changes devices with another climber without checking with staff
payload.explanation: Unusual sounds from safety equipment always require inspection before further use.

payload.snippet: Sofia is at a bonfire party. A younger child starts throwing sticks into the fire.
options: She moves the younger child away from the fire and tells a supervising adult
She tells the child to stop but takes no further action
She throws water on the fire to reduce the risk
She stands between the child and the fire alone
payload.explanation: A child near a fire requires adult supervision — moving them and alerting an adult is the correct two-step response.

payload.snippet: Tyler finds his little sister has been eating berries from a bush in the garden. He does not know if they are safe.
options: He calls Poison Control or his parents immediately, noting which bush and how many berries
He waits to see if his sister feels sick before calling anyone
He gives his sister milk to neutralise any poison
He picks more berries to show a doctor later
payload.explanation: When unknown plant material has been eaten, immediate contact with Poison Control prevents delay in treatment.

payload.snippet: Grace is walking home alone and notices a car driving slowly alongside her for a second time.
options: She walks quickly toward the nearest open shop or busy place and calls a parent
She ignores it and continues walking home
She shouts at the driver to leave her alone
She stops walking and takes out her phone on the pavement
payload.explanation: Trusting your instincts about a following vehicle and moving toward people immediately is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Alex and his friends find an old shed at the back of a park with the door ajar and rusty tools inside.
options: He tells his friends not to go in and they walk away
He enters to see if anything valuable is inside
He pushes the door fully open to look in from the doorway
He throws a rock inside to check for animals before entering
payload.explanation: Abandoned structures with rusted materials are structural and tetanus hazards — leaving immediately is correct.
