calls out the imbalance loudly during a group session in front of everyone
stops submitting his own work to avoid the inevitable disappointment of being ignored
tells the other group members about the pattern to validate their frustration
payload.explanation: Speaking to the facilitator privately is the constructive and respectful first step.

payload.snippet: Nina reads a published novel for school that she believes glamourises dangerous behaviour in a way that could influence vulnerable young readers.
options: writes a detailed critical review explaining exactly how and why the portrayal is dangerous
demands the book be removed from the curriculum immediately
refuses to complete the assigned work related to the book
tells parents of other students about the book without the school's knowledge
payload.explanation: A detailed critical review engages thoughtfully with the text and contributes to the wider debate about what is appropriate.

payload.snippet: Tom is on the editorial team of the school newspaper and is pressured by a senior member to publish a story about a student that Tom knows is untrue.
options: refuses to publish the story and explains clearly that it is factually inaccurate
publishes the story but adds a disclaimer saying it may not be accurate
publishes the story since the senior member has authority over editorial decisions
tells the student who is the subject of the story without addressing the editorial issue
payload.explanation: Refusing to publish known falsehoods is a fundamental principle of responsible journalism.

payload.snippet: Ava is asked to judge a school story competition and discovers that the anonymised entry she likes best is actually from her closest friend.
options: continues judging it on its merits and scores it the same as she would have anonymously
gives her friend's entry extra marks to ensure it wins
deliberately marks her friend's entry lower to avoid any appearance of bias
withdraws from the judging panel to avoid any conflict of interest
payload.explanation: Judging on merit regardless of authorship is the definition of fair and ethical judging.

payload.snippet: Ben is writing a story that incorporates a real and traumatic event from his own life and finds the writing process is re-triggering painful feelings.
options: pauses the writing and talks to a trusted adult about how the process is affecting him
pushes through since finishing the story will help him process the trauma
abandons the story entirely and never writes about personal subjects again
tells no one and continues writing alone trying to suppress the difficult feelings
payload.explanation: Pausing and talking to a trusted adult about the emotional impact is the healthy and correct response to creative work that re-triggers pain.

payload.snippet: Grace is reviewing a book for her school's reading club newsletter when she finds the author has included a thinly veiled negative portrayal of a real person she recognises.
options: flags this to the supervising teacher before publishing her review
publishes the review naming the real person she believes the character is based on
includes a mention in her review that the character may be based on a real person
contacts the publisher directly to ask whether the character is based on a real person
payload.explanation: Flagging to the teacher before publishing ensures responsible handling of a potentially libellous observation.

payload.snippet: Max is helping moderate an online school book club when he discovers a member has been posting spoilers for books that other members are still reading.
options: privately messages the member explaining the spoiler rule and asks them to stop
removes all the spoiler posts immediately without contacting the member first
bans the member from the group immediately for breaking the community rules
ignores it since spoilers are inevitable and readers should be more careful
payload.explanation: A private message explaining the rule and asking the person to stop is the fair and respectful first response.

payload.snippet: Lily is a guest author at a school event when a student asks her a question about her creative process that she finds very personal and uncomfortable.
options: politely explains she would prefer to keep that aspect of her process private
answers the question fully since the audience has a right to know about her process
changes the subject abruptly without acknowledging the question was asked
gives a clearly false answer to protect her privacy while still appearing open
payload.explanation: Politely declining to answer a question that feels too personal is the professional and dignified response.

payload.snippet: Zoe discovers that a popular book in her school's reading programme contains a stereotype about a group she is part of that she finds personally hurtful.
options: speaks to the teacher about how the portrayal made her feel and asks what support is available
removes the book from the school library shelf herself to protect others
publicly tells her class the book is harmful and no one should complete it
says nothing and reads the rest of the book in silence trying to ignore the impact
payload.explanation: Speaking to the teacher about personal impact creates a dialogue and may lead to better class discussion of the text.

payload.snippet: Sam is writing a biographical story about a real living person who has not given permission for their story to be told.
options: researches what is publicly known, focuses only on public facts, and considers whether to proceed
writes the story in full detail since it is creative fiction and not a factual report
changes the name of the real person and publishes without other changes
asks the person for permission before writing anything further
payload.explanation: Researching what is public, using only those facts, and considering carefully whether to proceed are all professionally appropriate steps.

payload.snippet: Finn discovers that the author of a book series he loves has recently expressed publicly harmful views that conflict with everything the books seemed to stand for.
options: continues to engage with the books critically while being honest about his conflicted feelings
immediately destroys all copies of the author's books he owns
pretends he never liked the books and denies having recommended them to friends
defends the author's views since he respects them too much to criticise them
payload.explanation: Engaging critically while being honest about conflicted feelings is the mature and intellectually honest response.

payload.snippet: Ruby is asked to read her creative writing to the school at an assembly and the piece contains deeply personal material she is not sure she wants to share publicly.
options: asks the teacher whether she can read a different piece or share part of it only
reads the full piece since she was asked and feels she cannot refuse
refuses without explanation and submits an excuse to avoid the assembly entirely
reads the full piece and immediately regrets it but says nothing to anyone
payload.explanation: Asking about alternatives or partial sharing is a legitimate and self-respecting conversation to have with the teacher.

payload.snippet: Owen finds out that a book he spent months writing for a competition was not shortlisted and he is devastated by the outcome.
options: reads the feedback carefully and asks if it is available to improve his next submission
gives up writing entirely since months of work was not recognised
tells everyone the competition was unfair and the judges were wrong
contacts the competition to argue that his entry deserved a place on the shortlist
payload.explanation: Reading feedback and using it to improve is the resilient and productive response to competition disappointment.

payload.snippet: Sophie reads a book recommended to her as being about people like her but finds the portrayal shallow, inaccurate, and written by someone who clearly has no lived experience of that community.
options: writes an honest review explaining the gap between the book's claim and its reality
refuses to write a review since engaging with the book gives it more attention
contacts the publisher to demand the book be withdrawn from sale
tells friends in the same community to avoid the book without giving reasons why
payload.explanation: An honest review that articulates the problem clearly is the most useful contribution to the wider conversation.

payload.snippet: Jake is a writing mentor helping younger students and one student's story clearly describes what sounds like a real and difficult home situation using fictional characters.
options: raises this sensitively with a safeguarding lead or teacher after the session
discusses the story's themes with the student directly asking whether it is autobiographical
stays quiet since the story is officially fiction even if it might be real
asks the student's friends whether the fictional story might be real
payload.explanation: Raising with a safeguarding lead protects the child — it is not the mentor's role to investigate directly.

payload.snippet: Chloe is a class librarian and discovers a student has been taking books home and selling them online for profit.
options: tells the school librarian and a teacher about what she has discovered
confronts the student directly in front of the class
removes the student's borrowing privileges herself without telling any adult
says nothing since books are cheap to replace and the student probably needs the money
payload.explanation: Telling the school librarian and a teacher enables a proper response — Chloe should not act unilaterally.

payload.snippet: Ethan writes a story for class that his teacher says is brilliant but also says it contains ideas that are too mature for the class assignment.
options: asks the teacher what would make the story appropriate without compromising his voice
rewrites the story to be entirely different so the maturity concern goes away
submits it unchanged since the teacher said it was brilliant and that matters more
shows the story to his parents to get a second opinion on the teacher's assessment
payload.explanation: Asking what specific adjustments are needed is the collaborative and craft-focused response.

payload.snippet: Isla discovers that a famous author's most celebrated book was substantially written by someone else who received no credit for their contribution.
options: researches the claim carefully from multiple credible sources before forming any opinion
immediately dismisses her admiration for the author based on the unverified claim alone
shares the claim widely on social media before verifying whether it is accurate
defends the author since famous people are often the target of false accusations
payload.explanation: Researching carefully from multiple credible sources before forming an opinion is the critical thinking standard.

payload.snippet: Leo witnesses a swimmer being pulled underwater by a strong current at a beach that has no lifeguard on duty.
options: calls emergency services immediately and directs bystanders to throw floating objects from shore
swims out immediately to try to reach the struggling swimmer
runs along the shore to get in front of the current to cut off the swimmer
shouts instructions to the swimmer about how to escape the current themselves
payload.explanation: Calling emergency services and coordinating shore-based rescue is correct — swimming to someone in a rip current risks your own life.

payload.snippet: Mia is a swimming instructor and one of her students has a panic attack in the water during a group lesson.
options: moves all other students to the shallow end and calmly helps her student to the pool edge
ends the lesson for everyone and asks all students to get out immediately
calls for a colleague and keeps talking calmly to the student while supporting them
asks the student's parent who is watching to come in and help
payload.explanation: Moving other students to safety while keeping calm and supporting the student to the edge is the correct dual-focus response.

payload.snippet: Kai is white-water rafting when the raft overturns and everyone is in the fast-moving river.
options: keeps his feet up and pointed downstream, and goes with the current toward calmer water
swims directly to the nearest bank regardless of the current direction
tries to swim back to the overturned raft upstream to right it
grabs any nearby rock to stop himself from moving downstream
payload.explanation: Feet-up, pointing downstream is the correct whitewater swimming position — fighting the current exhausts you.

payload.snippet: Nina is a lifeguard when she sees a swimmer in difficulty at the far end of her zone but she cannot reach them before another lifeguard crosses into her zone.
options: enters the water immediately with her rescue equipment and calls to the other lifeguard simultaneously
waits to see if the other lifeguard responds before entering the water herself
blows her whistle to alert the other lifeguard and waits on the pool deck
enters the water without her rescue equipment since time is critical
payload.explanation: Entering the water with rescue equipment immediately while communicating with the other lifeguard is the correct response — equipment is essential.

payload.snippet: Tom is sailing with his family when a boom swings suddenly and knocks his mother unconscious and she falls into the water.
options: throws a life ring toward her, shouts man overboard, and calls emergency services
dives in to support her head above water since he is the strongest swimmer
takes control of the boat and tries to sail back toward her position
tries to pull her back onto the boat without assistance from anyone
payload.explanation: Throwing a life ring, shouting the alert, and calling emergency services activates the fastest and most comprehensive response.

payload.snippet: Ava discovers that a private swimming club in her town has been excluding children from specific ethnic backgrounds from membership under unofficial policy.
options: reports this to the relevant anti-discrimination authority and supports affected families if asked
confronts the club committee at a public meeting about their unofficial policy
starts a social media campaign to expose and shame the club publicly
organises an alternative inclusive swimming event rather than engaging with the club
payload.explanation: Reporting to an anti-discrimination authority triggers a formal investigation — public confrontation or social media campaigns are secondary options.

payload.snippet: Ben is scuba diving in a coral reef when his diving partner begins to ascend too quickly toward the surface.
options: grabs his partner's tank and slows their ascent while signalling to the dive master above
ascends quickly alongside his partner to provide support at the surface
signals frantically to the dive master and hopes they can intervene in time
continues his dive and alerts the dive master when they reach the surface
payload.explanation: Slowing the ascent by holding the tank while signalling is the correct response — rapid ascent causes life-threatening decompression sickness.

payload.snippet: Grace is a swim coach when she notices one of her elite swimmers is using a training technique that risks a serious shoulder injury.
options: stops the session immediately and speaks with the swimmer about the technique
finishes the session and raises the technique concern in the next training debrief
lets the swimmer complete the set using the technique but does not repeat it in future training
asks the swimmer's parent to watch the next session and observe the technique themselves
payload.explanation: Stopping immediately and addressing the technique protects the swimmer from injury — finishing the set first multiplies the risk.

payload.snippet: Max is on a solo open-water swim when he starts to feel the early signs of hypothermia — confusion and clumsiness.
options: aborts the swim immediately and signals to the safety boat for assistance
focuses intensely on his technique to warm up through physical effort
switches to a faster stroke to generate more body heat as quickly as possible
continues for five more minutes to see whether his body acclimatises to the temperature
payload.explanation: Aborting immediately and signalling is critical — hypothermia impairs judgment rapidly and continuing is extremely dangerous.

payload.snippet: Lily is diving into a hotel swimming pool when she notices at the last moment that the depth is much shallower than the markings suggest.
options: aborts the dive and grabs the pool edge to stop herself from entering the water
completes the dive at a shallower angle to reduce the impact on entry
enters the water feet first rather than head first to reduce the danger
shouts to warn other divers on the board behind her before entering the water
payload.explanation: Aborting a dive at the last moment is difficult but the only correct response — both a shallow dive and feet-first entry still risk serious injury in very shallow water.

payload.snippet: Zoe is a water polo referee when she notices that a player on one team has been deliberately injuring opponents underwater where she cannot see clearly.
options: stops the match, addresses the observed behaviour directly with both coaches, and issues a formal warning
continues the match but positions herself differently to observe the underwater behaviour better
whispers to the injured players to tell her immediately if it happens again
stops the match and tells the player's coach without issuing a formal warning first
payload.explanation: Stopping the match and addressing it formally protects players and creates an official record of the behaviour.

payload.snippet: Sam is the only adult present when a young child slips and falls into a deep pool at a private garden party.
options: jumps in to retrieve the child immediately since trained help is not available and every second counts
shouts for another adult to help before doing anything himself
throws every floating object he can find into the pool toward the child
calls emergency services first and then jumps in
payload.explanation: Jumping in immediately is the correct response when you are the only adult and a young child is in the water — call services after retrieving the child.

payload.snippet: Finn is leading a school kayaking trip when he notices the weather is deteriorating rapidly and the return route will soon become dangerous.
options: turns the group around immediately and heads back to shore before conditions worsen further
pushes the group to paddle faster to complete the route before the weather arrives
finds a sheltered bay and waits to see how the weather develops before deciding
sends the strongest paddlers ahead to scout the route while the rest of the group waits
payload.explanation: Turning around immediately is the correct decision — conditions deteriorate faster than they appear to from the water.

payload.snippet: Ruby discovers that the swimming pool her club trains at has not had its water quality tested for several months.
options: raises this formally with the pool management and advises her club members until testing is confirmed
trains as normal since the pool looks clean and no one has reported illness
tests the water herself using a home testing kit and trains if the result seems acceptable
reports the pool to environmental health authorities before speaking to pool management
payload.explanation: Raising it formally with management first and advising caution is proportionate — escalating to authorities is appropriate only if management does not respond.

payload.snippet: Owen's swim team is preparing for a championship when the team coach pressures a swimmer who has a shoulder injury to compete and hide the injury from officials.
options: supports the injured swimmer to report the injury to officials and decline to compete if necessary
says nothing since it is ultimately the injured swimmer's own decision to make
tells the coach privately that this puts the swimmer at serious risk
reports the coach's pressure to the governing body without first supporting the swimmer directly
payload.explanation: Supporting the swimmer to self-advocate and report the injury protects their health and keeps the competition fair.

payload.snippet: Sophie is in a tidal estuary when the tide turns much faster than predicted and her group is cut off from the shore.
options: keeps the group calm, moves to the highest ground available, and calls emergency services
leads the group in wading back through the incoming tide immediately
tells the group to swim across the tidal channel since the shore is only a short distance away
climbs a tree and waits for the tide to retreat before attempting to return
payload.explanation: Moving to high ground and calling emergency services is the correct response to tidal entrapment.

payload.snippet: Jake is at a pool when he notices a child he does not know sitting alone near the deep end looking distressed and tearful.
options: goes over and asks if the child is okay and whether they need help finding an adult
tells a pool staff member from a distance without approaching the child himself
leaves the child alone since they are not in immediate physical danger
takes the child to the changing rooms to find their parent or guardian
payload.explanation: Approaching the child directly and asking if they need help is the most immediate and caring response.

payload.snippet: Chloe is a competitive open-water swimmer who is offered a performance-enhancing substance by a teammate who says it is undetectable.
options: refuses clearly and reports the offer to the team's coach or the competition authority
refuses but says nothing about the offer to avoid getting her teammate in trouble
asks for more information about the substance before making any decision
declines the substance but says nothing to anyone and trains harder instead
payload.explanation: Refusing and reporting the offer is required by anti-doping rules — staying silent while knowing about a doping offer has consequences.

payload.snippet: Ethan's water sports centre is running a dangerous activity without the legally required safety certification and participants do not know.
options: tells the participants and the relevant safety authority about the missing certification
participates himself since the activity looks safe even without the certification
tells only the participants so they can make their own informed decision
calls the relevant safety authority without warning the participants first
payload.explanation: Informing both participants and the safety authority ensures immediate protection and formal enforcement.

payload.snippet: Isla is competing in an open-water swimming race when she witnesses another competitor in serious difficulty well behind her current position.
options: stops her race, ensures the swimmer is seen by safety crews, and assists if she can
continues racing and trusts the safety boats to have seen the swimmer in difficulty
waves to the safety boat and keeps racing since she has already flagged the issue
swims back to the swimmer in difficulty even though it means abandoning her race
payload.explanation: Stopping and ensuring the safety crew has seen the swimmer is the correct racing response — abandoning the race to assist is also a valid choice if the swimmer is in immediate danger.

payload.snippet: Ben is skiing on a blue run when he catches an edge and tumbles hard, sliding twenty metres before stopping. He cannot move his right leg and there is no ski patrol visible anywhere.
options: He stays still, keeps his skis across the slope as a visual signal, and uses his phone to alert ski rescue.
He tries to stand and ski slowly to the bottom on one leg to find the ski patrol hut.
He removes both skis and walks carefully down the icy slope to the resort.
He waves his poles and hopes a passing skier will stop and carry him down.
payload.explanation: Remaining still prevents further injury; crossed skis signal distress; calling ski rescue is correct protocol.

payload.snippet: Maya is ice fishing with her uncle when the ice shifts with a loud crack and water appears in a widening line between her and the shore.
options: She lies flat immediately to spread her weight and rolls toward the shore without standing.
She stands and runs fast toward the shore before the crack widens further.
She jumps across the crack to the shore side before it gets too wide.
She stays perfectly still and calls for her uncle to throw a rope.
payload.explanation: Lying flat distributes weight over cracking ice and rolling is safer than running or jumping.

payload.snippet: A walker is found collapsed in a snow-covered field with suspected hypothermia — he is shivering violently and confused about where he is.
options: She calls 999, moves him gently out of the wind, removes wet layers, and wraps him in dry blankets from her pack.
She briskly rubs his arms and legs to generate friction heat right away.
She gives him a large flask of hot tea and tells him to drink it quickly.
She removes all his clothing to check for injuries before calling the ambulance.
payload.explanation: Hypothermia requires 999, shelter from wind, dry insulation, and gentle handling — not friction or hot drinks.

payload.snippet: Tom is driving on a rural road when his car slides off into a snow-filled ditch. The car is stable, the engine is running, and it is minus ten degrees outside.
options: He keeps the engine running for heat but opens a window slightly and checks the exhaust is not blocked by snow.
He turns the engine off to save fuel and wraps himself in the car mat.
He gets out and walks toward the nearest lights he can see in the distance.
He revs the engine hard and rocks the car trying to get it free from the ditch.
payload.explanation: Running the engine for heat is correct but a snow-blocked exhaust can cause fatal carbon-monoxide poisoning.

payload.snippet: Anna is leading a group of young children on a winter nature walk when one child slips into a shallow but fast-flowing icy stream.
options: She reaches out with her walking pole for the child to grab, keeping herself on the bank.
She jumps in immediately to lift the child out before the cold sets in.
She sends the fastest child to run for help while she watches.
She unzips her coat and throws it over the stream to make a rope.
payload.explanation: Reaching with a pole keeps the rescuer safe while assisting the child — entering icy water is dangerous.

payload.snippet: Oliver has been training for a winter triathlon and goes for an early-morning run in minus eight degrees. He notices his ears and nose have gone completely numb and white halfway through the route.
options: He turns back immediately, covers his ears and nose with his hands, and heads home to rewarm gently.
He continues his planned route because completing training is important for his race preparation.
He rubs his ears hard and fast to restore circulation before turning back.
He runs faster to raise his core temperature and restore blood flow to his face.
payload.explanation: White numb skin is frostnip — stop activity, protect the area, and rewarm gently without rubbing.

payload.snippet: A burst pipe has flooded the hallway with water on a night of minus fifteen degrees outside. The water is rapidly freezing on the wooden floor.
options: She turns off the water at the stopcock, mops what she can, and calls an emergency plumber.
She pours boiling water over the floor to melt the ice and stop it spreading.
She opens the front door to let cold air set the ice so she can sweep it out.
She uses the electric fan heater on the floor to melt the ice overnight.
payload.explanation: Stopcock, mop, and emergency plumber is the correct burst-pipe response — adding heat causes further damage.

payload.snippet: Jake is supervising a group of teenagers ice-skating when one falls awkwardly and reports that her back is hurting and she cannot feel her feet.
options: He tells her not to move, keeps her warm, and calls for an ambulance immediately.
He helps her very gently off the ice and onto a bench to rest.
He asks her to wiggle her toes and if she can he helps her to stand.
He skates to the rink exit and asks the reception to call a taxi.
payload.explanation: Suspected spinal injury requires stillness, warmth, and emergency services — never move the casualty.

payload.snippet: The school's caretaker finds the outdoor steps covered in thick black ice just as children start arriving for the day.
options: He stands at the steps to redirect children to the side entrance while a colleague spreads grit.
He shouts at arriving children to walk very carefully on the ice.
He puts a cardboard box over the worst patch and monitors the rest.
He closes the school and sends a text message to all parents right away.
payload.explanation: Redirecting children away from hazard while the fix is applied is the correct duty-of-care response.

payload.snippet: Clara's family is hiking in a winter mountain national park when visibility drops to near zero in a sudden whiteout blizzard with strong winds.
options: They stop immediately, use the GPS to mark their position, shelter behind a large rock, and call mountain rescue.
They continue walking quickly in the direction they were heading to reach the summit shelter.
They spread out to cover more ground and search for a descent path.
They follow the stream downhill, knowing water always leads to a lower valley.
payload.explanation: Stopping, sheltering, marking position, and calling mountain rescue are the correct whiteout protocols.

payload.snippet: Ben finds an injured barn owl sitting in deep snow in the field, unable to fly, with one wing drooping.
options: He wraps it loosely in his scarf, places it in a box with air holes, keeps it dark and quiet, and contacts a local wildlife rescue.
He warms it up quickly with the hand warmers in his pocket.
He splints the wing with two pencils and tape from his rucksack.
He leaves it where it is so the parent owls can come back to help it.
payload.explanation: Wrapping loosely, darkening, and contacting wildlife rescue is correct injured-bird protocol.

payload.snippet: Maya is supervising a younger sibling on the sledge run when she notices a patch of bare ice leading directly into a low stone wall.
options: She shouts to her sibling to lean right to steer away and stands ready to intercept if needed.
She runs onto the sledge run ahead of the sibling to block the wall.
She tells the sibling to grab both sides and close their eyes.
She waits to see if the sibling steers naturally before deciding to intervene.
payload.explanation: Giving immediate clear steering instructions while being ready to intercept is the correct supervisory response.

payload.snippet: Tom has been clearing the roof of heavy snow for an hour when he feels the ladder shift under him as he descends.
options: He grips the ladder firmly, steps down one rung at a time, and shouts to someone below to hold the base.
He jumps off the ladder from his current height to get down quickly.
He climbs back to the roof and waits for someone to notice.
He leans toward the wall to stop the ladder from falling further.
payload.explanation: Controlled one-rung descent while calling for a ladder-holder is the correct roof-ladder safety procedure.

payload.snippet: Anna notices the village road has become completely impassable during the night blizzard and the only trained nurse in the village lives on the other side.
options: She organises a group of villagers to shovel a safe path through the snow to the nurse's house.
She sends the nurse a message explaining the situation and wishes her luck.
She drives her 4x4 over the snow-covered road, as slowly as possible.
She waits for the county council gritter, which is expected sometime tomorrow morning.
payload.explanation: Community action to clear a path ensures the nurse can reach patients who may need urgent care.

payload.snippet: Oliver is helping his dad fit winter tyres when he notices the jack is positioned on a frozen patch that has begun to melt under the car's warmth.
options: He points this out and they lower the car, move it to firm ground, and re-jack safely.
He stands clear and watches while his dad completes the tyre change quickly.
He wedges a flat stone under the jack foot to stabilise it on the ice.
He pours cold water on the jack foot to refreeze the ice quickly.
payload.explanation: A shifting jack is a life-safety hazard — the car must be lowered and the jack repositioned on firm ground.

payload.snippet: Clara is first on the scene when a cyclist has skidded on black ice and is lying on the road, conscious but dazed and wearing a helmet.
options: She calls 999, warns oncoming traffic, and keeps the cyclist still and warm without removing the helmet.
She removes the helmet carefully to check for head injuries underneath.
She moves the cyclist to the pavement to clear the road for traffic.
She gives the cyclist water and helps them sit up against the kerb.
payload.explanation: 999, traffic warning, immobilise, keep warm, and leave the helmet on are correct road incident first-aid steps.

payload.snippet: Lily is leading her scout patrol on a winter night hike when she realises her compass and the group's footprints have both disappeared under fresh snow and she does not recognise any landmark around her.
options: She halts the group, uses her phone's GPS app to locate their position, identifies the safest route back to the car park, and messages the scout leader their coordinates.
She picks the direction with the most stars visible overhead and leads the group confidently forward.
She splits the patrol into pairs to spread out and search for a recognisable landmark.
She keeps moving at pace because stopping in cold weather causes body temperature to drop rapidly.
payload.explanation: GPS and messaging known location to the leader are the correct responses when lost on a winter night hike.

payload.snippet: Tom's elderly grandfather slips on black ice on the front step and lands heavily on his hip. He is conscious but cannot get up and is lying on frozen ground.
options: Tom calls 999 immediately, covers his grandfather with a coat and blanket to prevent cold injury while on the ground, and stays on the line guiding the responders.
Tom wraps his arms under his grandfather's arms and tries to lift him to a sitting position.
Tom asks a neighbour to help pull grandfather inside as quickly as possible.
Tom tells grandfather to try to roll onto his side and crawl to the doorstep.
payload.explanation: Moving someone with a suspected hip fracture risks worsening the injury — 999, insulation, and staying put are correct.

payload.snippet: The ice rink surface has developed a dangerous rough patch in the centre that has already tripped two skaters. The session supervisor notices but the ice-resurface machine is out of service.
options: She closes the rink, places cones and rope around the damaged area, and announces an adjusted skating zone for the remainder of the session.
She asks the strongest skaters to stay away from the area and relies on them to warn others.
She speeds up the session end by fifteen minutes and makes no announcement to avoid panic.
She has the maintenance crew lay rubber matting over the rough patch while skaters continue.
payload.explanation: Marking the hazard, restricting the skating zone, and communicating clearly is the correct duty-of-care response.

payload.snippet: Oliver discovers that the path through the woods to the village has a section where meltwater has flooded over a wooden footbridge, forming a thick sheet of invisible wet ice after the overnight freeze.
options: He marks both approaches to the bridge with brightly coloured sticks from his bag and reports the hazard to the parish council by phone.
He chips away at the ice with his boot heel to create a rough surface so others can cross.
He ties his scarf across one approach as a marker and crosses quickly on the other side.
He waits at the bridge to warn approaching walkers in person until someone else takes over.
payload.explanation: Visible hazard markers on both approaches and an official report ensure all users are warned and the problem gets fixed.

payload.snippet: Ben is lifeguarding a community outdoor pool when a swimmer raises their arm — the international signal for distress — from the deep end but does not appear to be sinking. Three other swimmers are nearby and the second lifeguard is occupied with a minor cut at the first-aid station.
options: He blows his whistle to clear the area, throws the rescue tube immediately, shouts for the other lifeguard, enters only if the tube throw is unsuccessful, and keeps eyes on the casualty at all times.
He waits ten seconds to confirm the swimmer cannot self-rescue before taking any action.
He tells the nearest strong swimmer to assist while he fetches the second lifeguard.
He enters the water immediately and swims to the distressed swimmer as fast as he can.
payload.explanation: A raised-arm signal demands immediate tube-throw response, cleared area, and eyes-on — never delay to confirm distress.

payload.snippet: Maya is running a summer outdoor play session for thirty children aged four to ten when she counts heads and finds a five-year-old is missing. The session is in a park with a road on one side and a pond on the other.
options: She immediately assigns a trusted helper to watch all remaining children, calls 999, and begins a systematic search with the other adult starting at the pond — the nearest water hazard.
She searches the whole park herself first before calling 999 so she can give the police a full picture.
She asks all the older children to spread out and search in pairs while she calls the parents.
She calls the parents first so they can authorise her to leave the other children with helpers to search.
payload.explanation: Missing child near water: 999 immediately, maintain supervision of other children, prioritise search from water hazard outward.

payload.snippet: Tom is working at a summer outdoor wedding as the catering lead when the temperature hits forty degrees and the ice supply runs out. Guests have been drinking alcohol in the heat and two elderly guests already look unwell.
options: He immediately switches all service to soft drinks and water, isolates the two unwell guests in a shaded area with fans, and calls 999 if either shows signs of confusion or skin change.
He carries on with the menu plan but asks the bar staff to encourage water between drinks.
He announces that hot food service is suspended and redirects guests to the shaded marquee.
He calls the caterer's supplier for an emergency ice delivery and monitors the guests closely.
payload.explanation: Alcohol in extreme heat is a medical amplifier — removing service, cooling identified casualties, and having 999 ready is the priority.

payload.snippet: Anna is hiking alone on a remote coastal path in a summer heatwave when she twists her ankle badly on loose scree, cannot weight-bear, is three kilometres from the nearest road, and has half a litre of water left.
options: She finds shade, texts her exact location and grid reference to a contact, calls mountain rescue, stays put, and sips water sparingly while waiting.
She attempts to limp back to the road as staying put in the heat will worsen her dehydration.
She drinks all the water immediately to maintain full cognition and then calls for rescue.
She makes a makeshift splint from her walking pole and attempts to continue the route to raise help.
payload.explanation: Injured and alone: shelter, share location, call rescue, conserve water, and stay put — moving a broken ankle worsens outcome.

payload.snippet: Oliver is the senior responsible adult on a school summer trip when the coach driver unexpectedly falls ill with what appears to be a cardiac event, stopping the coach on the motorway hard shoulder with thirty children on board.
options: He calls 999, starts CPR if the driver is unresponsive and not breathing, keeps children calm and seated, sends one teacher to the rear emergency exit as a safety officer, and does not exit children to the hard shoulder.
He exits all children to the motorway verge immediately to remove them from the stalled vehicle.
He calls the school first to get authorisation before contacting emergency services.
He calls 999, lays the driver flat across the seats, and asks the children to move to the back of the coach.
payload.explanation: Hard shoulder is more dangerous than a stalled coach — keep children seated inside; CPR and 999 are the correct adult response.

payload.snippet: Clara is volunteer-managing a community outdoor lido that is legally required to close if the water quality E. coli reading exceeds 200 CFU per 100ml. Today's test returns a reading of 280. The pool is packed with 200 swimmers on the hottest day of the year.
options: She closes the pool immediately, posts the reading on the information board transparently, directs swimmers to changing rooms, and contacts the local authority's public health team.
She closes the pool but tells swimmers only that there is a technical issue to avoid panic.
She retests the water immediately and waits for a second reading before deciding whether to close.
She limits swimming to adults only while she investigates and waits for the public health guidance.
payload.explanation: An above-threshold pathogen reading triggers mandatory immediate closure and transparent communication — retesting does not override the first result.

payload.snippet: Ben is running a summer holiday camp and one of the children discloses during a group session that an adult at home hits them when they are bad and shows bruising on their arms that was not there yesterday.
options: He thanks the child calmly, listens without asking leading questions, notes what was said word for word privately, and reports immediately to the camp's designated safeguarding lead.
He calls the parents to discuss what the child has said and to give them the chance to explain.
He photographs the bruising as evidence and stores it on his personal phone for the report.
He waits until the end of the day to gather more information from the other children first.
payload.explanation: Child safeguarding: listen, note verbatim, do not investigate or contact parents — report immediately to the DSL.

payload.snippet: Maya is kayaking with a group of beginners in a sheltered sea cove when the wind suddenly picks up and one kayaker capsizes. The capsized kayaker is wearing a PFD, is conscious, and is calling for help, but the other beginners are starting to drift toward open water.
options: She shouts clear instructions for beginners to paddle toward the beach, paddles directly to the capsized kayaker, helps them re-enter or tows them to shore, and keeps a head count throughout.
She gets the capsized kayaker to hold her stern toggle and tows everyone together to shore.
She shouts to the capsized kayaker to float on their back and then rounds up all the drifting beginners first.
She calls the coastguard immediately and waits for professional rescue before approaching the capsized kayaker.
payload.explanation: In a group kayak incident: secure the immediate casualty, give clear instructions to the group, maintain a count — sequence matters.

payload.snippet: Tom is a sports coach running a summer football camp in direct sun when a twelve-year-old player collapses mid-drill, recovers briefly, then has a second collapse with a brief seizure lasting thirty seconds.
options: He calls 999 immediately, notes the seizure duration, places the player in the recovery position, keeps others back, and does not put anything in the player's mouth.
He calls the player's parents immediately and tells them to meet him at the nearest hospital.
He gives the player water and asks them to sit up and report how they feel after the seizure ends.
He times the seizure and if it lasts under two minutes decides not to call 999 to avoid over-reaction.
payload.explanation: A seizure following exercise collapse in heat needs 999, recovery position, timing, and nothing in the mouth — not food, drink, or a 'wait and see' approach.

payload.snippet: Anna is a summer camp nurse and a thirteen-year-old camper arrives with an allergic rash covering both arms after eating lunch, reporting she feels itchy in her throat. The camper has not brought her prescribed antihistamine.
options: She calls 999 immediately, stays with the camper, monitors her breathing, and prepares the camp's emergency EpiPen in case anaphylaxis progresses.
She gives the camper liquid antihistamine from the camp's general first-aid stock.
She contacts the camper's parents for authorisation before using the emergency EpiPen.
She asks the camper to breathe slowly and walk with her to the camp office for the antihistamine records.
payload.explanation: Throat itch with spreading rash is anaphylaxis risk — 999 first; use EpiPen if authorised in camp protocol without waiting for parents.

payload.snippet: Oliver is working at a summer outdoor festival as a medic when he is approached by a friend of a festivalgoer who says their friend has taken something and is now unresponsive in a tent. He finds a young adult unconscious, breathing slowly and shallowly.
options: He calls for the festival's advanced medical team immediately, places the person in the recovery position, stays beside them monitoring breathing rate, and does not leave until the team arrives.
He asks the friend what substance was taken and then decides whether 999 or the festival medics are more appropriate.
He props the person upright so their airway does not get blocked and fans them to maintain consciousness.
He waits to see if the person rouses within five minutes before escalating to the advanced team.
payload.explanation: Drug-related unconsciousness with slow shallow breathing is a respiratory depression emergency — recovery position, advanced medics, do not leave.

payload.snippet: Clara discovers that the community paddling pool she manages has been vandalised and glass fragments have been scattered in the water overnight before the morning session opening.
options: She locks the gate, places hazard signs, calls the police to report criminal damage, and arranges a full drain and professional inspection before any reopening.
She uses a pool net to remove all visible glass, refills with fresh water, and opens with an extended staff pre-swim inspection.
She calls the council's parks department and opens the pool with a reduced maximum depth while awaiting guidance.
She closes only the section nearest to where the glass appears to be and allows the rest of the pool to open normally.
payload.explanation: Glass in public water requires full closure, police report, drain, and professional inspection — no partial operation is acceptable.

payload.snippet: Anna is a summer camp medic on duty when a camper arrives with a string of blisters across both shoulders that she says came from a plant she brushed against on yesterday's nature walk. The blisters are tense, fluid-filled, and painful to touch.
options: She photographs the blisters, does not rupture them, covers them with a non-adherent dressing, records the incident, and drives the camper to the nearest minor injuries unit for assessment.
She pops the blisters with a sterile needle, cleans the area with antiseptic, and applies cream from the first-aid stock.
She identifies the plant as likely hogweed from the pattern and treats locally without seeking further medical assessment.
She applies a cooling gel dressing and monitors the camper for twenty-four hours before deciding whether medical attention is needed.
payload.explanation: Plant-contact blisters — particularly hogweed phototoxicity — need professional assessment, not home lancing.

payload.snippet: Tom is a junior ranger leading a summer dawn bird-survey walk when a member of the group spots what appears to be a red kite tangled in baling twine in a hedgerow. The bird is alive but exhausted and cannot free itself.
options: He keeps the group back, calls the RSPCA emergency line, and stays to monitor the bird without handling it until the officer arrives.
He wraps the bird in his jacket to calm it and carefully cuts the twine with his penknife.
He gets the group to form a screen around the hedgerow while he films the bird for identification.
He marks the hedgerow on his GPS and leads the group on, returning after the survey to check if it freed itself.
payload.explanation: Injured wild raptors require RSPCA response — handling them incorrectly causes further injury and is illegal without a licence.

payload.snippet: Maya is a summer swimming instructor supervising an eight-year-old beginner in the outdoor pool when the child suddenly inhales a large volume of water while practising a back float and begins coughing violently. She brings the child to the pool edge — the coughing subsides but the child looks pale and slightly dazed.
options: She keeps the child out of the water, monitors them closely, calls for the duty manager, and strongly advises the parent to take the child to hospital for assessment for secondary drowning.
She sits the child down, gives them water, and resumes the lesson once the coughing has fully stopped.
She tells the parent the child recovered well but to watch their breathing overnight at home.
She files an incident report after the session and advises the parent to call 111 if concerned.
payload.explanation: Any significant water inhalation in a child warrants a hospital assessment for secondary drowning, even when immediate symptoms resolve.

payload.snippet: Oliver is coaching a junior cricket team on a summer evening when a twelve-year-old is struck directly in the chest by a fast delivery. The ball hit exactly over the heart. The player goes down immediately and loses consciousness for a few seconds before coming round looking confused.
options: Oliver calls 999 immediately, places the player in the recovery position if conscious, does not let him stand or walk, and requests AED availability on site.
Oliver helps the player sit up as they are conscious now, gives them water, and watches for ten minutes before deciding.
Oliver checks for broken ribs by pressing on the chest and then allows the player to rest at the boundary.
Oliver calls the parents and asks them to collect the player and take them to a walk-in centre.
payload.explanation: A direct precordial blow causing even brief unconsciousness is a commotio cordis risk — 999 and AED readiness are mandatory.

payload.snippet: Clara is running a summer outdoor art workshop when a participant reports that the solvent used to clean the printmaking equipment has splashed into her eye. The participant is blinking rapidly and her eye is red and watering heavily.
options: Clara immediately guides her to the nearest eye-wash station, irrigates the eye continuously for at least fifteen minutes, and calls 999 or arranges transport to hospital.
Clara tells her to blink rapidly and cover the eye with a clean pad while she looks up the safety data sheet.
Clara applies eye drops from the first-aid kit and monitors the redness for thirty minutes.
Clara wipes the eye gently with a wet wipe and advises her to see a pharmacist later in the day.
payload.explanation: Chemical splash to the eye requires immediate continuous irrigation for fifteen minutes minimum and urgent hospital assessment.

payload.snippet: Ben is organising a large outdoor summer picnic for two hundred guests. Halfway through the event, twelve guests report that they feel nauseous and two have already been sick, all having eaten the prawn salad served forty-five minutes ago.
options: Ben removes all remaining prawn salad from service immediately, records the names of affected guests, calls 111 for advice on the mass-illness situation, and preserves a sample of the prawn salad in the refrigerator for testing.
Ben tells the affected guests to go home and rest, continues the event, and files a report with the caterer tomorrow.
Ben announces a general advisory for all guests to stop eating prawn salad but continues serving other food normally.
Ben clears all food from the tables immediately and ends the picnic to avoid further illness.
payload.explanation: Suspected food poisoning cluster requires: remove the food, log casualties, call 111, preserve a sample — the event need not end but the implicated food must be stopped.

payload.snippet: Tom is supervising an outdoor summer theatre rehearsal in a park when a lightning strike hits a tall tree forty metres away. No one is hurt but the tree catches fire and smoke begins rising.
options: He immediately leads all cast and crew to the designated outdoor shelter (a substantial building), calls 999 to report the tree fire, and does not allow anyone to return to the park until fire services confirm it is safe.
He keeps the rehearsal going while he calls the fire service, as the fire is contained to the tree.
He moves the group fifty metres further from the tree and resumes rehearsal in a safer spot.
He checks whether anyone is hurt first, then decides whether the fire is serious enough to call 999.
payload.explanation: A lightning strike tree fire in a public park needs 999 and full evacuation to a building — the storm is still a live hazard.

payload.snippet: Anna is managing an outdoor summer sports camp for children with varying physical abilities. The forecast shows UV index eleven at peak hours. Two children have vitiligo, making their depigmented patches extremely vulnerable to severe burn within minutes.
options: She moves all outdoor activity to before 10am and after 3pm, ensures the two children with vitiligo have factor fifty-plus sunscreen reapplied every ninety minutes to all exposed patches, and provides UPF-rated clothing for the midday break.
She advises the two children's parents in advance and leaves it to the parents' discretion how much to cover.
She applies standard factor thirty sunscreen to all children including those with vitiligo every two hours.
She keeps all children indoors during peak UV hours and runs all scheduled outdoor activities in the gym instead.
payload.explanation: Vitiligo patches burn within minutes in UV index 11 — targeted factor 50+, UPF clothing, and scheduled outdoor timing are the medically informed management steps.

payload.snippet: Anna is driving alone on a rural road in a rainstorm when she hits a deep pothole hidden by surface water. Her front-left tyre blows out instantly and the car begins to pull hard to the left at fifty miles per hour.
options: She grips the wheel firmly, takes her foot off the accelerator without braking, lets the car slow naturally, and steers to a safe stopping point well off the road.
She brakes hard immediately to stop the car before it drifts off the road.
She steers to the right to counteract the pull and maintains her current speed.
She turns off the engine immediately and steers to the side of the road.
payload.explanation: A blowout at speed requires no sudden braking — grip, lift, slow naturally, and steer off the road.

payload.snippet: Oliver is a first aider at an outdoor music festival when he is called to a young woman who was struck by lightning a few minutes ago. She is unconscious and not breathing. His defibrillator is at the first-aid tent forty metres away.
options: He begins CPR immediately, sends a bystander at a run for the AED, and continues until the AED arrives or the patient starts breathing.
He waits for the AED before starting CPR as lightning victims may carry a residual electrical charge.
He checks her pulse for sixty seconds first to be certain CPR is needed.
He starts CPR but shouts for everyone nearby to back away in case of residual electrical charge.
payload.explanation: Lightning strike victims carry no residual charge and need immediate CPR — do not delay for AED or worry about touching them.

payload.snippet: Maya is the duty officer at a youth outdoor activity centre when a severe flood warning is issued for the river running alongside the site. She has sixty children and twenty adults on the site and the normal road access is next to the river.
options: She evacuates everyone immediately via the uphill emergency track to the car park on high ground, accounts for all sixty children and twenty adults, and calls the emergency services to update them on their position.
She monitors the river level for thirty minutes to see how fast it is rising before deciding to evacuate.
She moves everyone to the centre's highest building and waits for emergency services to arrive by boat.
She sends adults to the car park via the normal road and keeps children in the highest building until transport arrives.
payload.explanation: A severe flood warning on a site next to a river means immediate high-ground evacuation of everyone before the road floods.

payload.snippet: Jake is on a hill-walk with two friends when one friend slips on a muddy path and slides three metres before stopping, sitting up and saying her wrist hurts and looks misshapen.
options: Jake keeps her still, immobilises the wrist by supporting it gently without straightening it, calls mountain rescue, and keeps her warm with extra layers while they wait.
Jake asks her to flex the wrist slowly to check if it is a sprain or a break.
Jake splints the wrist with two walking poles and helps her walk out to speed up the rescue.
Jake calls his parents to drive to the car park while he helps his friend limp out from the hill.
payload.explanation: A visibly misshapen wrist is a likely fracture — immobilise, do not move the casualty on a hill, call mountain rescue.

payload.snippet: Clara is coaching a junior athletics session outdoors when continuous rain turns the long-jump sand pit into a waterlogged slurry. A child takes a run-up and lands in the deep wet sand, twisting and falling sideways with a yelp.
options: Clara stops the session, assists the child to the side, checks for injury, and does not resume use of the sand pit until it is drained and made safe.
Clara rakes the top layer of sand to redistribute the water and resumes the session carefully.
Clara lets children jump but only if they land two-footed and on the dry far edge of the pit.
Clara asks the child if she can walk and if so continues the session after a five-minute rest.
payload.explanation: A waterlogged long-jump pit is a hazard requiring session stop and proper drainage before any further use.

payload.snippet: Tom is cycling across a flooded underpass that appears shallow when the water suddenly reaches his pedals and the bike stalls. He dismounts into water that is now thigh-deep and moving.
options: He abandons the bike, wades diagonally toward the nearest wall, uses it to support himself, and moves steadily toward the exit without fighting the current.
He keeps hold of the bike and uses it as a float to help stay upright in the current.
He turns back toward the entrance immediately and wades against the current.
He calls 999 and waits exactly where he is so rescuers can find him more easily.
payload.explanation: Abandon the bike, use the wall for support, and move diagonally with the current to exit — do not fight moving floodwater.

payload.snippet: Anna is supervising a primary school residential trip when overnight rain causes the wooden fire-escape stairs on the accommodation block to become extremely slippery. She tests them at six a.m. and judges them too dangerous to use without grip aid.
options: She applies the grit from the emergency box kept at the accommodation entrance, tests them again, and advises the trip leader to identify an alternative ground-floor exit route for the morning just in case.
She tells children to hold both rails and take the stairs slowly, monitoring each one as they descend.
She places a warning cone at the top and bottom and uses the stairs herself throughout the morning.
She closes off the fire-escape stairs entirely and leaves the interior staircase as the only exit route.
payload.explanation: Gritting, retesting, and identifying an alternative exit addresses the hazard without leaving people without an escape route.

payload.snippet: Oliver is running a kayaking session on a river when the water level rises by thirty centimetres in twenty minutes due to rain upstream. He is three kilometres from the put-in and there are six novice paddlers with him.
options: He immediately guides the group to the bank, pulls all kayaks out of the water, and calls the kayak club emergency contact to arrange vehicle extraction rather than paddling back.
He keeps paddling downstream to the take-out point as the water is flowing faster and will make the trip shorter.
He anchors kayaks to a tree and waits on the bank for the level to stabilise before paddling on.
He sends his strongest paddler ahead to the take-out to arrange extraction while the others wait.
payload.explanation: A rapidly rising river level requires immediate bank exit and vehicle extraction — not continued paddling or waiting.

payload.snippet: Maya is at a park when she notices that a large tree near the children's play area is leaning noticeably further than she has ever seen it, with fresh root pull visible on one side after three days of heavy rain.
options: She immediately guides all children away from the tree's fall zone, calls the council parks emergency number, and stays to warn other park users until staff arrive.
She ties a rope around the trunk and stakes it to the ground to reduce the lean.
She estimates the fall zone herself and positions children at what she thinks is a safe distance.
She photographs the tree and emails the council's non-emergency address with a request for inspection.
payload.explanation: A rain-loosened leaning tree with root pull is a falling hazard requiring immediate clearance and an emergency parks call — not email.

payload.snippet: Jake is driving in heavy rain on a motorway when he enters a large patch of standing water at sixty miles per hour and the car begins to aquaplane, losing all steering response.
options: He releases the accelerator smoothly, keeps the wheel straight, and waits for traction to return before making any steering corrections.
He brakes firmly and steers gently right to get off the standing water patch.
He turns the steering wheel gradually left then right to regain grip through the tyres.
He lifts his foot off the accelerator and applies the handbrake to slow in a straight line.
payload.explanation: Aquaplaning requires: lift off the accelerator, straight wheel, wait for grip — any braking or turning worsens loss of control.

payload.snippet: Clara is a teacher on a school residential when she finds a twelve-year-old student sitting outside a locked cabin in heavy rain, soaking wet and refusing to come inside. When asked, the student discloses she has hurt herself with a sharp object on her arm.
options: Clara calmly brings her inside without drawing attention, assesses the injury, gives first aid if needed, and follows the school's safeguarding protocol by informing the designated safeguarding lead immediately.
Clara asks her to roll up her sleeve to confirm the injury before taking any further action.
Clara gives her dry clothes, starts a supportive conversation, and decides whether to inform the safeguarding lead in the morning.
Clara informs the group of teachers and asks one to come and support the conversation.
payload.explanation: Self-harm disclosure requires immediate safeguarding reporting, not assessment delay or group disclosure.

payload.snippet: Ben is leading a team of six on a corporate outdoor challenge event when torrential rain causes a small wooden bridge they need to cross to start moving and creaking underfoot.
options: He stops the group at the bridge approach, tests the bridge's stability alone, and if in any doubt leads the group on a longer detour around the water obstacle.
He has the group cross one by one as quickly as possible to minimise load time.
He holds the side rail and judges the bridge safe enough for the group after his test.
He asks the two heaviest group members to wait while the others cross and then reconsiders.
payload.explanation: A moving creaking bridge in flood conditions should be treated as unsafe — test alone, then detour if any doubt.

payload.snippet: Tom is helping at a rainy outdoor market when he notices that the temporary electrical cable powering the food stalls has been lying in a puddle for the past hour. Several vendors are still plugged in and trading.
options: He tells the nearest vendor to switch off at the plug, warns others not to step in the puddle, and calls the market manager to disconnect at the distribution board.
He lifts the cable out of the puddle with his rubber boot and walks it to a dry area.
He puts a cardboard box over the puddle so vendors and customers do not step in it.
He photographs the hazard and sends it to the market organiser's phone number.
payload.explanation: A cable in a puddle with live connected equipment is a life-safety electrical hazard requiring immediate power-off at the board.

payload.snippet: Maya is a senior lifeguard at an outdoor pool during heavy rain when a lightning detection alarm activates. She has thirty swimmers in the pool and two young swimmers in the shallow end who are not responding to verbal instructions to exit.
options: She blows three short whistle blasts, enters the pool only to physically guide the two unresponsive swimmers out, then evacuates all staff and swimmers to the indoor changing facilities.
She calls the two swimmers' parents first and asks them to come and collect their children.
She keeps all other swimmers in the pool while she deals with the two who are not listening.
She turns off the pool lights and PA system so the children understand it is a serious situation.
payload.explanation: Lightning alarm requires immediate pool evacuation — verbal-only override is not enough for non-compliant swimmers.

payload.snippet: Oliver is leading a walk along a coastal path when persistent rain has made the cliff-edge path slick with mud. A section of the path has a two-metre drop on the left side and no barrier.
options: He turns the group back the way they came, finding a safer inland route, and does not continue along the exposed muddy edge.
He has the group press against the cliff wall and move quickly past the exposed section.
He ties a rope between group members so anyone who slips will be caught by the others.
He goes first to test the path and then signals for the group to follow one by one.
payload.explanation: A muddy exposed cliff-edge path is not passable safely — turn back and find an alternative route.

He brakes firmly and steers gently right to get off the standing water patch.
He turns the steering wheel gradually left then right to regain grip through the tyres.
He lifts his foot off the accelerator and applies the handbrake to slow in a straight line.
payload.explanation: Aquaplaning requires: lift off the accelerator, straight wheel, wait for grip — any braking or turning worsens loss of control.

Clara asks her to roll up her sleeve to confirm the injury before taking any further action.
Clara gives her dry clothes, starts a supportive conversation, and decides whether to inform the safeguarding lead in the morning.
Clara informs the group of teachers and asks one to come and support the conversation.
payload.explanation: Self-harm disclosure requires immediate safeguarding reporting, not assessment delay or group disclosure.

She sends adults to the car park via the normal road and keeps children in the highest building until transport arrives.
payload.explanation: A severe flood warning on a site next to a river means immediate high-ground evacuation of everyone before the road floods.

He keeps hold of the bike and uses it as a float to help stay upright in the current.
He turns back toward the entrance immediately and wades against the current.
He calls 999 and waits exactly where he is so rescuers can find him more easily.
payload.explanation: Abandon the bike, use the wall for support, and move diagonally with the current to exit — do not fight moving floodwater.

payload.snippet: Clara is responsible for a group of six children at an outdoor birthday party in a public park. While she is counting, she realises one five-year-old is missing. The last time she saw the child he was near the pond at the bottom of the slope.
options: She calls loudly, assigns one adult to stay with the other five, and runs directly to the pond to check before expanding the search.
She assigns all adults to search different sections of the park simultaneously.
She calls the child's parents immediately and asks them to come to the park.
She tells the remaining children to spread out and look for their friend.
payload.explanation: When a child near water is missing, the water hazard must be checked first — always.

payload.snippet: Tom is a volunteer at a school sports day helping to supervise the climbing wall activity when a nine-year-old reaches the top but the belayer's hand slips and the child drops two metres before the system catches them with a jolt. The child is dangling and crying.
options: He calls for the trained climbing instructor immediately, keeps the child calm and still while suspended, and does not attempt to lower the child himself.
He reaches up and unclips the child's harness so they can climb down the rope themselves.
He asks the belayer to slowly lower the child while he steadies the child from below.
He tells the child to let go of the wall and lower themselves hand-over-hand down the rope.
payload.explanation: Suspending a frightened child after a drop requires a trained instructor — keep them calm and do not improvise a lowering.

payload.snippet: Anna is at an outdoor play area when she witnesses an older child systematically intimidating and threatening younger children to stay off the equipment, making several of them cry. The child's parent is present and watching but not intervening.
options: She calmly speaks to the park warden or reports to the supervisor and does not confront the parent directly.
She directly challenges the older child in front of their parent to make the situation stop.
She takes the younger children to the far side of the park and calls the park closed for the area.
She tells the older child loudly that their behaviour is wrong so other parents can hear.
payload.explanation: Reporting to a park authority rather than confronting the parent avoids escalation and ensures proper handling.

payload.snippet: Oliver is leading a junior ranger forest-school session at a woodland playground when a child climbs a dead tree at the edge of the site. The tree visibly sways and the bark crumbles under the child's grip.
options: He calls the child down in a calm steady voice, moves the group away from the tree, and marks it for removal.
He has two other children hold the base of the tree while the climbing child descends.
He climbs the tree himself to assess whether it is structurally safe enough for play.
He waits until the child reaches a low branch before giving instructions, to avoid startling them.
payload.explanation: A dead swaying tree is a structural hazard — calm retrieval and marking are required immediately.

payload.snippet: Maya is working as a playground supervisor when she observes a new child join the group who appears to have fresh bruising on both forearms in a pattern inconsistent with playground falls — multiple circular marks in a line.
options: She documents what she sees accurately, does not question the child directly, and reports immediately to the school's designated safeguarding lead.
She asks the child in private what caused the bruises to understand what happened.
She photographs the bruises for the record and then monitors the child for the rest of the session.
She calls the child's parents to report the bruising pattern and see if they can explain it.
payload.explanation: Patterned bruising requires safeguarding reporting — do not interrogate the child or contact parents.

payload.snippet: Ben is helping install a new outdoor play structure at a community centre when he notices the ground anchors provided are a different specification than the drawing shows. He raises this with the site manager who tells him to fit them anyway and sign off the installation.
options: He refuses to sign off on the incorrect specification and asks the site manager to put the instruction in writing before he proceeds.
He fits the anchors as instructed and notes his concern in a site diary in case something goes wrong.
He installs the anchors as told, planning to replace them at the next inspection.
He calls the manufacturer directly and asks whether the alternative anchors are actually safe to use.
payload.explanation: Installing incorrect safety-critical anchors and signing off creates personal liability — require written instruction and refuse sign-off.

payload.snippet: Jake is supervising children at an adventure playground when one child starts a dare game that has escalated to jumping from a platform two metres high onto the grass below. Three children have already jumped before he notices.
options: He stops the game immediately, checks each child who jumped for injury, fills in an incident report, and informs the parents of all three.
He stops the next child from jumping and monitors the three who already jumped for the rest of the session.
He finishes supervising and completes an incident report at the end of the session.
He ends the session early and asks the children to wait for parents without explaining why.
payload.explanation: Immediate stop, injury checks for all participants, incident report, and parent notification are all required.

payload.snippet: Clara is running an after-school playground session when it starts raining heavily and the wooden decking on the assault course becomes extremely slippery. One child has already fallen.
options: She closes the wooden section immediately, moves children to the covered area, and files an incident report about the fall.
She tells children to remove their shoes to get better grip on the wet wood.
She keeps the session going but positions herself at the wet section to catch anyone who slips.
She ends the session and waits for the rain to stop before anyone continues playing.
payload.explanation: A wet wooden surface with a known fall requires immediate closure of that section and an incident report.

payload.snippet: Tom is playing at a skate park when he sees a child he knows from school sitting alone behind the toilet block looking distressed, with their phone lit up in their hand. When he asks, the child says an older person keeps messaging them asking them to meet.
options: He sits with the child, looks at the message if the child shows him, and walks with the child to tell a trusted adult immediately.
He tells the child to block the number and not to reply, then leaves them alone.
He tells the child to meet the person in a public place so they can see who it is.
He takes a photo of the screen for evidence and reports it to the police app on his own phone.
payload.explanation: An adult soliciting a child online for a meeting is a safeguarding matter — accompany the child and tell a trusted adult immediately.

payload.snippet: Oliver is at a community playground when he sees a child have a seizure lasting about forty-five seconds near the swings. The child comes round and seems confused and tired. No adult is immediately visible.
options: He keeps bystanders back, notes the duration, keeps the child in the recovery position if needed, calls 999, and stays with the child until an adult arrives.
He helps the child to the bench and gives them water while waiting for them to recover.
He runs to find the child's parent before calling 999 so they can authorise medical help.
He puts the child in the recovery position, waits for five minutes, and calls 999 only if there is another seizure.
payload.explanation: A first seizure in a child requires 999 regardless of apparent recovery — do not delay for parental authorisation.

payload.snippet: Maya discovers that the protective rubber surfacing under the climbing frame has been partially lifted at one corner, exposing a concrete edge that children could fall onto.
options: She stands near the hazard to redirect children away from it and calls the park authority to report the exposed concrete.
She pushes the rubber surfacing back down and stomps on it to reattach it temporarily.
She places a warning cone over the lifted section and hopes the park authority will notice it.
She redirects children verbally and sends a photo to the park's social media page.
payload.explanation: A supervisor must physically block access to an exposed hard surface and report it officially — DIY repairs to safety surfaces create liability.

payload.snippet: Ben is at an outdoor playground when he notices a water feature has a pump that is making a loud grinding noise and has a visible electrical cable lying across the wet ground near the splash area, where young children are playing.
options: He moves all children away from the wet area immediately, calls for the park warden, and makes sure no one touches the cable or the water until the warden arrives.
He asks a child to hold the cable off the ground so it does not touch the water.
He switches the pump off at the power button on the unit to remove the electrical hazard.
He tells children to step over the cable carefully and continues watching the area.
payload.explanation: A wet cable near an electrical pump with children present is a live electrical hazard — clear the area immediately and call a warden.

He helps the child to the bench and gives them water while waiting for them to recover.
He runs to find the child's parent before calling 999 so they can authorise medical help.
He puts the child in the recovery position and calls 999 only if there is a second seizure.
payload.explanation: A first seizure in a child requires 999 regardless of apparent recovery — do not delay for parental authorisation.
