payload.explanation: A retrospectively-identified clinical concern requires colleague consultation and professional advice on disclosure — unilateral monitoring or immediate disclosure without guidance may both be inadequate or disproportionate.

payload.snippet: Clara is at a birthday dinner when she realises the restaurant has charged the group for a bottle of wine that was not ordered. The birthday person's parent is about to pay without noticing.
options: She quietly points out the discrepancy to the adult and suggests they ask the server to check before paying.
She says nothing to avoid causing a fuss at a birthday dinner.
She tells the server directly without involving the adult.
She assumes the restaurant would correct it automatically on a later statement.
payload.explanation: Pointing out a billing error discreetly to the responsible adult is the correct approach — saying nothing or bypassing the adult are both wrong.

payload.snippet: Oliver's school friend has a birthday party and only invites half the class, which the school's pastoral policy discourages. Several uninvited classmates are visibly upset the following Monday.
options: He does not discuss the party publicly at school and is sensitive when talking to those who were not invited.
He tells the uninvited classmates who was invited so they know the full picture.
He brings party favours to share with uninvited classmates to compensate.
He tells his friend they should have invited the whole class.
payload.explanation: Discretion and sensitivity toward those not invited is the correct peer response — commentary on the host's list is not helpful.

payload.snippet: Anna is celebrating a landmark birthday when a close friend gives a speech that includes an embarrassing story about Anna that Anna had told in confidence.
options: She thanks her friend publicly for the speech, then privately and calmly tells her friend the story was something she had shared in confidence and had not wanted shared more widely.
She interrupts the speech to correct the record.
She thanks her friend publicly and says nothing privately.
She tells mutual friends what happened and lets the message reach her friend indirectly.
payload.explanation: A private, calm conversation after the public moment is the correct way to address a confidence breach without creating a scene.

payload.snippet: Jake is at a child's birthday party as a supervising adult when he notices that the face painter has run out of hypoallergenic paint and is using a standard craft product on the children's skin.
options: He stops the face painting activity and checks with the parents of any children who have already been painted about known skin sensitivities.
He allows the face painter to continue since no child has complained.
He tells children to let him know if their face feels itchy.
He asks the face painter to continue with only the children whose parents are present.
payload.explanation: Non-hypoallergenic products on children's skin is a safety issue — stopping and checking with parents is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Maya is planning a joint birthday with a friend and they have agreed on a shared budget. When the invoices arrive, Maya discovers her friend has booked several extras beyond the agreed scope.
options: She has an honest conversation with her friend about the cost increase before the event and agrees how the extra cost will be handled.
She pays her share of the agreed budget only and lets her friend cover the extras.
She cancels the joint booking since the agreement was broken.
She agrees to split the full cost to avoid conflict, then feels resentful about it.
payload.explanation: An honest conversation about unexpected cost increases — before the event — is the correct way to resolve a budget breach in a joint arrangement.

payload.snippet: Tom is at a birthday celebration in a public venue when a member of the group begins acting in a way that is drawing alarmed looks from nearby guests and clearly making venue staff uncomfortable.
options: He speaks quietly to the person and suggests they step outside for a few minutes to cool down.
He tells venue staff the person is a guest and asks them to ignore the behaviour.
He ignores the situation since it is not his role to manage other guests.
He calls the person out in front of the group to address the behaviour.
payload.explanation: Discreetly addressing a guest whose behaviour is causing concern — by stepping outside — is the least disruptive and most respectful response.

payload.snippet: Clara is a baker who is hired to make a birthday cake. The day before the event, she realises she has run out of a key ingredient and her usual supplier cannot deliver in time.
options: She contacts the client immediately, explains the situation honestly, and presents the options available — such as a design modification or a shorter timeline substitute ingredient.
She substitutes the ingredient without telling the client and hopes they do not notice.
She cancels the cake and refunds the client the day before their event.
She asks the client to go and buy the ingredient themselves to meet her timeline.
payload.explanation: Honest early communication and offering options is the professional response to a supplier failure — silent substitution or last-minute cancellation both fail the client.

payload.snippet: Oliver is organising a surprise 60th birthday party for a parent when he discovers that the parent has recently been diagnosed with a serious illness and may not be well enough to attend their own surprise party.
options: He speaks privately with the parent's partner or closest family member to understand the parent's current capacity and preferences before proceeding with or changing the plans.
He proceeds with the party since cancelling would be worse for morale.
He cancels the party without speaking to anyone and notifies guests by message.
He tells the guests at the event that the birthday person may not attend, the day before.
payload.explanation: A sensitive health situation requires consultation with the inner circle before any party decision — proceeding or cancelling without input may go against the person's wishes.

payload.snippet: Anna's birthday party venue double-books the date and calls the week before to say they cannot accommodate her event.
options: She asks the venue what they propose to resolve the issue, and if they cannot offer an adequate alternative, she requests a full refund and begins arranging an alternative independently.
She demands the venue honour her booking since she has a contract.
She accepts the first alternative the venue suggests without negotiating.
She takes the situation to social media immediately to apply pressure.
payload.explanation: Asking the venue for a solution first is the correct approach — immediate legal threats or public pressure bypass the negotiation process.

payload.snippet: Jake is invited to a birthday party via a group chat and accidentally sends a private message about the birthday person to the group instead of in a direct message.
options: He acknowledges the mistake in the group immediately, apologises to the birthday person directly, and does not try to delete or minimise the error.
He deletes the message quickly before anyone can screenshot it.
He pretends he was joking about a different person.
He leaves the group to avoid the immediate fallout.
payload.explanation: Immediate acknowledgement and a direct apology to the affected person is the correct response to a message sent in error.

payload.snippet: Maya is attending a milestone birthday party when she realises the venue is not meeting fire safety standards — the emergency exit is blocked by furniture for the event set-up.
options: She quietly brings it to the attention of a staff member or the venue manager.
She moves the furniture herself during a quiet moment.
She identifies the fire exits herself and tells her group where to go in an emergency.
She waits to see if anyone else raises it.
payload.explanation: A blocked fire exit is a safety compliance issue that must be raised with staff — taking personal action or waiting are both inadequate.

payload.snippet: Tom's cousin is throwing a birthday party and asks Tom to cover for him with his parents if he extends the party past the agreed curfew.
options: He tells his cousin he is not comfortable being asked to deceive his cousin's parents, and will not agree to cover for him.
He agrees since family loyalty comes first.
He says yes to keep the peace but plans to tell the truth if directly asked.
He tells his cousin's parents before the party so they can address it.
payload.explanation: Declining to deceive another person's parents on their behalf is the correct boundary — agreeing or pre-emptively involving the parents are both wrong in different ways.

payload.snippet: Jake is a venue manager when a birthday party booking for twenty children includes a bouncy castle. On the day, thirty-two children arrive and the operator says the weight limit is for twenty.
options: He speaks to the party organiser, enforces the bouncy castle's stated capacity limit, and arranges an alternative activity for the additional children who cannot safely use it.
He allows children on in rotating groups since the weight limit is a maximum at one time.
He asks the bouncy castle operator if the limit is flexible for a few extra smaller children.
He tells the organiser the additional children will not be able to participate in that activity and offers no alternative.
payload.explanation: Bouncy castle weight limits are safety specifications — enforcing the limit and providing an alternative is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Maya is a teenager who discovers that a friend has been telling people her upcoming birthday is a 'no gifts' event in order to pocket any money given directly, while privately expecting guests to give gifts anyway.
options: She speaks to her friend privately and explains why this is dishonest, giving the friend an opportunity to communicate clearly with the guests.
She tells the other invited friends what is happening so they can decide for themselves.
She attends without a gift since the official invitation said no gifts.
She does not attend to avoid being part of the dishonest situation.
payload.explanation: A private honest conversation with the friend is the appropriate first step — telling others or making unilateral decisions both bypass the direct approach.

payload.snippet: Tom is at an outdoor birthday event when a group of uninvited teenagers gatecrash and begin drinking alcohol among the guests.
options: He tells the adult in charge immediately so they can decide how to address the situation.
He asks the uninvited group to leave himself.
He alerts only the birthday person's parents after trying to talk to the group.
He films the situation on his phone in case evidence is needed later.
payload.explanation: Uninvited guests drinking alcohol at an event require adult intervention — a teenager addressing the group directly or filming before involving adults are both inadequate first steps.

payload.snippet: Clara is a fifteen-year-old whose parent has hired a professional photographer for her birthday party without asking Clara first. Clara is very uncomfortable being photographed.
options: She speaks to her parent privately before the party begins and explains her feelings, asking whether the photographer's role can be limited.
She refuses to interact with the photographer throughout the party without explaining why.
She tells the photographer directly not to photograph her.
She goes along with it to avoid causing conflict at her own party.
payload.explanation: A private conversation with the parent before the party allows for a practical adjustment — refusing the photographer directly or silent endurance both bypass the right communication channel.

payload.snippet: Oliver is an adult supervising a teenager's house party when he discovers that a guest has brought alcohol that is now being shared with the minors at the party.
options: He confiscates the alcohol, speaks privately with the guest who brought it, and decides whether that guest should remain at the party.
He tells all the guests that the alcohol must stop immediately but takes no further action.
He contacts the parents of the guest who brought the alcohol.
He calls the police since minors are consuming alcohol at a private event.
payload.explanation: Confiscating the alcohol and addressing the source directly are the correct first steps — police involvement is disproportionate for a first response to underage drinking at a private party.

payload.snippet: Anna's large birthday party is nearly over when she notices that several guests have left without saying goodbye and that a significant amount of food and drink is missing from a table that was not accessible during the event.
options: She checks whether the food was accidentally moved and, if genuinely missing, mentions it to her parents without making accusations to guests.
She contacts the guests who left without goodbye and asks whether they took anything.
She posts about the missing food on the group chat for the party.
She decides it was probably eaten during the party and does not raise it.
payload.explanation: Checking for innocent explanations first and raising it quietly with parents is the correct approach — public accusations or group message posts risk unfair blame.

payload.snippet: Jake is a child at his own birthday party when his parent begins drinking heavily throughout the event and their behaviour becomes noticeably erratic in front of the guests.
options: He quietly asks a trusted family friend or relative at the event to help manage the situation.
He tells his parent publicly to stop drinking.
He ignores the situation and hopes the guests do not notice.
He asks the guests to leave so his parent can be addressed privately.
payload.explanation: Quietly enlisting a trusted adult already present is the most appropriate and protective response for a child in this situation.

payload.snippet: Maya is planning a significant birthday trip abroad for a group of friends when one friend reveals she cannot afford the trip cost but has been going along with the plans to avoid being left out.
options: She has a private, honest conversation with the friend and explores whether a modified trip or alternative celebration can include everyone.
She proceeds with the original trip and offers to lend the friend the money.
She quietly plans a cheaper alternative trip without asking the group whether they would prefer it.
She tells the group about the cost issue without identifying which friend raised it.
payload.explanation: A private conversation and exploring flexible options together respects the friend's dignity — loans without discussion or unilateral plan changes both bypass the friend's agency.

payload.snippet: Maya is a trained first aider on a camping expedition when a fellow camper falls and complains of significant pain in their lower leg after twisting it awkwardly on uneven ground. The bone is not visibly displaced.
options: She immobilises the leg using available materials, keeps the casualty still and warm, and calls mountain rescue or emergency services given the remote location.
She assesses the ankle for a sprain, applies a compression bandage, and asks the casualty to try putting weight on it.
She splints the leg and assists the casualty in walking slowly to the nearest road.
She administers painkillers from the group first aid kit and monitors for an hour before deciding whether to call for help.
payload.explanation: In a remote setting, suspected lower-limb fracture requires immobilisation, warmth, and immediate emergency services — testing weight-bearing or assisted walking risks further injury.

payload.snippet: Tom is supervising a children's overnight camp when a child wakes up at 3am distressed and insisting they heard sounds outside the tent. Tom cannot identify the source.
options: He listens, checks around the tent perimeter with his torch without alarming the child, and stays with the child until they feel safe, while making sure other supervisors are aware.
He tells the child there is nothing to worry about and that they were dreaming.
He takes the child outside to show them nothing is there.
He wakes the whole group to do a head count in case someone is missing.
payload.explanation: Taking the child's concern seriously, checking calmly, and remaining with them is the correct response — dismissing or over-escalating both handle the situation poorly.

payload.snippet: Clara is a campsite manager who discovers one of her site's composting toilets has been blocked for twenty-four hours and campers have begun using the surrounding woodland as a toilet instead.
options: She arranges emergency chemical toilet delivery, clearly communicates the temporary alternative to all campers, and has the composting unit serviced as a priority.
She puts a note on the blocked toilet and monitors the situation for another day before arranging alternatives.
She asks campers to wait until the blocked toilet is fixed, expected by end of day.
She closes the section of the campsite where the toilet issue has occurred.
payload.explanation: A broken sanitation facility requires an immediate alternative, clear communication, and priority repair — asking campers to wait or closing the area without an alternative both fail duty of care.

payload.snippet: Oliver is leading a teenage camping expedition when his group reaches a river crossing that looks higher than expected due to recent rainfall. The crossing is on the planned route.
options: He stops the group, assesses the current depth and flow rate, and does not proceed if it is above knee height or fast-flowing — instead identifying an alternative route or wait option.
He crosses first to test the depth and signals if it is safe.
He asks the strongest swimmer in the group to assess the crossing.
He has the group cross holding hands since the route is scheduled and the group is expected.
payload.explanation: River crossings above knee height or with strong current are dangerous regardless of the planned route — individual testing or chain crossings do not make it safe.

payload.snippet: Anna is a bushcraft instructor when a student cuts their hand deeply on a knife during a whittling session. The bleeding is significant and does not stop after five minutes of direct pressure.
options: She maintains direct pressure, elevates the hand above heart level, calls emergency services, and keeps the student calm and still.
She applies a tourniquet above the wrist since the bleeding is severe.
She applies a butterfly closure dressing and drives the student to the nearest walk-in centre.
She applies a clean dressing and tells the student to press firmly while she assesses the rest of the group.
payload.explanation: Significant bleeding that does not stop with direct pressure and elevation requires emergency services — tourniquets on hands are contraindicated and self-driving is not appropriate.

payload.snippet: Jake is a camp manager when a parent calls demanding their child be allowed to leave the supervised multi-day camp early without the other parent's knowledge, citing a family dispute. The consent form was signed by both parents.
options: He declines to release the child based on one parent's verbal instruction, explains that both parents signed the consent form, and advises the requesting parent of the official process for changing the arrangement.
He releases the child to the requesting parent since they are a legal guardian.
He contacts the other parent to verify the request before making any decision.
He asks the child whether they want to go with the requesting parent.
payload.explanation: Releasing a child from a multi-consent arrangement based on one parent's verbal request risks the child's safety — the consent process must be followed.

payload.snippet: Maya is leading an adult hiking group in a forest when fog descends rapidly and the navigation app loses satellite signal. No member of the group has a physical map.
options: She stops the group, takes a compass bearing to confirm their last known direction, and follows a watercourse downhill if the bearing is unclear — avoiding movement without a reference.
She continues navigating from memory of the route map she reviewed before setting out.
She asks the group to spread out slightly to find a landmark.
She calls mountain rescue immediately since the group has no map and no signal.
payload.explanation: Stopping, taking a compass bearing, and using natural navigation features are the correct responses to sudden low-visibility fog with no digital navigation — spreading out increases risk of separation.

payload.snippet: Tom is at a forest campsite when a neighbouring camper shows signs of severe heat exhaustion — pale and clammy skin, rapid weak pulse, and confusion — after a long day in direct sun.
options: He calls 999 immediately, moves the casualty to shade, removes excess clothing, fans them and applies cool wet cloths, and gives them water to sip if they are conscious and able to swallow.
He gives the casualty a sports drink, fans them, and monitors for twenty minutes before calling 999.
He tells the campsite warden and waits for their guidance.
He moves the casualty to a cool stream nearby and has them sit in the water.
payload.explanation: Confusion combined with rapid weak pulse indicates severe heat exhaustion approaching heatstroke — 999 call, shade, cooling, and hydration if conscious are all correct immediate responses.

payload.snippet: Clara is an expedition leader whose group has a participant who has run out of their prescription medication on day three of a seven-day remote trip.
options: She contacts the participant's GP and the expedition's emergency support line to establish whether safe continuation without the medication is possible, and arranges emergency resupply or evacuation as advised.
She tells the participant to ration the remaining doses over the remaining days.
She asks other participants if any have a similar medication they can share.
She continues the expedition and asks the participant to monitor their symptoms.
payload.explanation: Running out of prescription medication in a remote setting requires medical advice before any decision — rationing, sharing, or symptom monitoring without guidance are all potentially dangerous.

payload.snippet: Oliver is a campsite warden who discovers that a group of campers has dug a fire pit in an area the site rules prohibit due to underground cables.
options: He approaches the group calmly, explains the underground cable risk, asks them to extinguish the fire, fills the pit under his supervision, and ensures the group is re-sited in a designated fire area.
He puts the fire out himself without speaking to the group and fills the pit.
He notes it in the incident log and monitors whether they repeat the behaviour.
He issues a verbal warning and allows the group to keep the fire going in the pit they have dug since it is already started.
payload.explanation: An illegal fire pit over underground cables is a serious hazard requiring immediate extinguishment, pit filling, and relocation — documentation without action or allowing it to continue are both wrong.

payload.snippet: Anna is a first aid trained camp counsellor when a child complains of severe abdominal pain, nausea, and a slight fever after a meal.
options: She removes the child from activity, contacts the camp medical lead, and does not administer any medication pending medical assessment.
She gives the child an antacid and tells them to lie down until it passes.
She monitors the child for an hour and contacts the parents if no improvement.
She asks the child what they ate and checks the other campers from the same meal for similar symptoms.
payload.explanation: Severe abdominal pain, nausea, and fever in a child requires medical assessment — self-treatment, monitoring only, or group symptom checks do not substitute for prompt clinical evaluation.

payload.snippet: Jake is leading a kayaking session at a lake when the wind picks up sharply and several kayakers are struggling to paddle back to shore and beginning to drift.
options: He calls all kayakers to raft up immediately, tows the struggling kayakers together, and uses a safety line to bring the group back to shore in a controlled manner.
He tells the stronger paddlers to return to shore first and send help back.
He shouts paddling instructions from the bank to the drifting kayakers.
He enters the water himself to push each kayak back individually.
payload.explanation: Rafting up and controlled towing keeps the group together and manages the risk — splitting the group or instructing from shore both leave struggling kayakers at greater risk.

payload.snippet: Clara is a solo camper who wakes at 3am to find her tent has been moved during the night — possibly by strong winds — and she is now very close to a cliff edge she cannot see clearly in the dark.
options: She stays still, uses her torch to assess the hazard slowly from within the tent, and does not move the tent until she has a clear picture of the ground ahead in daylight or with good light.
She immediately moves the tent away from where she estimates the edge to be.
She gets out of the tent and walks further into the field to assess her position.
She calls mountain rescue since she cannot be sure of her exact location.
payload.explanation: In low visibility near a cliff edge, staying still and assessing with a torch before any movement is the correct response — moving in the dark risks the edge.

payload.snippet: Oliver is on a group camping trip when a participant reveals they have been feeling ill for two days and suspect they ate something contaminated before the trip. They have been using the shared camp kitchen throughout.
options: He immediately restricts the ill participant from shared food preparation, cleans all shared utensils and surfaces, and monitors whether other participants develop similar symptoms.
He asks the participant to prepare only their own meals going forward.
He checks whether the participant has a temperature and decides based on how ill they seem.
He tells the group about the possible contamination and lets everyone decide for themselves.
payload.explanation: A possible foodborne illness with shared kitchen exposure requires restricted food-handling, full surface cleaning, and symptom monitoring — partial restriction or individual decision-making are not adequate.

payload.snippet: Anna is leading a youth group camping trip when she discovers that two participants have been secretly communicating with an unknown adult online from the campsite's wifi and have arranged to meet them the following morning.
options: She confiscates the devices, cancels the meeting, informs the group's safeguarding lead, and contacts the participants' parents that evening.
She speaks to the participants about the danger without contacting parents, since they came forward voluntarily.
She contacts the participants' parents but proceeds with the next day's activity once the meeting is cancelled.
She monitors the situation and decides whether to act based on what the unknown adult says if they arrive.
payload.explanation: A planned meeting with an unknown adult arranged online by young people is a safeguarding concern requiring immediate device removal, meeting cancellation, safeguarding lead notification, and parental contact.

payload.snippet: Jake is on a coastal camping trip when he notices the tide has come in significantly further than expected, cutting off the route back to the main beach path. Several members of his group are near the waterline.
options: He calls all group members to high ground immediately and contacts the coastguard to report their position and request guidance.
He assesses the depth of the water and attempts to wade back if it appears shallow.
He waits for the tide to retreat before moving the group.
He looks for an alternative coastal path along the cliff top without contacting the coastguard first.
payload.explanation: An unexpected coastal cut-off requires immediate high ground and coastguard contact — wading, waiting without contact, or independent route-finding all risk the group's safety.

payload.snippet: Maya is a camping group leader when one participant admits they have a prescription medication that needs to be kept refrigerated, which they did not mention before the trip. There is no refrigeration available.
options: She contacts the participant's doctor or a pharmacist to understand the impact of non-refrigeration over the trip duration, and arranges evacuation or resupply if the medication cannot be safely kept without refrigeration.
She puts the medication in the coolest part of the campsite and monitors the participant's health.
She asks the participant to take a higher dose while the medication is less effective to compensate.
She tells the participant the trip was planned without refrigeration and the decision to stay is theirs.
payload.explanation: Prescription medication requiring refrigeration is a medical management issue — placing in a cool spot without clinical advice or leaving the decision to the participant are both inadequate.

payload.snippet: Tom discovers mid-trip that a campsite they are using is on privately owned land and they do not have the landowner's permission. A 'No Camping' sign is partially hidden by overgrowth.
options: He informs the group, packs up immediately, and either contacts the landowner to apologise and seek permission, or relocates to a permitted campsite.
He checks whether the landowner is nearby before deciding whether to move.
He stays for the night since the sign was not visible when they arrived.
He moves on early the following morning before the landowner is likely to be up.
payload.explanation: Camping on private land without permission requires either seeking immediate permission or relocating — hidden signs or early departure do not make trespass acceptable.

payload.snippet: Clara is a first-time solo camper who wakes to find a large dog standing over her sleeping bag growling. The dog is loose and its owner is nowhere nearby.
options: She stays completely still, avoids direct eye contact, and speaks in a calm, low voice until the dog backs away, then slowly moves to put a barrier between herself and the dog.
She shouts loudly to scare the dog away.
She pushes the dog away firmly.
She throws food from her pack to distract the dog.
payload.explanation: With an aggressive dog, stillness, avoidance of eye contact, and calm voice are the correct de-escalation responses — shouting, pushing, or food-throwing can increase aggression.

payload.snippet: Oliver is the adult in charge of a teenagers' camping trip when a thunderstorm rolls in during a hike, well away from the campsite, and the group has no immediate shelter.
options: He moves the group away from isolated trees and high ground, has everyone crouch low in a spread pattern at least ten metres apart, and does not shelter under trees or use metal poles.
He leads the group quickly back to the campsite under the trees to shelter from the rain.
He pitches a tarp between two trees to provide cover for the group.
He asks everyone to huddle together under a tarp to share warmth and wait out the storm.
payload.explanation: Lightning safety in open terrain requires spreading out, low crouching away from trees and high points — sheltering under trees or grouping together both increase lightning risk.

payload.snippet: Clara is organising her room when she finds a large stash of unhealthy snacks she had been hiding from her parents, accumulated over several months.
options: She disposes of most of them and tells her parent honestly about the habit.
She eats the rest quickly before her parent finds out.
She hides them in a better location.
She tells her parent the snacks were always there and she did not buy them.
payload.explanation: Honesty about a hidden habit — even one driven by embarrassment — allows the underlying issue to be addressed.

payload.snippet: Oliver finds during a room clean that a significant amount of pocket money has been disappearing into impulsive small purchases he cannot account for.
options: He tells his parent honestly and asks for help creating a spending plan.
He tells his parent his money was lost or stolen.
He asks for more pocket money to make up the shortfall.
He hides the evidence and resolves to be more careful going forward.
payload.explanation: Acknowledging a spending habit problem and seeking help is more productive than concealing it.

payload.snippet: Anna is clearing her room when she discovers she has received money from relatives for several birthdays that was tucked away and never banked or acknowledged.
options: She tells her parent and writes thank-you messages to the relevant relatives, even if the occasion was months ago.
She keeps the money without telling anyone.
She puts it in her savings without mentioning the thank-you delay.
She tells only the relatives who might notice she has not acknowledged it.
payload.explanation: Late thank-you messages are still better than none — and discovered money should be disclosed to a parent.

payload.snippet: Jake is doing a deep clean when he finds items that belong to a friend who visited months ago and since moved to a different city.
options: He contacts the friend, describes the items, and arranges to post them if the friend wants them back.
He keeps the items since the friend probably does not remember them.
He throws them away since returning them would cost more than they are worth.
He gives them to a local charity shop.
payload.explanation: Making a reasonable effort to return items belonging to others — even when inconvenient — is the honest approach.

payload.snippet: Maya is doing a major room overhaul when she finds several pieces of her sibling's clothing that ended up in her wardrobe. Her sibling has been looking for them.
options: She immediately returns all of them and apologises for not noticing sooner.
She keeps the ones that fit her.
She puts them back without mentioning she found them.
She blames the washing process for mixing up the clothes.
payload.explanation: Returning a sibling's clothing promptly and apologising is both honest and fair.

payload.snippet: Tom finds a collection of screenshots he had saved of an argument between classmates that he had used to gossip with friends months ago. He regrets his role in spreading it.
options: He deletes the screenshots and reflects on the impact of sharing private information.
He keeps the screenshots in case they are useful later.
He shares them with one more person since they are already old.
He deletes them but tells no one since it is in the past.
payload.explanation: Deleting harmful screenshots and reflecting on the behaviour is the responsible step — even after the fact.

payload.snippet: Clara is helping a parent with a whole-house clean when she finds items in her room she did not realise were expensive, including some that look like antiques.
options: She shows the items to her parent and lets them decide on their value and fate.
She sells them online since she found them in her own room.
She hides the most interesting ones for herself.
She throws them away since they look old and unused.
payload.explanation: Items of potential value found in your room must be shown to a parent — they may belong to the family or have sentimental significance.

payload.snippet: Oliver does a full room tidy and finds a signed permission slip for a school trip that was never submitted. The trip is next week.
options: He gives it to his parent immediately and contacts the school to ask if late submission is possible.
He signs it himself and submits it the next day.
He does not submit it and tells his teacher he did not receive permission.
He waits to see if the school chases it.
payload.explanation: A late permission slip must be shown to a parent immediately — self-signing is forgery and missing the trip silently is avoidable.

payload.snippet: Anna discovers during a room clean that she has been hoarding packaging, paper, and containers for a craft project she has never started. The volume has become unreasonable.
options: She honestly assesses which items she will realistically use soon, recycles the rest, and sets a date for the project.
She keeps everything since she will definitely use it.
She throws all of it away since it was never used.
She moves it all into the garage without asking.
payload.explanation: A realistic self-assessment of hoarding intentions — and setting a concrete project date — is more honest and practical than keeping everything or discarding all.

payload.snippet: Jake finds paperwork in his room showing that he owes money to a school tuck shop account that went into deficit without him realising.
options: He shows his parent the paperwork and asks for help settling the debt.
He hides the paperwork and hopes the school forgets about it.
He settles it himself from his own pocket money without telling his parent.
He tells the school the paperwork is an error.
payload.explanation: Involving a parent when money is owed to a school account is the correct and transparent response.

payload.snippet: Maya is doing a deep room clean and her parent discovers items belonging to other children in the class that Maya had taken without asking.
options: She is honest about having taken them, returns all the items, and apologises to the children.
She claims she was looking after them for the other children.
She returns them secretly without the children knowing.
She throws them away to destroy the evidence.
payload.explanation: Honest admission, return, and apology are all required when belongings have been taken without permission.

payload.snippet: Tom finds a bag of plastic packaging he had meant to recycle for months. It has been growing behind his door.
options: He sorts it and takes it to the correct recycling facility or collection point.
He puts it all in the general bin since it has been there too long.
He continues putting off recycling it indefinitely.
He hides it in a drawer since dealing with it is too much effort.
payload.explanation: Following through on recycling intentions — even late — is better than sending recyclables to landfill.

payload.snippet: Maya finds a piece of jewellery in her room that she knows belongs to her parent but is worth a significant amount. She is not sure how it got there.
options: She returns it immediately and tells her parent where she found it.
She keeps it in a safe place but does not tell her parent in case they think she took it.
She puts it back in her parent's room without mentioning it.
She sells it online since she needs money.
payload.explanation: Returning valuable belongings immediately and explaining where they were found is the honest and safe response.

payload.snippet: Tom does a full room clean and realises that the dust and mess have been aggravating his asthma. He did not know this was a possible trigger.
options: He tells a parent and they arrange a deep clean together, then discuss a more regular cleaning schedule.
He takes his inhaler before cleaning and does not mention the trigger.
He cleans his room himself and measures whether his asthma improves.
He asks a doctor to prescribe stronger medication to manage the increased symptoms.
payload.explanation: Telling a parent about a health trigger and addressing it at the source is more effective than managing the symptom alone.

payload.snippet: Clara is cleaning her room when she finds evidence that a sibling has been going through her private belongings without permission.
options: She speaks to her parent about what she found and asks for help setting clearer privacy boundaries.
She goes through her sibling's belongings in retaliation.
She confronts her sibling loudly in front of the family.
She moves her belongings to a locked box without telling anyone why.
payload.explanation: Involving a parent and setting clear privacy expectations addresses the problem — retaliation or silent workarounds do not.

payload.snippet: Oliver discovers during a room tidy that his room has an unpleasant musty smell. After investigation he believes the smell is coming from inside the wall.
options: He tells his parent so they can check for a possible damp or mould problem inside the wall.
He buys a large plug-in air freshener to mask the smell.
He moves furniture away from the wall and monitors the situation.
He pours water around the skirting board to see if it gets worse.
payload.explanation: A smell from inside a wall may indicate damp or mould and requires an adult to investigate properly.

payload.snippet: Anna is clearing her room and finds that a significant amount of her belongings have migrated into shared family spaces over many months.
options: She retrieves her belongings and returns them to her room, and sets a habit of keeping her things out of shared spaces going forward.
She leaves them in the shared spaces since they are not in anyone's way.
She asks a sibling to move them since they were there first.
She puts the shared-space items in a bag and donates them.
payload.explanation: Retrieving your own belongings from shared spaces and preventing future drift is both responsible and considerate.

payload.snippet: Jake is doing a full room clean when he finds a sealed letter addressed to him that was never opened from over a year ago.
options: He opens it and acts on its contents if action is still needed.
He throws it away unopened since it is too old to matter.
He opens it but, since it is a year old, decides nothing in it can still be relevant.
He shows it to a parent before opening since he is not sure what to do.
payload.explanation: Opening an unread letter regardless of age is the correct step — it may still contain important or sentimental content.

payload.snippet: Maya's room has become a holding area for items belonging to other family members. She has been asked to clean but the items are not hers to move.
options: She tells a parent and asks for help deciding where those items should go before she begins her own tidying.
She moves everything into the hallway without asking.
She puts everything in a box labelled 'not mine' without telling anyone.
She tidies around the items as if they are furniture.
payload.explanation: Getting adult guidance before moving other people's belongings avoids conflict and ensures the items end up in the right place.

payload.snippet: Tom is cleaning his room when he finds an old friend's phone number on a piece of paper. The friend moved away two years ago and they lost touch.
options: He considers whether to reach out — and if so, does so through a parent if the friend is young.
He calls the number immediately.
He throws it away since two years is too long to reconnect.
He gives the number to mutual friends to pass on.
payload.explanation: Deciding whether to reconnect thoughtfully — and doing so appropriately for the age — is the mature response to a found contact.

payload.snippet: Clara is a student who discovers that several classmates have access to the answer key for a homework task, leaked by a previous student. She is under significant academic pressure.
options: She does not use the answer key, completes the homework from her own understanding, and considers whether to tell a teacher about the leak.
She uses the answer key since everyone else is using it.
She uses it for the questions she is unsure of only.
She tells a friend but decides it is not her responsibility to report it.
payload.explanation: Using a leaked answer key is academic dishonesty regardless of how many others use it — reporting the leak addresses the systemic issue.

payload.snippet: Oliver is a student under significant exam pressure when a parent insists on sitting with him every evening to supervise homework, which is actually making his anxiety worse.
options: He tells his parent honestly how the supervision is affecting him and asks if they can agree on a different arrangement — such as checking in after he finishes.
He says nothing and continues with the supervision to avoid conflict.
He tells his parent the homework is already done so they leave him alone.
He locks himself in his room to avoid the supervision.
payload.explanation: An honest conversation about the impact of well-intentioned oversight — and proposing an alternative — is healthier than avoidance or deception.

payload.snippet: Anna receives an academic integrity warning from her school for a homework task that she submitted, which closely matched another student's work. She did not copy — both students independently reached similar answers.
options: She provides evidence of her own working process and independent sources to the teacher, calmly and clearly.
She accuses her classmate of copying her work.
She accepts the warning quietly to avoid further attention.
She argues that coincidental similarity is the teacher's problem to prove.
payload.explanation: Providing documented evidence of independent work is the correct response to an academic integrity concern you know is unwarranted.

payload.snippet: Jake is struggling with a subject and finds a homework help website that does not write the work for students but explains concepts clearly. His teacher has not mentioned it.
options: He uses the site to understand the concept and then completes the homework in his own words.
He uses the site's worked examples and submits them directly.
He avoids using any online resource in case it counts as cheating.
He asks his teacher whether the site is permitted before using it.
payload.explanation: Understanding via online resources and then writing your own response is legitimate academic use — submitting their examples is not. Asking a teacher is a sensible option if unsure.

payload.snippet: Maya is given a major homework project worth a significant portion of her grade. She is going through a difficult personal period and is genuinely struggling to function.
options: She speaks to her form tutor or a school counsellor about what she is going through and asks about possible accommodations or an extension.
She submits whatever she can manage without telling anyone about her situation.
She copies a significant portion from online to meet the minimum requirements.
She waits until the day before to ask for an extension, making it harder for the school to help.
payload.explanation: Disclosing a personal difficulty early — and asking for academic accommodations through proper channels — enables appropriate support.

payload.snippet: Tom is completing homework and realises the question has a genuine ambiguity — two interpretations are both defensible.
options: He picks the interpretation he finds more interesting, makes his reasoning explicit in the answer, and notes the alternative interpretation.
He guesses which interpretation the teacher wants and answers that way.
He answers both interpretations in full to cover himself.
He emails the teacher to ask what the question means before starting.
payload.explanation: Choosing an interpretation, being transparent about the choice, and acknowledging the alternative demonstrates strong critical thinking.

payload.snippet: Clara finds that one of her teachers consistently sets homework that exceeds the recommended time limit for her year group, causing significant stress.
options: She notes the time she spends on each task over two weeks as evidence, then raises it with her form tutor or parent as a factual concern.
She completes only the portion of the homework that fits the time limit.
She tells her classmates to complain about the workload.
She asks the teacher directly in front of the class whether the workload is appropriate.
payload.explanation: Documenting the issue with evidence and raising it through the proper pastoral channel is the correct way to address a systemic workload concern.

payload.snippet: Oliver is a student who realises he has been doing well on homework but failing tests on the same topics, suggesting he is getting help at home rather than learning independently.
options: He tells his parent he needs to do homework independently — even if harder — so that his test performance and homework better reflect his actual knowledge.
He continues with parental help since homework marks benefit his overall grade.
He pretends to do homework independently while accepting help quietly.
He asks his teacher to weight tests more heavily than homework.
payload.explanation: Recognising that helped homework masks a knowledge gap — and choosing to learn independently — is an act of academic integrity.

payload.snippet: Anna is doing a homework assignment that requires her to take a position on a controversial ethical topic. She genuinely finds the topic very uncomfortable.
options: She chooses a position she can support with reasoning and evidence, notes that she finds the topic complex, and submits her best attempt.
She refuses to complete the assignment due to personal discomfort.
She asks the teacher to assign her a different question.
She writes a neutral 'both sides' answer to avoid committing to a position.
payload.explanation: Engaging seriously with uncomfortable academic material — choosing a supported position while noting its complexity — is stronger than avoidance or a neutral non-answer.

payload.snippet: Jake discovers that a classmate has been submitting AI-generated homework as their own work and has told Jake in confidence, swearing him to secrecy.
options: He tells the classmate that he cannot make that promise and that academic integrity is important, without immediately reporting them — giving the classmate the chance to stop.
He keeps the secret since the classmate trusted him.
He immediately tells the teacher since the confession was clearly a disclosure.
He starts using AI himself since it is unfair that his classmate benefits.
payload.explanation: Declining to make a secrecy promise and giving the classmate a chance to stop is a fair first response — immediate reporting and silent complicity are both premature.

payload.snippet: Maya is completing a take-home essay when she notices she has accidentally included a paragraph that she copied verbatim from her notes as a placeholder. She is about to submit.
options: She catches it, replaces the verbatim paragraph with her own writing, and checks the rest of the essay for similar errors before submitting.
She submits with the copied paragraph since it was unintentional.
She removes the paragraph entirely and leaves the section blank.
She changes a few words in the copied paragraph to make it look original.
payload.explanation: Finding and properly fixing a verbatim note-copied paragraph before submission is the honest and correct response — unintentional copying is still plagiarism if submitted.

payload.snippet: Tom is given a homework assignment that he later discovers was not actually set by his teacher but was a prank by a classmate who faked the homework sheet.
options: He verifies with the teacher before completing it, and tells the teacher what happened without immediately naming the classmate.
He completes the fake homework anyway since the work will not hurt him.
He tells everyone in the class the homework is a prank.
He immediately names the classmate who he suspects did it.
payload.explanation: Verifying homework with the teacher before completing it, and reporting the prank without pre-emptively naming someone, are both correct steps.

payload.snippet: Maya is given a homework task that she believes is genuinely beyond her current ability despite revising the material. She is worried about asking for help.
options: She attempts the homework and submits what she has, then emails the teacher honestly to say she found the material very challenging and asks for additional support.
She submits a minimal attempt and says nothing.
She asks a friend to explain their answers and then copies the approach.
She waits until the next lesson to tell the teacher, by which point the deadline has passed.
payload.explanation: Honest disclosure of genuine difficulty — before the deadline — allows the teacher to provide timely support.

payload.snippet: Tom discovers that his school's homework submission platform records metadata showing he submitted his homework at 11:58pm, when he had claimed it was done at 5pm in class.
options: He does not try to explain the metadata discrepancy dishonestly — if asked, he tells the teacher he finished it later than he said.
He claims the platform timestamp is wrong.
He says he accidentally resubmitted a draft version at midnight.
He pre-emptively tells the teacher the platform timestamps are unreliable.
payload.explanation: Metadata from submission platforms is a factual record — attempting to explain it dishonestly compounds a minor issue into an integrity problem.

payload.snippet: Clara is completing assessed coursework at home when a friend texts offering to send their version for Clara to 'check her work against'.
options: She declines, explaining that sharing assessed work between students would compromise both of their academic integrity.
She accepts and looks only at the structure, not the answers.
She accepts since her friend offered willingly.
She accepts but tells the friend she will not actually use any of it.
payload.explanation: Receiving another student's assessed work — even to check structure — creates a risk of unintentional copying and should be declined.

payload.snippet: Oliver is completing homework that involves analysing a real news event. He realises his analysis leads him to a politically controversial conclusion he is not sure he should write.
options: He writes the analysis honestly based on the evidence and reasoning, clearly labelling it as his own interpretation.
He changes his conclusion to a more neutral position to avoid controversy.
He writes the controversial conclusion without flagging it as his interpretation.
He avoids the topic and analyses a different event.
payload.explanation: Academic analysis requires honest reasoning — sanitising a conclusion or avoiding an uncomfortable topic both undermine intellectual integrity.

payload.snippet: Anna is given assessed homework and her parent works professionally in the exact subject area. Her parent offers very detailed and specific help.
options: She accepts general encouragement and subject area direction but ensures all specific content and wording is her own.
She accepts the detailed help since the expertise is genuine and available.
She asks her parent to write a draft that she then edits.
She refuses all help to be certain of full independence.
payload.explanation: Parental subject expertise can inform direction without doing the work — the line is where specific content and wording come from someone other than the student.

payload.snippet: Jake is completing homework for multiple subjects and prioritises one he finds easier, leaving the harder one until too late.
options: He reflects on the pattern, finishes what he can, and plans to start with the hardest subject first in future.
He submits only the easier homework and hopes the other teacher forgets.
He asks for extensions on both homework tasks.
He blames the amount of work set rather than his prioritisation.
payload.explanation: Recognising a prioritisation error and planning to reverse the order in future is honest self-improvement.

payload.snippet: Maya's school has a homework policy that limits total weekly homework to a set number of hours. She is regularly given significantly more than the policy allows.
options: She tracks her homework time accurately, shows the evidence to her form tutor, and asks for the policy to be enforced.
She does only the policy amount and tells each teacher she has reached the limit.
She says nothing since the workload is the same for everyone.
She complains on social media about the school's homework load.
payload.explanation: Documenting the issue with evidence and raising it through pastoral channels is the correct approach to a policy breach.

payload.snippet: Tom is given a homework task that requires him to discuss a topic from multiple perspectives. He personally finds one perspective deeply offensive.
options: He completes the task by representing all required perspectives fairly and academically, noting in his response that one perspective conflicts with his personal values.
He omits the perspective he finds offensive.
He includes the perspective but uses dismissive language toward it.
He tells the teacher he cannot complete the task in good conscience.
payload.explanation: Academic tasks require fair representation of required perspectives — noting personal values alongside the academic analysis is honest without compromising the task.

payload.snippet: Tom is new to a school where social groups are very established and exclusionary. Despite genuine effort, he has not made friends after several months.
options: He speaks honestly to a school counsellor about the situation and asks for support with strategies and, if needed, adult facilitation.
He concludes the school is too unfriendly and asks to transfer.
He tries to manufacture social conflict to disrupt the existing groups and find entry.
He accepts the isolation and focuses entirely on academic performance.
payload.explanation: A school counsellor can provide both strategies and facilitation — persistent exclusion after genuine effort warrants adult support.

payload.snippet: Clara's new friendship is with someone who clearly has significant emotional needs and relies heavily on Clara for emotional support beyond what feels sustainable.
options: She tells her friend she cares about them but cannot be their only source of support, and gently encourages them to also seek adult support.
She gradually fades from the friendship to avoid the difficult conversation.
She cuts off the friendship to protect her own wellbeing without any explanation.
She accepts the role as primary support and manages the strain alone.
payload.explanation: Honest, compassionate communication about your own limits — and encouraging professional support — is healthier than fading away or burning out.

payload.snippet: Oliver meets a new friend at a youth group who asks him to keep their location private from their parents, claiming their parents are controlling.
options: He tells a trusted adult in his own life about the request without necessarily revealing the friend's identity, and seeks guidance.
He keeps the secret since the friend's home life sounds genuinely difficult.
He tells the friend he cannot keep that kind of secret and encourages them to speak to a trusted adult themselves.
He contacts the friend's parents directly to tell them where their child is.
payload.explanation: A request to hide location from parents is a safeguarding concern — seeking guidance from your own trusted adult, while encouraging the friend to speak to one too, is the correct balanced response.

payload.snippet: Anna has been close friends with a new person for three months when she discovers the person has been lying about fundamental aspects of their background.
options: She asks her friend directly about what she has discovered, gives them the opportunity to explain, and then decides how to proceed based on their honesty.
She ends the friendship immediately since the lies mean nothing can be trusted.
She pretends she has not found out and continues as before.
She tells everyone they know about the dishonesty before speaking to the friend.
payload.explanation: Giving a friend the opportunity to explain and be honest — before making a decision — respects their agency and may provide important context.

payload.snippet: Jake's new friend group has a clear leader whose approval everyone seeks, including Jake. Jake notices the leader sometimes manipulates group dynamics.
options: He decides to invest in one-on-one friendships within the group rather than competing for the leader's approval.
He befriends the leader most intensively to secure his position in the group.
He publicly challenges the leader's influence to redistribute social power.
He withdraws from the group entirely since the dynamic is unhealthy.
payload.explanation: Investing in genuine individual friendships within a group is more sustainable than competing for a single person's approval.

payload.snippet: Maya is forming a new friendship when the friend begins testing her loyalty by asking her to exclude another classmate.
options: She tells her friend she is not comfortable excluding others as a loyalty test and that her friendships do not work that way.
She complies once to show loyalty and then tries to steer the friendship differently.
She chooses the classmate being excluded over the new friendship.
She avoids both people to stay out of the conflict.
payload.explanation: Setting a clear boundary about exclusion-as-loyalty-test early is more honest and sustainable than compliance or triangulation.

payload.snippet: Tom discovers that the new friend he has been spending a lot of time with has been involved in shoplifting and is pressuring Tom to join in.
options: He firmly declines and tells his friend he will not be part of it, and distances himself from the friendship if the pressure continues.
He agrees once to avoid social rejection and resolves to never do it again.
He reports his friend to the police immediately.
He says nothing and hopes the friend will stop on their own.
payload.explanation: A firm clear refusal — and distancing if the pressure continues — is the correct response to peer pressure toward illegal activity.

payload.snippet: Clara's new best friend is going through a difficult time and has become increasingly unpredictable and sometimes unkind toward Clara.
options: She acknowledges her friend is struggling, maintains her own boundaries about how she can be treated, and checks in with a trusted adult about how to support a distressed friend without absorbing the impact.
She puts up with the unkindness since her friend needs her.
She ends the friendship since she cannot cope with the unpredictability.
She tells all their mutual friends how her friend has been behaving.
payload.explanation: Maintaining your own boundaries while seeking adult guidance on supporting a struggling friend protects both people.

payload.snippet: Oliver moves to a new city and starts at a new school where he is immediately targeted by a clique who spread a false rumour about him before he even speaks to most people.
options: He focuses on building genuine one-on-one connections with people before the rumour's narrative takes hold, and speaks to a trusted adult if it escalates.
He confronts the clique leaders directly and publicly to disprove the rumour.
He starts counter-rumours about the clique members.
He avoids everyone until the rumour dies down naturally.
payload.explanation: One-on-one trust-building is more effective than public confrontation or avoidance when a new environment is hostile.

payload.snippet: Anna is forming a friendship with someone from a very different socioeconomic background, and financial differences are creating awkwardness around shared activities.
options: She suggests activities that work for both their budgets without drawing attention to the difference.
She always pays for both of them without discussing it.
She asks her friend directly why they cannot afford more expensive activities.
She stops suggesting plans since it is too complicated.
payload.explanation: Suggesting budget-accessible activities without spotlighting the difference respects both friends' dignity.

payload.snippet: Jake discovers that a new friendship he values was partly formed on false pretences — he had exaggerated aspects of his life to seem more impressive.
options: He gradually and naturally corrects the false impressions over time and moves the friendship toward a more honest foundation.
He maintains the false impression since the friendship would fall apart if the truth emerged.
He confesses everything at once to clear his conscience.
He ends the friendship to avoid being found out.
payload.explanation: Gradually correcting false impressions and building on genuine ground is more sustainable than maintaining pretence or dramatic confession.

payload.snippet: Maya is befriending a new classmate when she realises her other friends are pressuring her to drop the new friendship because they do not like the person.
options: She tells her existing friends she values their opinions but will make her own friendship decisions.
She drops the new friendship to maintain group harmony.
She hides the new friendship from her existing friends.
She confronts her existing friends publicly about their control.
payload.explanation: Asserting your right to form your own friendships — calmly and directly — is a fundamental social boundary.

payload.snippet: Tobias transfers mid-term to a new school where the class already has settled friendship groups. At break, he sits on a bench reading; a girl named Freya glances at his book and recognises the cover.
options: Freya asks Tobias about the book and they discover they both love the series
Freya decides not to interrupt his reading
Tobias ignores Freya when she approaches
They stare at each other awkwardly and walk away
payload.explanation: A shared interest is a natural opening for starting a new friendship.

payload.snippet: Amara and her family have just moved from a different country. At school she speaks quietly because she worries her accent will make others laugh, but her desk partner Lena keeps smiling at her answers in class.
options: Lena tells Amara her answers are brilliant and asks where she learned so much
Lena mimics Amara's accent playfully
Lena asks the teacher to move seats
Lena never speaks to Amara so she does not feel pressured
payload.explanation: Genuine compliments across cultural differences break down self-consciousness and invite connection.

payload.snippet: Marcus joins a football team mid-season when the other players already know each other well. In the first practice he misses an easy shot; some boys groan, but the team captain Eli jogs over.
options: Eli claps Marcus on the back and says everyone has off moments
Eli tells the coach Marcus should sit on the bench
Eli ignores Marcus and resets the drill
Marcus storms off the pitch feeling humiliated
payload.explanation: Encouragement from a leader reassures a new member that mistakes are part of learning.

payload.snippet: Nia is new to a coding club and watches everyone type quickly; she feels too slow and considers quitting, but the girl beside her, Zara, notices and slides her laptop closer so Nia can see the steps.
options: Nia thanks Zara and follows along, gaining confidence step by step
Nia closes her laptop and tells the teacher she is sick
Zara turns her screen away to protect her own work
Nia copies Zara's full code without understanding it
payload.explanation: A small act of inclusion can stop someone from giving up something they enjoy.

payload.snippet: Dev and his new friend Callum disagree about which board game to play; Dev wants chess because he is good at it, but Callum suggests a new game neither of them knows.
options: They agree to try the new game so neither has an unfair advantage
Dev insists on chess since it was his idea to play
Callum walks home because Dev will not compromise
They play both games but Dev deliberately lets Callum lose chess
payload.explanation: Trying something new together levels the playing field and makes friendship fairer.

payload.snippet: Sofia's class does a pair project; she is paired with a new girl, Hana, who is very quiet. Sofia talks fast and keeps taking over; she notices Hana has stopped writing.
options: Sofia pauses and asks Hana what ideas she has
Sofia finishes the project on her own so it gets done faster
Sofia tells the teacher Hana is not contributing
Sofia slows down only when the teacher walks over
payload.explanation: Pausing to invite a quieter partner's input strengthens both the friendship and the project.

payload.snippet: Jonah notices a new boy, Eli, eating alone every day for a week. Jonah's friends say it would be awkward to invite him over, but Jonah feels bad every time he passes Eli's table.
options: Jonah invites Eli to sit with his group
Jonah keeps walking because his friends told him not to
Jonah asks a teacher to move Eli's seat
Jonah leaves a note on Eli's tray without speaking to him
payload.explanation: Acting on empathy despite peer pressure can change someone's school experience completely.

payload.snippet: Rosa and Mia have been friends for only two weeks when Mia says something that accidentally hurts Rosa's feelings about her drawing. Rosa goes quiet.
options: Mia realises what she said and apologises sincerely
Mia says Rosa is being too sensitive
Rosa pretends nothing happened so their new friendship is not ruined
Mia changes the subject and never mentions it again
payload.explanation: Addressing a hurtful comment quickly, even in a new friendship, builds honesty and trust.

payload.snippet: Tom is travelling abroad when his passport, wallet, and phone are all stolen. He has no money, no ID, and no way to contact home.
options: He contacts the nearest British embassy or consulate for emergency consular assistance, and asks a fellow traveller or hotel to allow him to make a call home.
He waits at the place of the theft hoping the thief returns what he took.
He tries to borrow money from a stranger and find his own way home.
He contacts his travel insurance company first since they pay for emergencies.
payload.explanation: The British embassy or consulate is the first contact for a UK citizen abroad with no ID or money — they can arrange emergency travel documents and contact family.

payload.snippet: Clara discovers mid-way through a long-haul flight that her travel documents for the destination country are not in her bag.
options: She informs the cabin crew immediately and asks them to contact the destination airport's immigration team about the situation.
She hopes the documentation issue will be overlooked on arrival.
She waits until landing and explains to immigration on arrival.
She looks through all her carry-on bags thoroughly before telling anyone.
payload.explanation: Informing cabin crew immediately — so the destination can be notified before landing — gives the most options for resolving a documentation issue.

payload.snippet: Oliver is the guardian of a child on a day trip when the child goes missing in a crowded public venue.
options: He immediately alerts the venue's security team, stays at a fixed location so the child can find him, and contacts the police if the child is not located within a few minutes.
He searches the venue himself before involving security.
He contacts the child's parents first before alerting security.
He retraces the route they walked together.
payload.explanation: Alerting venue security immediately is the critical first action — they have communication systems and staff coverage a single searcher does not. The police must also be contacted quickly if the child is not found.

payload.snippet: Anna finds a bag in a bus station that is unattended and has been there for over thirty minutes.
options: She does not touch the bag and alerts the station staff immediately.
She checks inside the bag for identifying information.
She moves the bag to a more visible location so the owner can find it.
She continues with her journey and tells no one.
payload.explanation: An unattended bag in a public transport hub must be reported to staff immediately — it must not be touched or moved.

payload.snippet: Jake discovers that a valuable item has gone missing from his home and the only people who have been in the property recently are family members.
options: He checks carefully before making any accusation, including all storage spaces and whether he himself may have misplaced it.
He confronts the family member he most suspects directly and immediately.
He secretly checks the belongings of the person he suspects.
He reports it to the police as a theft before speaking to the family.
payload.explanation: A thorough self-check before any accusation is essential — false accusations of theft within a family cause serious damage and many 'thefts' turn out to be misplacements.

payload.snippet: Maya is at a festival when her bag containing her medication, phone, and ID is stolen. She is there alone.
options: She goes to the festival's medical and security team, explains her situation including the medication need, and asks them to contact police and help her reach her emergency contact.
She tries to retrace her route and find the bag herself.
She borrows a stranger's phone to call home before reporting to security.
She waits near the main stage hoping her friends will find her.
payload.explanation: Festival security and medical teams are equipped for this situation — they can handle the medication emergency, police contact, and emergency communication simultaneously.

payload.snippet: Tom loses an expensive item that belongs to his employer. He is worried about the professional consequences.
options: He tells his employer honestly and immediately, provides a full account of what happened, and discusses next steps including any potential liability.
He looks for the item for several days before disclosing to give himself time to find it.
He claims the item was stolen to reduce his liability.
He replaces the item from his own money before telling his employer.
payload.explanation: Immediate honest disclosure — rather than delayed admission, false theft claims, or silent replacement — is the professional and ethical response.

payload.snippet: Clara is on a hiking trail when she realises she has lost the map and her phone has no signal.
options: She stays on the marked trail, uses the sun or landscape to maintain directional awareness, and waits at a waypoint if she becomes genuinely unsure of direction.
She leaves the trail to look for a higher point with phone signal.
She backtracks entirely to the starting point.
She continues walking at pace hoping to reach the end before dark.
payload.explanation: Staying on the marked trail is the cardinal rule when navigation fails on a hike — leaving the trail or rushing in uncertain conditions both increase risk.

payload.snippet: Oliver finds a signed cheque for a large amount inside a library book he has borrowed.
options: He returns the cheque and book to the library desk and reports where he found it.
He attempts to identify the payee and return it directly.
He destroys the cheque to prevent fraud.
He keeps it since it is uncrossed and bears no instructions.
payload.explanation: A found cheque must be handed to the library — attempting personal return, destruction, or keeping it are all incorrect.

payload.snippet: Anna loses her driving licence while moving house and cannot find it in the chaos of boxes.
options: She applies for an official replacement through the DVLA and does not drive until the licence is replaced or she has confirmed her provisional or entitlement through the DVLA system.
She drives without the licence since she has been driving for years and knows she is licensed.
She uses a photocopy of the old licence as a substitute.
She waits for the boxes to be fully unpacked before applying for a replacement.
payload.explanation: Driving without a valid licence in hand is a legal offence — an official replacement must be applied for immediately.

payload.snippet: Jake's company laptop goes missing after a work trip. He is not sure if it was lost or stolen.
options: He reports it to his company's IT security team immediately so the device can be remotely wiped, and to the police in case it was stolen.
He waits twenty-four hours in case it turns up before reporting it.
He reports it only to his line manager and lets them decide what to do.
He reports the theft to police but waits to tell IT until he has the police crime number.
payload.explanation: A missing company laptop is a data security incident — IT security must be notified immediately for remote wipe, regardless of whether it was lost or stolen.

payload.snippet: Maya finds an injured guide dog in the street without its owner. The dog has an identification tag.
options: She calls the number on the tag, keeps the dog calm and contained, and contacts a vet or RSPCA if the owner cannot be reached.
She takes the dog home until the owner is found.
She leaves the dog where she found it since it may find its own way home.
She takes the dog to the nearest police station.
payload.explanation: Calling the number on the tag is the correct first step — a vet or RSPCA should be contacted if the owner is unreachable, not police.

payload.snippet: Theo left his retainer on a cafeteria tray by accident and it has gone through the dishwasher cycle. His orthodontist appointment is in two days and a replacement costs hundreds of pounds.
options: Theo tells the school office immediately so staff can check the kitchen waste before disposal
Theo tells his parents the retainer broke on its own
Theo goes without telling anyone and hopes the gap is not visible at the appointment
Theo searches the bins alone at lunchtime
payload.explanation: Acting immediately and honestly gives the best chance of recovery and avoids compounding the problem.

payload.snippet: Clara finds a purse on the pavement containing cash, bank cards, and an ID. She is running late for school and does not have time to take it to a police station.
options: Clara takes the purse into the nearest open shop and asks staff to hand it in
Clara keeps the cash and leaves the rest on the ground
Clara puts the purse back so someone else deals with it
Clara texts her mum and waits on the pavement
payload.explanation: Handing found property to a responsible person ensures the owner has the best chance of recovery.

payload.snippet: Will borrows his dad's expensive drill for a school project and accidentally leaves it at his friend's house on Friday evening; his dad will need it Saturday morning.
options: Will texts his friend immediately asking if he can collect the drill that evening
Will tells his dad the drill was at school and collects it Monday
Will replaces it with a cheaper drill from a discount store
Will waits to see if his dad notices before saying anything
payload.explanation: Addressing a borrowed-item mistake the same day avoids the problem compounding.

payload.snippet: During a school trip, Ava's backpack containing her camera, phone, and passport is left on the coach while she explores a museum. A coach inspector locks the vehicle and takes it to a depot.
options: Ava tells a teacher immediately; the teacher contacts the coach company to retrieve the bag from the depot
Ava waits until the return journey to mention it hoping the coach returns
Ava borrows a classmate's phone to search for the depot on her own
Ava assumes everything will be fine and finishes the museum visit
payload.explanation: Immediate escalation to a responsible adult is essential for lost items containing travel documents.

payload.snippet: Noah's grandfather's pocket watch, kept safely on his bedside table, is missing after a family gathering. Noah suspects a young cousin may have picked it up while playing.
options: Noah quietly asks his cousin if they picked up something shiny, framing it as curiosity not accusation
Noah tells his parents his cousin stole it without speaking to the cousin first
